## TO THE MEDICAL COLLEGE OF BASEL.
### TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED LEADER, <note>original: "Decurioni"; a title derived from Roman administration, used here to denote a high-ranking member or administrator of the medical faculty.</note>
### TO THE MOST REFINED DISCIPLE OF ASCLEPIUS, <note>original: "Asclepiadae"; a term for physicians, referring to the followers or descendants of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing.</note>
### TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS HERBALIST AND ANATOMIST,

# CASPAR BAUHIN OF BASEL. <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624) was one of the most important botanists and anatomists of the Renaissance, famous for his "Pinax Theatri Botanici" which classified thousands of plants.</note>
# CASPAR SCHVENCKFELT,

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE.
## <note>original: "Epistola Dedicatoria"</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut headpiece featuring elaborate scrolling foliage and floral motifs symmetrically arranged from a central point.</image-desc>

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' contained within a square frame, decorated with intricate botanical scrollwork.</image-desc>

As I was considering, most distinguished Doctor and most worthy Dean, what I might offer to Your Excellence at this time in return for the countless favors you have bestowed upon me, this little work <note>original: "opella"; a humble diminutive often used by authors to describe their own books</note> occurred to me as most fitting. I have labored upon it over the past years in the sacred study of Medicine <note>original: "Medicinae"</note>, with the help of God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deo Opt. Max."; an abbreviation for *Deo Optimo Maximo*, a traditional invocation used since Roman times to acknowledge divine favor.</note>.

For when I decided—guided by a natural inclination as well as the advice and authority of my teachers—to devote myself to the sacred art of Medicine, I determined that I required a precise knowledge of pharmaceutical matters <note>original: "Rei pharmaceuticae"; referring to the study and preparation of medicines</note>. This is a field neglected by many physicians of our own age, resulting not only in a loss of their own reputation but, more importantly, in great harm to those who are sick.

Therefore, having thoroughly read the principal and most outstanding writers <note>original: "Scriptores"</note> in this field—including the Greeks and Arabs as well as the modern authors <note>original: "Neotericis"; referring to the Renaissance-era medical writers who were then updating and challenging classical knowledge</note>—I have...

<summary>In this opening of his dedicatory letter, Schvenckfelt expresses his gratitude to Caspar Bauhin and explains that he wrote this book to address a dangerous lack of pharmaceutical knowledge among contemporary doctors.</summary>
<keywords>medical education, pharmacy, 16th-century physicians, gratitude, classical authorities, Arabic medicine, Renaissance science</keywords>

-># THE DEDICATORY<-

(thinking that no small part) of their reputation would be diminished if they spent any care or labor in learning about simple and composite medicines <note>Simples are single medicinal ingredients (usually herbs), while composites are mixtures of multiple ingredients.</note> ) they leave this most beautiful and useful part of Medicine—indeed, the highly necessary part called **Pharmacy** <note>original: "Φαρμακευτικὴν" (Pharmakeutikēn)</note>—to be learned and handled by superstitious old wives and certain unskillful pharmacists. Let these men, I pray, listen to Galen <term>Galen of Pergamon: An influential Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose works formed the basis of Western medical science for over a millennium.</term>, the leader of Physicians; let them hear, I say, what he himself left written in the first book of *On Antidotes*, saying:

> In general, a Physician must be skilled in all plants, or at least most of them; since the power of composite medicines follows the powers of the simple ones, with only a small difference in ratio arising within the composition itself.

The great Fernel <term>Jean Fernel (1497–1558): A French physician who was among the first to describe the spinal canal and who coined the terms "physiology" and "pathology."</term> of our own time confirms the same thing, who says in his *Method of Healing*:

> The knowledge, collection, selection, cleansing, preservation, correction, and the diligence of mixing simple medicines are separately referred and belong to the Pharmacists; yet, it is necessary above all for the Physician also to be knowledgeable and skilled in these things: since...

among the ministers of the Art <note>Referring to the "Art of Medicine."</note> he might wish to retain and protect his own authority and dignity. For that reason, if in times past it did not shame or grieve the princes of Physicians, the most invincible Emperors, the most powerful Kings, and the most illustrious Dukes—namely **Galen** <term>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD): The most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</term>, **Hermes Trismegistus** <term>Hermes Trismegistus: A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical, alchemical, and medical texts were attributed.</term>, **Mithridates** <term>Mithridates VI: A King of Pontus famous for his obsession with poisons and his namesake "universal" antidote.</term>, **Gentius** <term>Gentius: An Illyrian king credited by early botanists with discovering the medicinal properties of the gentian root.</term>, **Lysimachus** <term>Lysimachus: A general of Alexander the Great and King of Thrace, often associated in early modern texts with the plant Lysimachia (loosestrife).</term>, and many other most excellent and highly skilled men in the art, whose names I now willingly and knowingly pass over—if, I say, it did not shame these men to collect *simples* <note>Individual medicinal ingredients, usually botanical, used to make more complex remedies.</note>, to examine their properties, and to construct medicines: Why then should we cast off this study from Medicine as if it were something foreign, without the knowledge of which a Physician can hardly be called such, let alone be or become perfect? 

But, to set these things aside and return to where I digressed: this *Treasury* <note>original: "Thesaurus." This likely refers to the title of the book itself, implying a collection of valuable medical secrets.</note>, most worthy Lord Dean, my patron always to be honored, although it is a small work and least worthy of Your Excellency; nevertheless, just as the great Divinities are sometimes content with an offering of grain and salt <note>A reference to the "mola salsa," a humble sacrificial offering used in ancient Roman religion when a worshipper could not afford a more expensive sacrifice.</note> if a greater means is not available to the worshipper, so also I do not doubt that Your Excellency [will accept] this very slightness of mine as a *sign and a token* <note>original: "σημείον, καὶ τεκμήριον" (sēmeion kai tekmērion)</note>...

## THE DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

*...and promoted me by his grace. I declare and profess this remarkable benevolence of Your Excellence* <note>original: "T.E." (Tua Excellentia)</note> *before God and men: that whatever progress I have made in this most celebrated **Academy of Basel** in the study of **Botany** <term>Botany: Historically referred to as "Res herbaria," the study of medicinal plants and their uses.</term> and **Anatomy**, I justly attribute all of it to Your Excellence as if to a nurturer. At the same time, I offer myself in the gratitude I owe and for any services that I can honorably perform; and I promise that as long as I live, I will direct all my efforts and plans toward this single goal: that, as far as I am able, things pleasing and acceptable first to God my Creator and to my parents, and then to Your Excellence, may always be done and said by me. Farewell in **CHRIST JESUS**, who may lead Your Excellence, along with all your household, safe and sound even unto the **years of Nestor**.* <note>A classical reference to Nestor, the legendary King of Pylos from Homer's Iliad, who was famous for his extreme longevity and wisdom.</note>

*Written from the renowned **Basel of the Rauraci**.* <note>original: "Rauracorum Basilea." The Rauraci were the ancient Celtic tribe of the region; Renaissance scholars often used these classical tribal names to refer to their cities.</note> *In the year of the last age 1587, on the very **Kalends of January**.* <note>January 1st, 1587.</note>

<summary>The author concludes his dedication by crediting the patron for his education in botany and anatomy at the University of Basel and offering his lifelong service in return. He closes with a traditional blessing for the patron’s long life and dates the letter January 1st, 1587.</summary>

<keywords>University of Basel, botany, anatomy, medical education, patronage, 16th-century medicine, Rauraci</keywords>

<meta>This page follows the conclusion of Caspar Schuenckfelt's dedication to his patron. It contains a laudatory poem (epigram) by his colleague or friend, Paul Cherler, which praises the author for summarizing the vast wisdom of medical history into a single, accessible volume.</meta>

# AN EPIGRAM OF MASTER PAUL CHERLER TO
## CASPAR SCHUENCKFELT,
### The Author.

> *Physicians—that renowned race of the gods—are to be greatly praised,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Who have composed various learned books:*
> *In which they diligently ward off every kind of disease,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And preserve healthy bodies in diverse ways.*
> *Nor meanwhile (since Virtue must be carried with praise)*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Do we exalt other men with any less praise,*
> *Who are accustomed to collect the divine inventions of wholesome medicine*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Into a systematic method <term>method: Refers to a "Methodus," a common Renaissance genre of textbook that organized complex subjects into logical, easy-to-learn structures.</term> with equal diligence.*
> *Since you are among their number, most learned **Schuenckfelt**,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*O young man, the rich hope of the medical company <note>original: "Medici chori" (the medical choir). In Latin poetry, a "choir" refers to a distinguished group or guild of experts.</note>:*
> *It is fitting for us to pay you the pleasing heraldry of well-deserved praise,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*On account of this work of beautiful diligence.*
> *In which you now reveal many mysteries of medical matters,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which Father **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC).</note> and **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire (129 – c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years.</note> possess.*
> *And those held by the Arabs: such as **Avicenna** and **Machaon** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a central figure of the Islamic Golden Age. Machaon was a legendary healer from the Trojan War; here, the poet groups him with historical medical authorities.</note>,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian or Assyrian physician; his works were essential to European pharmacy.</note>, the shining gem of the medical company:*
> *And what others hand down who flourish in our own time,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And who create learned books through recent art.*
> *So that you present, as it were, a thousand good doctors in one small volume:*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*A noble gift, a sweet benefit.*
> *Since you provide such things as a young man in your blossoming years,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*What will you bring forth when you are an old man, grayed in the art?*
> *Therefore, remember to remain steadfast in that study hereafter,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*So that you may be of benefit by producing various books.*
> *To weave the end beautifully with the beginning is a beautiful praise;*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*But to fall away from one's study is a shame.*
> *I ask you, friend **Caspar**, with my humble prayer through our friendship,*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*That you do not do so. Farewell.*

<summary>A commendatory poem by Paul Cherler praising Caspar Schuenckfelt for his diligence in synthesizing the medical knowledge of ancient Greeks, medieval Arabs, and modern scholars into a single useful volume.</summary>
<keywords>Paul Cherler, Caspar Schuenckfelt, medical history, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, Mesue, medical textbook, humanist poetry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sequence of commendatory poems (laudatory epigrams) written by the author's colleagues to celebrate the publication of his "Pharmaceutical Treasury." The catchword "Nomi" on the previous page refers to the start of the second poem's discussion of the "Nomine" (name/title) of the book.</meta>

# EPIGRAM
## On the Pharmaceutical Treasury of Caspar
## Schuenckfelt of Greiffenberg, Silesia. <note>original: "Gryphim. Sil." refers to Gryphibergum (Greiffenberg), the author's birthplace in the region of Silesia.</note>

*Just as Crete saw the wandering ways opened up*
*When Theseus was drawn into the palace halls,*
*And though he could not reach the inner recesses by his own skill,*
*He was helped, Ariadne, by your threads:*
*So may they receive a great reward for their labor, who follow*
*The threads drawn through the arts by the help of heavenly Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and handicrafts.</note>.*
*Especially in the fields of Medicine, where the paths*
*Have been made nearly impassable through grave errors.*
*Concerning which, this little book prepares to correct several,*
*And to mark the signs again upon the obscured paths.*
*Whoever you may be that reads this, with a harvest of the spirit,*
*Pray for the health of your author with a grateful mind:*
*But if you will not, at least deem him worthy of pardon, because*
*He succors those who have less skill than you do.*

->Caspar Firling of Glogau.<-

---

## THEOPHILUS GAUTERIUS <note>Likely Theophilus Ganter, a contemporary scholar or physician.</note>
### To Caspar Schuenckfelt, the Author.

*You rightfully bestow this little book, Schuenckfelt,*
*Certainly with a fitting name: yet perhaps*
*A more appropriate title could have been attached,*
*(If I may say so with your permission). Why so? You should have*
*Inscribed nothing but the naked name of "Treasury,"*
*And removed those words you added after it: not indeed so that*
*It would be judged worthy of that honor above all others—*
*Just as once the single city of Rome was called "The City"—*
*Not for that reason: but because this one book encompasses*
*What the word **TREASURY** signifies when standing alone.*
*For here truly, here, I say—even with Momus <note>The Greek god of satire and mockery, famous for finding fault in even the most perfect works.</note> as judge—*
*You have provided a life-giving breath <note>original: "$\alpha\upsilon\rho\alpha\nu$ $\epsilon\theta\eta\varsigma$". This is a clever bilingual pun. The poet is breaking the word "Thesaurus" into Greek components: "Thes" (from *tithemi*, meaning "you have placed or provided") and "Aura" (meaning "breath" or "breeze"). He suggests the book's title literally means "You have provided a breath of life."</note> to the dying patient.*

# EPIGRAM

## On the Pharmaceutical Treasury of Caspar Schwenkfeld of Greiffenberg, Silesia <note>Caspar Schwenkfeld (1563–1609) was a renowned Silesian physician and naturalist. "Gryphim. Sil." is an abbreviation for Greiffenberg, Silesia, his birthplace.</note>

> *As much as Crete once saw revealed for wandering ways,*
> *When Theseus was drawn into the palace halls,*
> *And could not reach the inner recesses by his own skill,*
> *Until he was aided, Ariadne, by your threads:*
> *So much reward for their labor do they seek, who follow*
> *The threads drawn through the arts by the help of heavenly Pallas.* <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and handicrafts.</note>
> *Especially in the fields of Medicine, where the tracks*
> *Have been made almost impassable by grave errors.*
> *Out of these, this little book prepares to correct some,*
> *And to mark the signs again upon the covered paths.*
> *Whoever you may be who reads this, with a fruitful mind,*
> *Pray for the health of your author with a grateful heart;*
> *If not that, at least deem it worthy of pardon, because*
> *It may help those who have less skill than you.*

->Caspar Firling of Glogau.<- <note>Glogau (Głogów) is a town in Lower Silesia.</note>

## THE. GAUTERIUS G. A.

### To Caspar Schwenkfeld, the Author.

> *You grant this little book, Schwenkfeld, by right indeed,*
> *With a most fitting name: yet perhaps,*
> *A more suitable title could have been attached,*
> *(By your leave I say it)—why so? You ought to have*
> *Inscribed nothing except the bare name of "Treasury,"*
> *And removed those words you added after: not indeed so that*
> *It would be judged by all as worthy of that honor*
> *Just as Rome was once called simply "The City,"*
> *Not so: but because this one book embraces*
> *What the word TREASURY denotes when it stands alone.*
> *For here truly—here, I say—even with Momus as judge,* <note>Momus was the Greek god of satire and mockery, known for finding fault with everything.</note>
> *You <unclear>give</unclear> <note>original: "δίδως"</note> a life-giving <term>breeze</term> <note>original: "αὔραν" (auran)</note> to a dying patient.*

## To the Reader.

*In the Catalog, kind Reader, which I have placed before*
*this work, I have added certain synonyms for medicinal herbs*
*<term>simples</term> <note>Plants or herbs used on their own for medical purposes, before being compounded into drugs</note>, in which, however, I was not overly meticulous,*
*since I know that Master Caspar Bauhin <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624) was a preeminent Swiss botanist who began the transition toward modern plant classification</note>, most skilled*
*in botany <note>original: "Rei herbariæ"</note>, is preparing an Epitome of Synonyms*
*from those authors who are commonly used by students,*
*which would have already been finished, had not a new*
*Anatomical Method, in which he is now entirely occupied,*
*caused a delay: just as also his brother, the most*
*distinguished Master Johannes Bauhin <note>Johannes Bauhin (1541–1613) was a physician and botanist, brother to Caspar; his major botanical work was published posthumously</note>, Chief Physician*
*<term>Archiater</term> <note>A Greek-derived title for a head physician, often to a royal or princely court</note> to the most illustrious Prince, Lord Frederick,*
*Count of Württemberg and Montbéliard, has a massive*
*work in hand, namely concerning the agreement and*
*disagreement of authors regarding the names of plants:*
*both of which works I hope will be published shortly,*
*and will be of the greatest benefit to students of*
*botany. Farewell.*

<summary>In this preface, the author explains that they have omitted an exhaustive list of plant synonyms because two definitive botanical works by the Bauhin brothers were expected to be published soon.</summary>

# ON THE PROPERTIES
# OF MEDICINES
## Derived from Simples,
### BOOK ONE.
#### CONCERNING SIMPLES IN GENERAL.
##### SECTION I.
##### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring ornate foliate scrolls and floral designs within a square border.</image-desc>

A medicine <note>original Latin: *medicamentum*; Greek: *pharmakon*</note>, according to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose systems dominated Western medical science for over a millennium</note> in Book 1 of *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, is defined as anything that is able to alter and change our nature.

Nourishment <note>original Latin: *nutrimentum*; Greek: *trophē*</note>, however, is that which increases, feeds, and preserves our physical substance. For whatever things, once taken into the body and concocted <note>original: *concocta*; the process of "cooking" or digesting food in the stomach to turn it into useable material</note> and converted into humors <note>The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine held must be balanced for health</note> that are compatible with our nature and suitable for nutrition, they adhere to the members <note>The parts or organs of the body</note> and are shaped to, or assimilated into, their substance; these [provide] <note>The text continues on the next page with the word "provide" (original Latin: *praebent*)</note> nourishment.

<summary>This opening page defines the fundamental distinction between a medicine, which changes the body's nature, and nourishment, which sustains and assimilates into the body's own substance.</summary>
<keywords>Galen, medicine, nourishment, humors, simples, pharmacology, digestion, assimilation</keywords>

# ON THE PROPERTIES OF SIMPLE MEDICINES

...provide: All other things have the power of a medicine <note>original Latin: *medicamentum*</note>. Since, however, it is not our purpose in this place to discuss nourishment <note>original Latin: *nutrimentum*</note>, we shall leave those aside and proceed to the classification of medicines.

Medicines are distinguished into Simples and Compounds.

*Simples* <note>original Greek: *hapla*</note> are, by their nature, sincere, pure, and not mixed with the properties of any other medicine. *Compounds* <note>original Greek: *syntheta*</note> are prepared from simples joined, mixed, and balanced together in a proper and fitting proportion. We shall deal with Simples in this first book, and with Compounds in Book 2.

Before we embark upon the specific properties of simple medicines, it seemed right to provide first a Catalog (serving as a precursor <note>original Greek: *prodromou*</note> to what follows) of those simples:

->whose use in our time<-
->is common in the apothecary shops.<- <note>original Latin: *officinis*; the "officina" was the storeroom or workshop of an apothecary where medicinal ingredients were kept and prepared</note>

<meta>catchword: Chapter</meta>

<summary>This page distinguishes between simple and compound medicines, defining simples as pure substances and compounds as balanced mixtures. It concludes by introducing a catalog of medicinal ingredients commonly used in contemporary pharmacies.</summary>
<keywords>pharmacology, simple medicines, compound medicines, apothecary, pharmaceutical catalog, Galenic medicine</keywords>

BOOK ONE. CHAPTER II.

# Catalog of those Simples which are in greatest use in Medicine in these times.

## General Table of the Catalog.

Medicines are derived from:

*   **Plants**
    *   From the **Whole**
    *   From **their parts**: and either from
        *   **Dissimilar parts** <note>original Latin: *dissimilaribus*; in Galenic medicine, these are complex parts made of different tissues, such as a whole leaf or branch</note> such as
            *   Leaves
            *   Stalks
            *   Branches
            *   Twigs } Chapter 2
            *   Flowers — Chapter 3
            *   Fruits — Chapter 4
            *   Roots — Chapter 5
            *   Seeds — Chapter 6
            *   Barks — Chapter 7
            *   Woods — Chapter 9
            *   Juices — Chapter 11
            *   Liquids — Chapter 12
            *   Resins — Chapter 13
            *   Gums — Chapter 14
        *   **Similar parts** <note>original Latin: *similaribus*; uniform substances that are the same throughout, like sap or pulp</note>
*   **Animals** either
    *   From the **Whole** such as the
        *   Leech <note>original Latin: *hirudine*</note>
        *   Wagtail <note>original Latin: *motacilla*; a small bird used in various folk and historical remedies</note>
        *   Fox <note>original Latin: *vulpe*; fox lungs were often prepared as a treatment for asthma and breathing difficulties</note> } Chapter 15
    *   From **their parts**
        *   **Organic parts** <note>original Latin: *organicis*; functional organs</note>
            *   Head
            *   Liver
            *   Testicles
            *   Kidneys
            *   Whole body } Chapter 16
        *   **Similar parts** <note>homogeneous tissues or fluids</note>
            *   Brain
            *   Bones
            *   Rennet <note>original Latin: *coagulo*</note>
            *   Inner lining of the stomach
            *   Hooves or nails
            *   Glue <note>original Latin: *glutino*; likely gelatin or isinglass</note>
            *   Shells <note>original Latin: *testibus*; likely referring to eggshells or sea shells, which were treated as uniform medicinal substances</note>
            *   Fat
            *   Marrow } Chapter 17
            *   Blood, etc.

### CHAPTER III.

## FLOWERS <note>Greek: *Anthoi*</note>

**Flowers are:**
*   **identified by** their **smell**, **taste**, and **natural color**.
*   **selected** when they are **fresh**, **mature**, and **not spoiled**.
    *   <margin>they should be gathered between flowering and seeding</margin>
*   **dried in the shade**.
*   **stored in linden-wood boxes** <note>original: *arculis tiliaceis*; linden wood was used because it is odorless and would not affect the scent of the flowers</note>.
*   **preserved for up to a year**.

<insert>
**Note Well:** **Red Roses** <note>original: *Rosae rubrae*</note> are dried with a **more intense heat**, because if they are dried with a slow heat, their color and their medicinal powers perish. Therefore, they are dried either in an **oven** or near a **furnace** in a warm **heated room** <note>original: *hypocaustum*; a room heated from below, common in early modern pharmacies for drying botanical samples</note>.
</insert>

**Fruits**, a term used chiefly for the products of larger plants, such as trees and shrubs:

            * Eastern
    * an oven <note>original: *clybano*; a drying kiln or portable oven</note>.

    * cabinets
    * boxes <note>original: *pixidibus*; typically small apothecary jars or turned wood boxes</note>
    * baskets.
* They are to be replaced every single year.

## C H A P T E R V.
### ROOTS, *RHIZAI* <note>original Greek: 'Ρ 'Ι 'Σ Α Ι (*rhizai*)</note>.

<image-desc>A hierarchical diagram categorizing the handling of "Radices" (roots). The word "Roots" is the primary subject, branching into four main actions: selection, gathering, storage, and preservation. Each action branches further into specific criteria and conditions, such as the state of the plant, the weather, and the orientation of the storage room.</image-desc>

**Roots**
* **are selected**
    * the most perfect of their kind.
    * well-conditioned <note>meaning healthy or in good state</note>.
    * not decayed.
    * not withered.
    * not wrinkled.
* **are gathered**
    * once the fruit has already been lost <note>after the fruiting season</note>.
    * when the leaves begin to fall.
    * in clear weather.
    * <gloss>gathered in Spring, according to Dr. Bohn <note>Johannes Bohn (1640–1718), a noted German physician and professor at Leipzig.</note>.</gloss>
* **are stored**
    * sliced }
    * whole } in a place that is:
        * elevated
        * clean
        * dry
        * facing
            * the South
            * or
            * the North.
* **are preserved**
    * smaller ones for a year.
    * larger ones for
        * two years.
        * three years.

<insert>
<gloss>(with the leaves removed)</gloss>
Certain roots are peeled so that they may dry more easily, such as **chicory**; some are even split, and the inner woody core is removed, as in **parsley**, **chicory**, etc.
</insert>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>ON THE FACULTIES OF SIMPLE MEDICINES</header>
<meta>catchword: Grapes</meta>

## CHAPTER VI.

### SEEDS <note>original: *Semina*, *Σπέρματα* (*spermata*)</note>,

**Selection, Gathering, and Preservation of Seeds**
*   **Seeds are selected** <note>original: *Semina eliguntur*</note> that are:
    *   mature
    *   well-conditioned
    *   sturdy <note>original: *corpulenta*</note>
    *   full
    *   not decayed.
*   **They are gathered from** <note>original: *leguntur ex*</note>:
    *   **fruits** which are:
        *   at peak ripeness
        *   gathered before they fall.
    *   **stalks** which are:
        *   already dry
        *   no longer green.
*   **Once dried, they are preserved** (for longer than leaves) <note>original: *siccata asservantur*</note>:
    *   in **glass vessels** and **small bags**: kept in a drier place.
    *   in **paper** and **parchment**: wrapped up.

*All seeds are composed of an oily substance, and for this reason, they can also be preserved for a longer time.*

**Sorrel**, that is, **Wood-sorrel** <note>original: *Acetosæ*, *Oxalydis*; *Oxalis* refers to the acidity of the plant, often used in cooling medicines</note>.

# BOOK ONE.

## CHAPTER VII.

### BARKS <note>Greek: $\phi\lambda\omicron\iota\acute{\alpha}$ (*phloia*)</note>.

<margin>In Spring, according to Dr. Broen <note>likely Johannes de Bruine (1630–1703), a Dutch physician and professor known for his works on pharmacy</note>.</margin>

**BARKS**
- **Are obtained, partly from:**
    - Trees
    - Fruits
    - Roots
    - Branches
- **Are gathered:**
    - When the fruits are most ripe.
    - When the herbs are stripped of their leaves.
    - When they are flourishing <note>in their period of most active growth</note>.
- **Are kept for a year.**

Of Celery <note>original: *Apii*; in this context, usually referring to Smallage or Wild Celery</note>.
Of Hazelnuts.

# CHAPTER XI.

## JUICES, <term>extracted plant fluids</term> <note>original: χυλοὶ (*chyloi*). This term refers to the vital juices or "humors" expressed from botanical matter for medicinal use.</note>

<image-desc>A taxonomic tree diagram using large curly brackets to classify "Succi" (juices) based on their consistency and preservation methods. The text branches from left to right, starting with a general definition and splitting into "Liqvidi" (Liquid) and "Sicci" (Dry) categories, which then further subdivide into specific examples and processes.</image-desc>

Juices, which are expressed from plants or parts of plants by crushing or pounding, are either:

*   **Liquid.** Those which are preserved either:
    *   by themselves, such as—
        *   Wine <note>original: *Vinum*</note>
        *   Vinegar <note>original: *Acetum*</note>
    *   mixed with salt, such as—
        *   Unripe grape juice <note>original: *Omphacium*. Used for its acidity and cooling properties.</note>
        *   Oil <note>original: *Oleum*</note>
    *   covered with a layer of oil <note>A common historical preservation method where a layer of oil on top of a liquid prevents air from reaching it, stopping spoilage.</note>, such as the juice of—
        *   Pomegranates <note>original: *Granatorum*</note>
        *   Lemons <note>original: *Limonum*</note>
        *   Roses <note>original: *Rosarum*</note>, etc.

*   **Dry.** Those which:
    *   are dried by—
        *   The Sun
        *   Age
        *   Fire.
    *   or <gloss>are thickened for the sake of preservation</gloss> by being cooked—
        *   with honey
        *   or with sugar
        *   } into a thick consistency.

# LIQUIDS (SAPS), <note>original Greek: ὀποί (*opoi*)</note>.

Liquids that flow out when a part of a plant is cut or bored into:
- **are selected:** when they are not old, and not weak or faded.
- **are collected:** by cutting the stem during its peak period of youthful vigor.
- **are stored:** in a dry place.
- **remain potent:** for three years at most.

---

**Vinegar**, <note>original Greek: ὄξος (*oxos*)</note>.
**Vinegar of Roses.**
**Vinegar of Elderberry.**
**Vinegar of Squill** <note>original: *Acetum Scillinum*. Made by macerating squill (sea onion) in vinegar; used for coughs and as a diuretic.</note>.
**Balsam**, the liquid of a certain shrub growing in Judea, Opobalsamum, Judean Balsam.
**Cedar liquid** <note>original: *Cedrinus liquor*. Often refers to the resinous oil of the cedar tree used for preservation.</note>.
**Elaterium**, see under **Juices** <note>A powerful purgative derived from the juice of the squirting cucumber.</note>.
**Euphorbium**, see under **Gums** <note>A caustic resin from the *Euphorbia* plant.</note>.
**Opium**, the Liquid or "Tear" flowing from the wounded heads of the black Poppy, also called Meconium <note>original: *Meconium*. Historically, this term referred specifically to the juice extracted from the whole poppy plant, which was considered less potent than the pure latex (opium).</note>.
**Opopanax**, called by the Latins the liquid of the Hercules-all-heal plant <note>original: *Panacis Heraclei*. A medicinal gum-resin used as an antispasmodic.</note>, Opopanacum of the Apothecaries.
**Wine.**

## CHAPTER XIII.
### R E S I N S, <note>original Greek: Ῥητίναι (*Rhētinae*)</note>.

<margin>Resins are either thickened [artificially] or naturally coagulated. According to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of the foundational pharmacopeia *De Materia Medica*.</note>.</margin>
**Fir resin**, an oily resin, <note>original Greek: *dakryon elatēs*—literally "tears of the fir tree"</note> according to Dioscorides.
**Colophony**, as named in the *Apothecary shops*. Dry or Greek pitch, <note>original Greek: *pissē kolophonikē*</note>. It is now nothing other than the dregs remaining from distilled turpentine or fir resin <note>A translucent, brittle resin (rosin) left after the volatile oils are distilled away.</note>.
**Larch resin**, or resin of the Larch tree, <note>original Greek: *pitynē larikinē*</note>.
**Mastic**, derived from the Lentisk tree, <note>original Greek: *mastichē*</note>.
**Pitch-flower**, the volatile "flower" or surface-skimming of liquid pitch <note>original: *Pissanthum*</note>.
**Pitch-oil**, liquid pitch mixed with oil, <note>original Greek: *pissa hygra*</note>.
**Dry Pitch**, called Naval Pitch in the *Apothecary shops*, <note>original Greek: *palimpissa* (re-boiled pitch), *pissa xēra* (dry pitch)</note>.
**Pine-cone resin**.
**Turpentine**, <note>original Greek: *terminthinē*</note>, which is also referred to simply and absolutely as "resin."

**Ammoniacum**, <note>original: *Ammoniacū*</note> called *Traston* and *Transma* by **Pliny** <note>A Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*. This resin comes from a plant related to fennel.</note>.

**Camphor**, <note>original: *Caphura* or *Cāphora*</note> which among the ancients was the "tear" of an **Indian tree**; our version is **man-made** <note>original: *factitia*. In this period, this often meant refined or processed by hand rather than occurring naturally in that form.</note>.

**Of ivy**.
**Myrrh**, <note>original Greek: μύῤῥα (*myrrha*), σμύρνα (*smyrna*)</note> the "tear" of the **Arabian tree**.
**Of the plum tree**.
**Sandarac** <note>original: *Sandaracha*</note> of the **Arabs**, called *Vernigo* by **Hermolaus** <note>Hermolaus Barbarus, a 15th-century scholar who updated botanical texts.</note>, and commonly called *Vernix* <note>Varnish</note> by **Dioscorides**. It is the dried gum of the **juniper**.
**Sagapenum**, also called **Serapinum** <note>A yellow-brown resin from an Umbelliferous plant</note>.

**Jaw of a Pike fish** <note>original: *Mandibula Lucii piscis*. The pike was often called the "water wolf" and its jaw was used in powdered form.</note>.
**Arabian Mummy**, from tombs, or **artificial Bitumen** <note>original: *Mumia Arabum, sepulcrorum, Pissaphaltum factitium*. In this period, "Mummy" referred to both the preserved flesh of the ancients and the asphalt-like resins used in embalming, both of which were prized as topical and internal medicines.</note>.
**Crab’s eyes** *in the apothecary shop* or **Crayfish stones** <note>original: *Oculi Cancrorum* or *Lapides Gammarorum*. Not actually eyes, but calcium carbonate stones found in the stomachs of crayfish during their molting cycle.</note>.
**Bone from a Stag’s heart** <note>original: *Os è corde Cervi*. This is actually a piece of cross-shaped cartilage found in the hearts of older deer that has hardened into bone; it was famously used to treat heart palpitations.</note>.
**Cuttlefish bone** <note>original: *Os Sepiæ*. The chalky internal shell of the cuttlefish, used as a dental abrasive or an antacid.</note>.
**Triangular bone of the human skull**. It is a small bone bearing a triangular shape at the back of the head near the **lambdoid suture** <note>original: *suturam lambdoideam*. The joint at the back of the skull. This specific bone is often called a "Wormian bone" or "Inca bone" today.</note>. Some attribute a miraculous power to the shavings of this little bone.
**Inner skins of chicken gizzards** <note>original: *Pelliculæ stomachorum gallinæ*. Used to aid digestion and treat stomach complaints.</note>.
**Perch-stones** <note>original: *Percarum lapilli*. Small calcified stones (otoliths) found in the head of the perch fish.</note>.
**Perna**, by others called <term>perna</term> <note>original: *πέρνα*. A Greek term for a leg or ham.</note>, which is **Pig's thigh**.
**Hare’s hair**.
**Lungs**—
- **of a Lamb**.
- **of a Pig**.
- **of a Bear**.
- **of a Fox** <note>original: *Pulmo vulpinus*. Fox lungs were a staple remedy for respiratory shortness of breath and asthma, following the logic that the long-winded fox would transfer its stamina to the patient.</note>.
**Skink kidneys** <note>original: *Renes Scincorum*. The skink, a desert lizard, was a vital ingredient in complex ancient panaceas like Theriac.</note>.
**Snake slough** <note>original: *Senecta Angvium*. The shed skin of a snake, used to treat skin diseases or to promote the "casting off" of illness.</note>.
**Pig's ankle bone** <note>original: *Talus suillus*.</note>.
**Hoof of an Elk**, and **of a Donkey**.
**Sweet-scented nail** <note>original: *ungvis odoratus*. Usually referring to the *Blatta Byzantia*, the operculum (lid) of a marine snail which, when burned, produces a musky odor used to treat "hysteria."</note>.
**Unicorn horn** <note>original: *unicornu Monocerotis*. This was the most expensive item in the pharmacy; while sold as "unicorn," it was almost always the tusk of a narwhal. It was believed to sweat in the presence of poison.</note>.

## CHAPTER XIX.

->METALLIC SUBSTANCES.<-

<margin>Metallic substances.</margin>

**Metallic substances**
{ **are chosen:**
   - **having the strongest color characteristic of their kind**
   - **endowed with the best quality:**
      - **of taste**
      - **of smell**
{ **are kept safely everywhere, though without dust.**

**Adarce** <note>original: *Adarce*; a salty, porous crust that forms on reeds in salt marshes, used in ancient medicine for skin conditions.</note>
**Copper** <note>original: *Aes*; Greek: <term>chalkos</term></note>.
**Burnt copper** <note>original: *Aes ustum*; copper calcined by heat until it becomes brittle and medicinal.</note>
**Flower of copper** <note>original: *Aeris flos*; Greek: <term>chalkou anthos</term> according to Dioscorides; the fine beads or granules that form on the surface of molten copper.</note>
**Verdigris** <note>original: *Aerugo aeris*; called *Ziniar* by the Arabs; the green corrosion or "rust" of copper.</note>
**Copper scale** <note>original: *Aeris squama*; Greek: <term>chalkou lepis</term>; commonly called copper *batitura*—the flakes that fall off when metal is hammered while hot.</note>
**Scraped verdigris**, or green of copper <note>original: *Aerugo rasilis* or *viride aeris*.</note>
**Alum** <note>original: *Alumen*.</note>
**Potash** <note>original: *Alumen catinae*; literally "alum of the crucible," often referring to potassium carbonate or refined salts used in glassmaking and alchemy.</note>
**Liquid alum**, also called **Rock alum** <note>original: *Alumen liquidum* or *Alumen rupeum*.</note>
**Antimony**, or **Stibium** <note>original: *Antimonium* or *Stibium*; Greek: <term>stimmi</term>, also called <term>gynaikeion</term> ("feminine") by Galen.</note>
**Prepared antimony**, or **Glass of antimony** <note>original: *Antimonii vitrum*; a translucent substance created by roasting antimony ore.</note>
**Anthrax**, or **Vein of red lead** <note>original: *Antrax seu vena Minii*; likely referring to cinnabar or ores containing red lead.</note>
**Silver filings** <note>original: *Argenti scobs*.</note>
**Silver leaf** <note>original: *Argentum foliatum*; thin sheets of silver used in gilding or medicine.</note>
**Native silver** <note>original: *Argentum nativum*; silver found in its pure state in nature.</note>
**Precipitated silver**, known as **Angelic Powder** <note>original: *Argentum præcipitatum* or *Pulvis Angelicus*; a chemical preparation involving the dissolution and precipitation of the metal.</note>

->### BOOK ONE.<-

**Alabaster stone** <note>original: *alabastritis*; a soft, translucent mineral often used for jars to hold precious ointments</note>, or **Alabaster** <note>original: *Lapis Alabastri*; noted as an "officinal" or standard pharmaceutical substance</note>.
**Cocks-stone** <note>original: *Alectorius*; a mythical stone said to be found in the gizzards of old roosters, believed to grant strength and invincibility</note>.
**Amianthus stone**, **Plume alum**, **Live linen**, **Fissile alum**, or **Plume alum** according to **Matthioli** <note>original: *Amianthus lapis, Alumen plumosum, Linum vivum, Alumen scissile, Alumen de pluma Mattio*; these terms refer to fibrous asbestos, which was called "live linen" because it could be woven into cloth that was cleaned by fire rather than water</note>.
**Armenian stone** <note>original: *Armenius lapis*; a blue mineral, often azurite, used both as a pigment and as a purgative to treat melancholia</note>.
**Toadstone** <note>original: *Bufonius*; historically believed to be found in the heads of toads and used to detect or neutralize poison, though usually these were the fossilized teeth of prehistoric fish</note>.
**Whetstones** <note>original: *Cotes*</note>.
**Jet** <note>original: *Gagates*; a type of lignite (fossilized wood) that becomes electrically charged when rubbed</note>.
**Hematite**, **Bloodstone**, or **Sanguine stone** <note>original: *Hæmatites, Lapis sangvinarius & sangvineus*; named for its blood-red color when powdered and used to stop bleeding</note>.
**Jewish stone** <note>original: *judaicus lapis*; a fossilized sea urchin spine found in Judea, traditionally dissolved in liquid to treat kidney stones</note>, also called **Phoenix-stone** by **Pliny** <note>original: *Phœnicites Plinii*</note>.
**Lapis Lazuli** <note>original: *Lapis Lazuli*; the deep-blue stone used for ultramarine pigment</note>, or **Deep-blue stone**, **Sky-blue stone**, or **Star-stone** <note>original: *kyanos (Greek), Lapis cyaneus, cæruleus, stellatus*; often described as "starred" due to its flecks of golden pyrite</note>.
**Magnet**, **Loadstone**, or **Iron-stone** <note>original: *Magnes, magnetis (Greek), herakleia (Greek - "the Herculean stone"), Sideritis*; famous for its natural magnetic properties</note>.

**Marble** <note>original: *Marmor*</note>.
**Honey-stone**, **Milk-stone**, **Galaxy-stone**, or **White-writing stone** <note>original: *Melitites, Morochtus, Galaxia, Leucographis*; a group of white or yellowish minerals described by **Pliny** for their medicinal uses</note>.
**Muscle-stone** <note>original: *Myites*; possibly referring to a stone shaped like a muscle or a mouse</note>.

**Serpentine** or **Snake-marble** <note>original: *Ophites, ophitēs (Greek), Marmor serpentinum*; named for its mottled green appearance resembling the skin of a snake</note>.
**Shell-stone** <note>original: *Ostracites*; a fossilized shell used for its abrasive or drying qualities</note>.
**Phrygian stone** or **False amber** <note>original: *Phrygius, Pseudolyncurius*; the latter is a substance mistaken for "lyncurium," a mythical gemstone said to be formed from lynx urine</note>.
**Pumice** <note>original: *Pumex*; described by **Theophrastus** as **Alkyonion** <note>Greek: *alkyonion*</note>, because it was believed to be formed from the hardened foam of the sea</note>.

**Chalk**, **Silver earth**, or **Silver chalk** <note>original: *Creta, Terra argentaria, Creta argentaria*; a fine white clay used by silversmiths for polishing and in medicine as a drying agent</note>.
**Red chalk** <note>original: *Creta rubra*</note>.
**Green chalk** <note>original: *Creta viridis*</note>.
**Eretrian earth** <note>original: *Erethria*; a medicinal clay from the city of Eretria in Greece, prized by ancient physicians for its cooling and astringent qualities</note>.
**Armenian clod**, **Armenian bole**, or **Oriental bole** <note>original: *Gleba Armenia, Bolus Armenus, Bolus orientalis*; a famous reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent and as a remedy against the plague</note>.
**Melian earth** <note>original: *Melia*; a white earth from the island of Melos</note>.
**Yellow ochre** or **Mountain clay** <note>original: *Ochra lutea, Lutum montanum*</note>.
**Red earth** <note>original: *Rubrica*; a variety of red ochre</note>
**for craftsmen** <note>original: *fabrilis*; used for marking or smithing</note>.
**from Sinope** <note>original: *sinopica*; a high-quality pigment and medicine from the Black Sea region</note>.
**Samian earth** <note>original: *Samia*; from the island of Samos</note>.
**Selinusian earth** <note>original: *Selinusia*; a white clay from Selinus in Sicily</note>.
**Sealed earth** or the **Lemnian seal**, **Sacred earth**, or the **seal of Galen** <note>original: *Sigillata seu Sigillum Lemnium, Terra sacra, sphragis Galeno*; a prestigious clay from Lemnos, traditionally pressed into tablets and stamped with a seal to guarantee its purity</note>.
**Silesian sealed earth** or the **Fat of the Sun of the Paracelsians** <note>original: *Sigillata Silesiaca, Axungia Solis Paracelsistratum*; a local German alternative to Lemnian earth, associated with the alchemical theories of Paracelsus</note>. The best of these, however, is from **Striegau** <note>original: *Strigensis*</note>. Indeed, many varieties are now being dug up in Silesia. For this reason, one must take care not to be deceived by **charlatans** <note>original: *Agyrtis*; wandering peddlers or quacks who sold fraudulent medicines</note>.
**Kiln-fired shards** <note>original: *Testae fornaceae*; ground pottery used for its drying effects</note>.
**Tripoli earth** or **Alana earth** <note>original: *Tripolis, Alana terra*; abrasive earths used for polishing metals</note>.

**Whetstone** <note>original: *Cotes*; used for sharpening tools and sometimes in medicinal preparations</note>.

**Muscle-stone** <note>original: *Myites*; likely a stone or fossil named for its resemblance to a muscle shell</note>.

# ON THE PROPERTIES OF SIMPLE MEDICINES
76

**Pyrite**, commonly called **Marcasite** <note>original: *pyrites*; literally "fire-stone." These are iron disulfide minerals that produce sparks when struck, often used in early medicine for their supposed "heating" qualities</note>.
**Sarcophagus stone**, or **Asian stone** <note>original: *Sarcophagos, Asius lapis*; Greek: *σαρκοφάγος*. A type of limestone from Assos in the Troad, famous in antiquity for its ability to "consume" the flesh of bodies buried within it</note>.
**Schist**, that is, **fissile stone** <note>original: *Schistus*; a stone that naturally splits into thin layers</note>.
**Selenite**, **Looking-glass stone**, or **Saint Mary’s Glass** <note>original: *Selenites, Specularis, Glacies D. Mariae*; Greek: *διαφανὴς* (transparent) per Galen, or *ἀφροσελήνος* (moon-foam). A translucent variety of gypsum that forms clear, leaf-like sheets, often used as windowpanes before glass was widely available</note>.
**Flint** <note>original: *Silex*; Greek: *χάλιξ* (pebble or gravel)</note>.
**Emery**, or **Smerillus** <note>original: *Smyris*; Greek: *σμύρις* per Galen. A very hard mineral used for grinding and polishing other stones</note>.
**Spongite**, or **Sponge-stone** <note>original: *Spongites, Lapis spongie*; small stones or fossilized fragments found inside sea sponges, believed to help break down kidney stones</note>.
**Tartar**, that is, the substance that clings to wine casks <note>original: *Tartarum*; the acidic crust (potassium bitartrate) that crystallizes during wine fermentation. It was a vital ingredient in alchemical and medical preparations</note>.
**Thracian stone**, a species of **Jet**, of a black color <note>original: *Thracius, Gagatidis species*; Greek: *Θρᾶσσα λίθος*. Described by ancient naturalists as a stone that was ignited by water and quenched by oil</note>.

### BOOK ONE 77

**Crystal** <note>original: *Chrystallus*. In this period, rock crystal was often believed to be water or ice so intensely frozen over centuries that it could no longer melt</note>.
**Garnet**, named *from the color of the pomegranate*; otherwise called the **Chalcedonian Carbuncle** <note>original: *Granatus, à pomi punici colore; aliàs Carbunculus Charcedonicus*. The name derives from "granatum" (pomegranate) because the stones resemble the red seeds of the fruit</note>.
**True Hyacinth** <note>original: *Hyacinthus verus*. This term was historically used for various blue or reddish-yellow stones, including sapphire and zircon</note>.
**Sky-colored Jasper**, called *thyites* by Dioscorides and Galen; otherwise called **Turquoise** <note>original: *Iaspis aërizusa*, Greek: *θυίτης*. The "air-colored" jasper was a common identification for turquoise in Renaissance lapidaries</note>.
**Jasper** *is of a green color*, known as *iaspis* <note>original: *Iaspis viridi colore est*, Greek: *ἰάσπις*. While jasper occurs in many colors, the green variety was most prized for its supposed medicinal power to stop bleeding</note>.
**Onyx**, **Onychite**, or **Onyx-stone** <note>original: *Onyx, Onychites, Lapis Onychinus*. The name comes from the Greek word for "fingernail," referring to its pinkish-white translucency</note>.
**Opal**.
**Ruby**, called *pyropos*, or the **Amethyst-colored Carbuncle** <note>original: *Rubinus*, Greek: *πυρωπὸς* (fire-eyed), *Carbunculus amethystizon*. "Carbuncle" was a general category for glowing red stones; those with a violet tint were compared to amethyst</note>.
**Sapphire**, or **Syrtite** <note>original: *Sapphyrus, Syrtites*. Historically, "sapphire" often referred to Lapis Lazuli, but here it likely refers to the blue corundum</note>.
**Sarda**, **Carnelian**, or **Sardine stone** <note>original: *Sarda, Corneolus, Sardinus*. A brownish-red stone often used for seal rings</note>.
**Sardonyx**, which *has a name mixed from Sarda and Onyx*.
**Emerald**, the *most precious of all gems, and nearly the most delicate* <note>original: *Smaragdus, gemmarum omnium pretiosissima, & fermè tenerrima*. Emeralds were highly valued not just for beauty but for their supposed ability to comfort and strengthen the eyesight</note>.
**Terebinth-colored stone** <note>original: Greek *Τερεβινθίζων*. A stone described as having the yellowish-green color of resin from the terebinth tree</note>.
**Topaz**, a *gem of a green color* <note>original: *Topafius, gemma viridis coloris*. In antiquity and the Middle Ages, "topaz" usually referred to what we now call Peridot, which is green, rather than the yellow-gold stone known as topaz today</note>.

-> *Five precious fragments.* <-
-> **Of Sapphires.** <-
-> **Of Garnets.** <-
-> **Of Emeralds.** <-
-> **Of Hyacinths.** <-
-> **Of Sardas.** <-
<note>In early medicine, these five gems—Sapphire, Garnet, Emerald, Hyacinth, and Sarda—were often ground together into a fine powder known as the "Five Precious Fragments." This expensive preparation was used in cordials to strengthen the heart and protect against melancholy and poison</note>.

**Pyrite**, commonly called **Marcasite** <note>original: *πυρίτης, Marchasita vulgò*. Early mineralogists often grouped these sulfide minerals together; pyrite was valued for its ability to strike fire</note>.
**Sarcophagus**, or the **Stone of Assos** <note>original: *Σαρκοφάγος, Assius lapis*. Pliny described this stone from the Troad as having the power to consume the flesh of corpses within forty days</note>.

### BOOK ONE.

**Crystal** <note>original: *Chryſtallus*. Usually referring to rock crystal or clear quartz</note>.
**Garnet** <note>original: *Granatus*</note>, named **from the color of the pomegranate**; otherwise called the **Chalcedonian Carbuncle** <note>original: *à pomi punici colore: aliàs Carbūculus Charcedonicus*. The name "garnet" comes from the Latin *granatum* (pomegranate) because the red crystals resemble the seeds of the fruit</note>.

**Sardonyx**, which **derives its name from a mixture of Sarda and Onyx** <note>original: *mixtum habet è Sarda & Onyche nomen*. This stone features the reddish layers of carnelian (sarda) and the white/black layers of onyx</note>.
**Emerald**, the **most precious of all gems, and almost the most delicate** <note>original: *Smaragdus, gemmarum omnium precioſiſſima, & fermè tenerrima*. Early naturalists observed that emeralds were softer and more prone to fracturing than diamonds or rubies</note>.
**Terebinthizon** <note>original: *Τερεβινθίζων*. A variety of jasper or other stone that resembles turpentine resin in its color or translucency</note>.
**Topaz**, a **gem of green color** <note>original: *Topaſius, gemma viridis coloris*. Note that in antiquity, "topaz" usually referred to what we now call Peridot, which is green, rather than the modern yellow or blue topaz</note>.

# ON THE POWERS OF SIMPLE MEDICINES.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->SEA SUBSTANCES<-

**Sea Foam** <note>original: *Alcyonium, sive Spuma maris*. In early medicine, this term referred to various sponge-like marine organisms or bryozoans, often believed to be the dried foam of the sea</note>.
**Fragrant Ambergris** <note>original: *Ambra odorata*. Known as *Ambarum* to the Latins or *Oriental Amber* (*Succinum orientale*). Unlike yellow amber from trees, this is a waxy substance produced by sperm whales, highly valued in perfumes and medicine</note>.
**Bitumen** <note>original: *Bitumen*, in Greek *asphaltos* (ἄσφαλτος). Also called **Judean Bitumen** (*Bitumen judaicum*). A natural mineral pitch found near the Dead Sea</note>.
**Shell of the Trumpet-Snail** <note>original: *Buccinarum testa*. Shells from the *Buccinidae* family of sea snails</note>.
**Crab Shell** <note>original: *Cancrorum testa*</note>.
**Clam Shell** <note>original: *Chamarum testa*. Specifically referring to the *Chama* genus of thick-shelled bivalves</note>.
**Chione Shell** <note>original: *Cionia testa*. Likely referring to the *Chamelea* or *Chione* genus of Venus clams</note>.
**Shell of Sea Snails** <note>original: *Cochlearum marinarum testa*</note>.

## C H A P T E R  I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' with symmetrical floral scrollwork and foliage patterns inside a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
It was stated earlier at the beginning of the first section, in chapter 1, that some medicines are **Simples** <note>Medicines consisting of a single natural ingredient, such as a specific herb or mineral</note> and others are **Compounds** <note>Medicines made by mixing multiple simples together</note>. Furthermore, Simples are considered either in general or in particular. In this first section, we have dealt with Simples generally; specifically, we have reviewed the catalog of those Simples which are commonly used in **apothecary shops** <note>original: *officinis*</note> in our time. It remains, therefore, that hereafter we deal with them in particular and examine the **Properties** <note>original: *Facultates*</note> of Simples.

Moreover, the properties <note>original: *facultates*; Greek: *Δυνάμεις* (dynameis)</note> of Medicines are nothing other than their productive causes, which they derive partly from their essence or substance, and partly from their accidents—that is, from their qualities or powers.

## C H A P T E R  I I.

->*Concerning Simples considered according to their essence.*<-

Simples considered according to their essence are either of a **thin** essence, or a **thick** essence, or of **dissimilar parts**.

<margin>**Animal parts.**</margin> Castoreum <note>original: *Castorium*; a yellowish secretion from beaver scent glands, traditionally used to treat hysteria and skin conditions</note>
Cuttlefish bone <note>original: *Sepiae testa*; the internal shell of a cuttlefish, often powdered for use in ointments or as a digestive aid</note>
<margin>**Excretions.**</margin> Honey <note>original: *Mel*</note>
Propolis <note>original: *Propolis*; "bee glue" collected from trees, used by bees to seal hives and by physicians for its antiseptic qualities</note>

A medicine of thin substance, if it is likewise hot—though below the third degree—such as Parsley <note>original: *Petroselinum*</note>, Hyssop <note>original: *Hyssopus*</note>, etc., when taken internally opens the small passages of the body and dissolves thin humors, dissipating them or digesting them through vapors. For this reason, it promotes sweating and urination, while it cuts through, thins, or breaks down thick humors. When applied externally, however, it thins and dilates the skin, and also draws out and dissolves spirits and humors from deep within the body. But if it is hot even in the fourth degree, it is considered Septic <note>original: *Septicum*; a substance so caustic or "hot" that it causes tissue to break down, blister, or "rot"</note>, which undoubtedly either burns, causes ulcers, excites blisters, or liquefies the flesh.

Truly, that which is of thin substance but tempered, or even likewise cold: when taken internally, it also opens and thins, but more sluggishly than the hot variety, or when applied externally to the body. Insofar as it is cold, it repels the flow of humors and restrains the force of eruptions; it does this more powerfully than that which is simply cold and astringent <note>original: *adstringens*; substances that contract body tissues</note>, for it carries the power of the cold deeper into the body. However, that which is cold and of a medium substance, such as
->Purslane <note>original: *Portulaca*; a succulent plant used for its cooling and soothing properties</note>, moderately repels the flow of humors, and stays and binds them.<-

# CHAPTER III.

->*Simples of Thick Essence.*<-

Simples having a thick and sticky essence are those whose substance clings and remains, and cannot penetrate deeply.

This leads into the start of Chapter III, which focuses on medicines with a "thick essence."</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

<margin>Animal parts.</margin> Castoreum <note>original: *Castorium*; a yellowish secretion from beaver scent glands used to treat nervous complaints</note>
Cuttlefish bone. <note>original: *Sepiæ testa*</note>
<margin>Excrements.</margin> Honey
Propolis. <note>original: *Propolis*; a resinous mixture produced by honeybees</note>

A medicine of thin substance, if it is likewise hot beyond the third degree <note>Ancient and Renaissance medicine graded the intensity of a plant's "complexion" (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) on a scale of one to four</note>, such as Parsley <note>original: *Petroselinum*</note>, Hyssop <note>original: *Hyssopus*</note> etc., when taken internally, opens the narrow passages of the body and dissolves thin humors <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health</note>, dissipates them or digests them into vapor, and for this reason promotes sweating and urine; but it cuts through, thins, or breaks down thick humors. When applied externally, however, it makes the skin porous and dilated, and also draws out and dissolves spirits <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to the subtle vapors or "pneuma" thought to circulate through the body to provide vitality</note> and humors from deep within the body. 

But if it is also hot in the fourth degree, it is considered Corrosive <note>original: *Septicum*</note>, because it certainly either burns, or causes ulcers, or raises blisters, or melts the flesh away. 

However, that which is of thin substance but tempered, or even equally cold: if taken internally, it also opens and thins [the humors], but more sluggishly than a hot medicine, or one applied externally to the body. Insofar as it is cold, it repels fluxions <note>The movement of harmful humors from one part of the body to another</note> and restrains the force of an eruption, and does so more powerfully than something that is simply cold and astringent, for it carries the power of the cold deeper into the body. But that which is cold and of a medium substance, such as Purslane <note>original: *Portulaca*</note>, moderately repels fluxion, and stops and binds the body.

Simple medicines having a thick and viscous essence are called those whose substance clings and persists, and cannot penetrate deeply.

<header>ON THE POWERS OF SIMPLE MEDICINES</header>

->Dregs <note>original: *Faex*; refers to the sediment of liquids like wine or oil used as a base for ointments</note><-
->Soot of Frankincense <note>original: *Thuris fuligo*; the carbon collected from burning resin, used to dry out wounds or treat eyes</note><-

A medicine that has attained a certain balance of heat and cold within a thick and earthy substance—such as **Armenian Bole** <note>original: *Bolus Armenus*; a medicinal red clay</note> or **Lemnian Earth** <note>original: *terra Lemnia*; a famous clay from the island of Lemnos used as an antidote to poison</note>—obstructs the internal passages and seals the pores of the skin; it soothes roughened areas and binds together parts that have separated. For such a substance is either "filling," a **plaster-like agent** <term>emplasticum: a sticky substance that clogs pores and adheres to the skin</term>, a smoothing agent, or even a gluey one. However, that which is moderately warm or cold, such as the **Rose** or **Myrtle**, tightens the looser parts and thereby strengthens them. 

But those substances that are excessively hot, such as those of the "fourth degree" <note>the highest level of intensity in the Galenic system of qualities</note>, like **Quicklime**, **Orpiment** <note>original: *Auripigmentum*; a yellow arsenic mineral</note>, and **Arsenic**, eat away at the flesh; these are **putrefactive** <term>septicum: an agent that causes tissue to rot or break down</term>, **caustic**, or **searing** <term>escharoticum: a powerful substance that burns the skin to create a scab or "eschar"</term>. 

On the other hand, substances that are excessively cold and dry, such as the **Oak Gall** or **Cypress Nut**, do not merely block the openings of the vessels when taken [internally], but actually contract and shut them, narrowing or "clotting" all the passages, and thickening the humors themselves beyond measure. Applied externally, such a substance thickens and binds the skin, restrains and even repels the force of a "fluxion" <note>an unhealthy flow of fluids to a body part</note>, and covers a wound with a scar.

### *Simple medicines possessing a dissimilar essence.*

Just as "Similar Simples" <note>simple medicines consisting of a single ingredient with a primary quality</note> are those which contain within themselves only one quality rather than many, so "Dissimilar" ones are those containing several. Thus, for example, the **Cabbage** <note>original: *Brassica*</note> possesses two powers: namely, those of purging and binding.

# CHAPTER I.

## ON SIMPLE MEDICINES, considered according to their Accidental Properties.

<note>original: *Accidens*; in the Aristotelian philosophy used by physicians of this era, an "accident" is a property or quality (like color, temperature, or taste) that a substance possesses, which is distinct from its essential nature.</note>

There are four primary types of Simple Medicines considered in respect to their accidental properties, which the modern authors <note>original: *Neoterici*; refers to medical writers of the Renaissance or later eras who built upon ancient Greek and Roman foundations.</note> have distinguished with names taken from their order: namely, into first, second, third, and fourth qualities.

## ON THE FIRST QUALITIES.

First Qualities are those which are propagated into mixtures immediately from the Elements themselves without any intermediary; they are the most simple and the first to be encountered by the senses, and they give rise to the other qualities. Some of these are judged to be Imbalanced, while others are Balanced.

->*Temperate Simples.*<-
<note>original: *Simplicia Temperata*; medicines that are "balanced" or "temperate" do not noticeably shift the body's internal temperature or moisture levels.</note>

Temperate Simples are determined to be those which do not have such manifest powers that they can rightly be called cold, hot, moist, or dry, or reach any specific degree in these qualities.

**Metals.** <note>original: *Metalla*</note> Silver <note>original: *Argentum*</note>
Gold <note>original: *Aurum*</note>

<meta>catchword: Cadmia</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the table of contents for the sections on moist medicines and begins Chapter 1, which defines the "First Qualities" of medicines (hot, cold, wet, dry) and introduces "Temperate" substances like gold and silver.</summary>
<keywords>Simple Medicines, Accidental Properties, First Qualities, Temperate Simples, Neoterici, Metals, Gold, Silver</keywords>

--- Page 127 ---

# C H A P T E R  II.

## On Intemperate Simples.

Those things are called **Intemperate** which heat, cool, moisten, or dry to such an extent that they reach a certain <term>degree</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a medicine's effect, from the 1st (mild) to the 4th (extreme).</note> in these qualities.
And of these, some are: &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**hot**, <note>original: *θερμὸν* (thermon)</note> such as Pepper
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**cold**, <note>original: *ψυχρὸν* (psychron)</note> such as Mandrake
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**moist**, <note>original: *ὑγρὸν* (hygron)</note> such as Oil
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**dry**, <note>original: *ξηρὸν* (xeron)</note> such as Sea water.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the qualities of medicinal substances, specifically transitioning from general definitions of intensity (the "degrees") to the specific properties and examples of substances categorized as "Hot."</meta>

<page-num>95</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

Since, however, the power and equally strong faculty of all those things which, for example, are called "hot" is not one and the same, practical use has distinguished four degrees and orders of them: the first, second, third, and fourth. These degrees or orders, which the Greeks call <term>taxis</term> <note>original: *τάξεις*; meaning ranks, orders, or arrangements.</note>, are explored and examined by taste, touch, and smell, as Galen teaches in the first of his *Prior Books on the Faculties of Simple Medicines* <note>original: *περὶ δυνάμεων τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων*; a foundational pharmaceutical text by the 2nd-century physician Galen.</note>. Furthermore, because the range <note>original: *latitudo*; refers to the spectrum of intensity within a single category.</note> of each class and order is not small, three parts are established: the beginning, the middle, and the end. Thus, among those things which are called "cold" in the third order, some consist in the beginning of this order, others in the middle, and others at the end.

---

## CHAPTER III.

### On Hot Simples.

Heat gathers together homogeneous things <note>substances of the same kind</note> and disperses or separates heterogeneous things <note>substances of different kinds</note>; it penetrates, opens, rarefies, thins, <term>digests</term> <note>original: *digerit*; in this context, it means to disperse or break down morbid matter or swellings.</note> or discusses, melts or <term>incises</term> <note>original: *incidit*; to "cut" through thick, sticky fluids or humors.</note>, dissolves, loosens, attracts, and draws apart. Furthermore, it burns, induces a crust <note>a scab or eschar</note>, stings, and so on. It can also cool by attracting and drawing out internal heat; it weakens, consumes, and destroys.

->Hot in the 1st Degree.<-

Those things are said to be Hot in the first degree which indeed change the body perceptibly—that is, those which affect our bodies with their heat lightly and obscurely rather than manifestly—yet in such a way that no effort of tasting follows <note>meaning they do not cause a sharp or painful sensation on the tongue</note>. Examples include:

<margin>Metals.</margin> <term>White lead</term> <note>original: *Cerusa*; lead carbonate, used historically in ointments despite its toxicity.</note>.
<term>Realgar</term> <note>original: *Sandaracha*; a red arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>.
<margin>Sea Products.</margin> Sea sponge.

<page-num>95</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

Since, however, not all things called "hot" (for example) possess a single power or an equally strong faculty, practical use has distinguished four degrees and ranks of them: the first, second, third, and fourth. These degrees or ranks, which the Greeks call *taxeis* <note>original: *τάξεις*; meaning arrangements or classifications</note>, are explored and examined through taste, touch, and smell, as Galen teaches in the first of his earlier books *On the Powers of Simple Medicines* <note>original: *περὶ δυνάμεων τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων*</note>. Furthermore, within each class and rank (as the range is not small), three parts are established: the beginning, the middle, and the end. Thus, among those substances called "cold" in the third degree, some belong at the beginning of this rank, others in the middle, and others at the end.

---

## CHAPTER III.

->Concerning Hot Simples.<-

Heat <note>original: *Calidum*; referring to the active quality of "hot" medicines</note> gathers together things of the same kind and breaks apart or separates those of different kinds; it penetrates, opens, thins, makes subtle, digests or dissipates, melts or cuts through <note>original: *incidit*; refers to "incisive" medicines that break up thick humors</note>, dissolves, loosens, attracts, and draws apart. Furthermore, it burns, induces a crust <note>original: *crustam*; likely referring to forming a scab or eschar on a wound</note>, stings, etc. It can even cool by attracting and drawing out internal heat; it weakens, consumes, and destroys.

->Hot in the 1st Degree.<-

Substances are said to be "Hot in the first degree" which produce a sensory change—that is, those which affect our bodies with their heat lightly and obscurely rather than in an obvious way. They are such that no difficulty in tasting them occurs. Examples include:
<margin>Metals.</margin> Ceruse <note>original: *Cerussa*; white lead, used historically in ointments and cosmetics</note>.
Sandarac <note>original: *Sandaracha*; likely referring here to "red arsenic" or a specific resin</note>.
<margin>Marine items.</margin> Sea sponge.

# CHAPTER 4.

->Hot in the 2nd degree.<-

To this degree are referred those things which already manifest a clear heating effect—that is, they impress the body more strongly and, as it were, introduce a certain toil <note>original: *laborem*; implying these substances cause a noticeable physiological reaction or "work" within the system compared to the mildness of the first degree.</note> to it, such as are:

Medicines that are **Hot in the second degree** are most suitable for those whose stomach is filled with phlegm <note>original: *pituita*; one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note>, as they possess the power to heat and dry. Likewise, they remove obstructions, thin out dense matter <note>original: *rarefaciunt*</note>, and open the passages of the skin <note>the pores</note>, yet they do so in a different manner than those that heat in the first degree. For these [second-degree] medicines dissolve the humors <note>original: *humo-* (humores)</note> slowly and with a pleasant warmth—

# CHAPTER V.

->Hot in the 3rd degree.<-

In this third degree are counted those Simples <note>natural medicinal ingredients not mixed with others</note> which act forcefully upon our body with heat; that is, they now clearly and effectively begin to change and alter the body's condition with significant effort, yet they do not heat to the highest possible extent.

# CHAPTER VI.

->*Hot in the 4th degree.*<-

To this degree belong simple medicines <note>original: *Simplicia*; individual ingredients used without mixing</note> that are supremely and extremely heating, so much so that they burn the skin and produce an eschar <note>original: *escharam*; a dry crust or scab of dead tissue produced by a burn or caustic substance</note>. Indeed, they almost destroy the tissue, driving the body from its proper temperament <note>the healthy balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note> and attacking it with great force.

<margin>Metals and Minerals</margin> <note>original: *Metalla*</note>
Adarce <note>original: *Adarce*; a salty, porous crust found on reeds in marshy areas, used for its cleansing properties.</note>
Arsenic <note>original: *Arrhenicum*; likely referring to orpiment or realgar, minerals containing arsenic.</note>
Quicklime <note>original: *Calx viva*; calcium oxide, which produces intense heat when mixed with water.</note>
Chalcantum or Vitriol <note>original: *Calchantum, Vitriolum*; metallic sulfates used as powerful astringents or caustics.</note>
Chrysocolla <note>original: *Chrysocolla*; literally "gold-glue," a mineral used in soldering and as a drying medicine.</note>
Melanteria <note>original: *Melanteria*; an earthy mineral related to vitriol, often used for making ink or as a caustic.</note>
Misy <note>original: *Misy*; a yellow, sulfurous mineral, typically an oxidized iron pyrite.</note>
Psoricum <note>original: *Psoricum*; a medicinal preparation of minerals used for skin conditions like the itch.</note>
Sal ammoniac <note>original: *Sal Armoniacum*; a salt used in various chemical and medicinal processes.</note>
Sandarac <note>original: *Sandaracha*; here referring to the "Greek" variety, which was red arsenic sulfide.</note>
Native sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur vivum*; natural, unrefined sulfur collected from volcanic sources.</note>

# CHAPTER VII.

## On Cold Simples.
<note>In early medicine, "simples" referred to medicinal ingredients consisting of a single herb, mineral, or substance, rather than a complex mixture.</note>

Cold gathers and binds together similar things; it cools, contracts, thickens, clogs, tightens, and binds. Furthermore, it numbs, makes the substance of the body immobile, and separates things that are continuous <note>The author likely refers to the way extreme cold can cause tissue to become brittle or crack</note>. Likewise, it can heat by forcing heat inward <note>This refers to the concept of *antiperistasis*, where external cold traps or concentrates the body's internal "innate heat"</note>, and it dries, stings, etc.

### Cold in the 1st degree.

To this first order belong those Simples that affect our body with cold only slightly or lightly, and which diminish the innate heat <note>the vital warmth believed to be centered in the heart and necessary for life</note>.

<margin>Earths</margin> Armenian Bole <note>original: *Bolus Armena*; a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent.</note>
Cimolian Earth <note>original: *Cimolia*; a white clay or "fuller's earth" used for its cooling and drying properties.</note>
Bricks <note>original: *Lateres*; often used in powdered form or heated to apply dry warmth, though here noted for their cooling nature when prepared differently.</note>

<margin>Metals</margin> Silver
Cadmia of silver <note>original: *Cadmia argenti*; a metallic oxide or residue collected from silver-smelting furnaces.</note>
Antimony <note>original: *Stimmi*; used since antiquity as both a medicine and a cosmetic.</note>

<margin>Gems</margin> Jacinth <note>original: *Hyacinthus*; a yellow, orange, or red gemstone, often zircon.</note>
Sapphire
Emerald

<margin>Roots</margin> Sea Holly <note>original: *Eryngii*.</note>
Green Licorice
Mallow

<margin>Leaves</margin> Sorrel <note>original: *Acetosa*.</note>
Mugwort <note>original: *Arthemisia*.</note>
Orach <note>original: *Atriplex*; also known as saltbush.</note>
Goat's Beard <note>original: *Barbula hirci*; a plant in the *Tragopogon* genus.</note>
Borage
Dwarf Olive <note>original: *Chamælea*; likely a species of *Daphne* or a similar small shrub.</note>

# CHAPTER X.

## Cold in the 4th degree.

These cool to such an extent that they extinguish life:
<margin>*Gems.*</margin> Diamond <note>In historical medicine, ground gemstones were occasionally used in tinctures for their supposed elemental properties.</note>.
<margin>*Roots.*</margin> Fungi <note>Mushrooms were often classified as "roots" of the earth and considered dangerously cold and moist.</note>.
<margin>*Leaves.*</margin> Hemlock <note>original: *Cicuta*; a famous and deadly poison.</note>.
Poisonous Bindweed <note>original: *Dorychnium*; a plant often confused with types of nightshade or convolvulus.</note>.
<margin>*Flowers.*</margin> Poppy.
<margin>*Fruits.*</margin> Henbane.
Thorn-apple <note>original: *Strammonea*; also known as Datura or Jimsonweed, known for its potent hallucinogenic and narcotic effects.</note>.
<margin>*Seeds.*</margin> Corn poppy <note>original: *Papaver erraticum*; the common wild red poppy.</note>.
<margin>*Juices.*</margin> Opium.

We use these for the most violent pains, which can be settled neither by soothing nor by warmer remedies. For these Narcotics <note>From the Greek *narkōtikos*, meaning "to make numb."</note> often lull the patient to sleep with wonderful success through their cold: they congeal the spirits, extinguish natural heat, and kill like poisons if used without care.

# CHAPTER XIII.

->Substances dry in the 3rd degree.<- <note>In the Galenic system, the "third degree" indicates a potent medicine that produces a very strong effect, often used for more stubborn or severe conditions</note>

**Metals.** <note>mineral and metallic substances used in pharmacology</note> Alum <note>original: *Alumen*; used topically to stop bleeding and dry out sores</note>
Iron Rust <note>original: *Ferrugo*; used to treat "fluxes" or discharges and to strengthen the stomach</note>

Common Salt <note>original: *Sal commune*</note>
Rock Salt <note>original: *Sal gemmae*; a pure, crystalline form of salt</note>
