Substances that are dry in the third degree <note>In the Galenic medical system, the "third degree" indicates a very high intensity of a quality, capable of significantly altering the body's balance</note> make the passages of the body narrower, block the transit of the humors, hinder the excretion of wastes, squeeze the vital juices out of the body, deprive the various parts of their nourishment, and by this reasoning cause wasting and consumption.

## CHAPTER XIV.
### Dry substances in the 4th degree.

In the third class, dry substances exert their greatest power without the addition of heat, just as moist substances do without the addition of cold. Therefore, in the fourth class, neither dry nor moist substances are placed [on their own], since they are considered "passive" qualities and are named as such: consequently, they do not attempt or approach this greatest work of themselves unless they are aided by significant heat or cold; otherwise, they are content with the power of being acted upon alone. They are, however, referred to this fourth order:

<margin>Metals</margin> Burnt copper <note>original: *Aes ustum*; copper or bronze calcined by fire to create a caustic powder used for cleaning wounds</note>
Flower of copper <note>original: *Aeris flos*; the fine scales that flake off hot copper, used to dry out weeping ulcers</note>
Orpiment <note>original: *Auripigmentum*; a yellow arsenic mineral used as a powerful corrosive and depilatory</note>
Lime <note>original: *Calx*; quicklime, used for its intense drying and caustic properties</note>
Chalcitis <note>original: *Chalcitis*; a copper-bearing mineral related to vitriol</note>
Chrysocolla <note>original: *Chrysocolla*; literally "gold glue," likely a green copper mineral like malachite used in eye salves</note>
Melanteria <note>original: *Melanteria*; a black vitriol or iron sulfate used as an astringent</note>
Misy <note>original: *Misy*; a yellow mineral ore, likely a sulfate of iron and copper</note>
Ochre <note>original: *Ochra*; an earth rich in iron oxide used as a drying agent</note>
Sandarac <note>original: *Sandaracha*; here referring to red arsenic (realgar), a toxic mineral used to treat skin growths</note>
Sory <note>original: *Sory*; a dark, mineral-rich earth related to copper vitriol</note>
Virgin sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur vivum*; raw, native sulfur as found in the earth</note>
Tutty <note>original: *Thutia*; zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces, used in healing ointments</note>

<margin>Leaves</margin> Garlic <note>original: *Allium*; famous for its intense heat and drying effects on the body</note>
Another species of Clematis <note>original: *Clematis altera*; likely "Virgin's Bower," used to blister the skin and treat leprosy</note>
Spurge <note>original: *Lactaria*; plants with a milky, caustic sap often used to burn off warts</note>
Spurge laurel <note>original: *Laureola*; an evergreen shrub with a very sharp, purging quality</note>
Cress <note>original: *Nasturtium*; known for its biting, pungent heat</note>
Pine-spurge <note>original: *Pithyusa*; a variety of euphorbia with an extremely drying sap</note>
Pennyroyal <note>original: *Pulegium*; a potent herb in the mint family used to stimulate menstruation</note>
Wild Rue <note>original: *Ruta sylvest.*; much more toxic and caustic than the common garden rue</note>
Sardinian herb <note>original: *Sardonia herba*; likely a species of buttercup that, if eaten, causes facial spasms resembling a "sardonic" grin</note>

## CHAPTER XV.
### On Moist Simples.

That which is moist provides moisture, softens, causes parts to cohere, glues them together, fills up [depleted areas], and so forth.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## Moist substances in the 3rd degree.

->Onion seed<- <note>original: *Cepar. sem.*; seeds of the common onion (*Allium cepa*)</note>
->Mushrooms<- <note>original: *Fungi*</note>
->White garden poppy<- <note>original: *Papaver sat. alb.*; *Papaver somniferum var. album*</note>
->Psyllium seed<- <note>original: *Pfillii sem.*; also known as fleawort</note>
->Sleep-inducing nightshade<- <note>original: *Solanum somnificum*; likely referring to a sedative plant like Winter Cherry or Mandrake</note>

These make the body sluggish and torpid, and they clearly dull and weaken all actions, from which arise nausea, vomiting, lientery <term>a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</term>, and so forth.

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## Moist substances in the 4th degree.

Just as dry substances do not possess their highest power unless they are aided by heat, so too moist substances do not have the highest moistening power unless an accompanying cold increases their action. Nevertheless, these can be referred to the fourth degree:

->Quicksilver<- <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; elemental mercury</note>
->Hemlock<- <note>original: *Cicuta*; a highly toxic sedative and paralytic</note>
->Dorycnium<- <note>original: *Dorychnium*; a plant described by ancient herbalists as a potent poison, possibly a type of convolvulus or nightshade</note>
->Opium<- <note>original: *Opium*; the dried latex of the poppy</note>
->Field poppy<- <note>original: *Papaver erraticum*; the common red corn poppy</note>

These are poisons. For they extinguish [innate] heat, just as water extinguishes fire.

->C H A P T E R I.<-

Secondary qualities <term>Secondary qualities: medical properties that result from the mixing of the four basic elements—earth, air, fire, and water—rather than from just one primary quality like 'heat' or 'cold'.</term> is the name given to the powers or faculties that arise immediately from the mixture and temperament of the Elements, or of the primary qualities, among themselves. Just as with the primary faculties, four degrees of power must be recognized in the secondary faculties: thus, within the categories of Astringents <note>substances that contract or tighten body tissues</note> or Thinning agents, there exist those of the first class, which act subtly; the second, which act clearly; the third, which act powerfully; and the fourth, which act to the highest and most extreme degree. Furthermore, within each class or order, there is a certain beginning, middle, and end. The distinctions between these qualities are many, as can be seen in the catalog placed at the start of this section.

<vocab>Secondary qualities, of the Elements, of Astringents, of Thinning agents, Putrefying agents, Pain-relievers, Destructive agents</vocab>

<summary>This page lists the final categories of secondary medicinal qualities—ranging from wound-healing to poisonous—and defines "secondary qualities" as complex powers arising from the mixture of primary elements. It establishes a four-tier system for measuring the intensity of these medicinal effects.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.
## CHAPTER II.

### *Softeners.*

A softener, <term>malaktikon</term> <note>original: μαλακτικόν</note>, is properly defined not as something that empties out what is distended and resisting through an abundance of fluid, nor something that merely moistens what is dry. Rather, it is that which warms, loosens, and dissolves things that have hardened together. Moreover, it consists of a moderate substance and is moderately hot beyond the third degree <note>In traditional medicine, the "degrees" (1–4) measured the intensity of a drug's primary qualities; a third-degree heat is quite powerful</note>, so that by dissolving the thinner portion of the bodily fluid, it does not cause the remainder to harden; it is dry in the second degree. For this reason, it must possess a smearing power (which they call <term>emplastic</term> <note>original: *emplasticam*; a sticky, resinous quality that allows a medicine to adhere to the skin like a plaster</note>), just as with substances that promote the formation of pus, though it should be hotter than those. It is also filled with an "airy" moisture and is devoid of all sharpness and every external taste or forceful quality: it is recognized by a fatty, oily, and somewhat sweet taste.

# CHAPTER III.

->Hardening Agents.<-

Hardening medicines, <note>Greek original: τὰ σκληρυντικὰ (ta sklēruntika)</note>, ought to be cold and moist, but in a certain way tempered in their dryness and moisture. Furthermore, substances that are cold and dry also harden, but they are not among those which are properly classified as Hardening agents. For these purposes, Hardening agents should be cold in the second or third degree, and moist in the first degree. <note>In the medical theory of this period, "degrees" measured the intensity of a substance's primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) on a scale of 1 to 4.</note>

Indeed, Hardening agents may be recognized by their taste, which indicates neither heat, nor bites or constricts the tongue. Since they must be cold, they are certainly not salty, nor sharp, nor bitter, nor sweet; and since no evacuation ought to occur for a thing to be hardened, there is also no need for constriction. For this reason, Hardening agents are neither harsh nor austere; perhaps they should not even be acidic, since they must not be <term>Thinning agents <note>original: *Attenuantia*; medicines used to break down or "thin" thick humors to aid their movement or expulsion</note></term>. Therefore, the taste of Hardening agents is a mixed variety, unless one prefers to call them tasteless.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Laxatives and Tensing Agents.
### <note>Greek original: χαλαστικά καὶ Συντατικά (chalastika kai syntatika)</note>

There is not just one species of **laxative** <note>In this historical context, "laxative" refers more broadly to medicines that loosen or relax any body tissue or tension, not just those that affect the bowels.</note> medicines, but as many as there are types of tensions. For since tension may arise from drying, cooling, **inflammation** <note>original: *phlegmone*; a term used in ancient medicine for a hot, red swelling caused by an excess of blood</note>, or a **hard tumor** <note>original: *scirrho*; a firm, painless swelling or "scirrhus"</note>: some loosen by moistening, some by heating, others by softening, others by purging tumors, and some through a combination of these.

The primary use of **Laxatives** is in **convulsions** which both cold and dryness induce, although a convulsion arising from other causes is sometimes treated with Laxatives.

---

## CHAPTER V.

### Rarefying Agents.

We call a medicine **rarefying** <note>Greek original: Ἀραιωτικόν (*araiotikon*); substances that make tissues more porous or less dense</note> if it dissolves and spreads out solid and compact matter, and separates its parts further from each other so that it makes small pores wider. The nature of these ought to be moderately warm, even in the **first degree** <note>A measure of intensity in Galenic medicine where the 1st degree is the mildest</note>, but not at all drying, and consisting of thin parts. They are recognized by the same qualities as Laxatives and **Emollients** <note>softening agents</note>, specifically by a taste denoting moderate heat.

BOOK ONE.

## CHAPTER VI.
### Dispersing Agents.

Medical practitioners have established two types of **Diaphoretics** <note>original: Διαφορητικά; also called *Discutientia, Dissolventia,* or *Resolventia*</note>: some are milder, which they call *rarefacientia* or **rarefying agents** (discussed in the preceding chapter); others are stronger, which they properly name **dispersing agents**. When taken internally, these substances do not only open blocked passages by cleansing and thinning the fluids, but they also drive the obstructing **humors** <note>the bodily fluids, such as blood, phlegm, and bile, which must remain balanced for health</note> toward the surface of the body, eventually dissolving them through sweat or breath. These substances are thin and hot in nature, allowing them to penetrate very quickly and enter into every part of the body. They are distinguished—just like "attracting agents"—by a sharp taste that burns the tongue, as they are made of fine particles and are extremely hot.

<margin>**Earths.**</margin> Bituminous earth <note>original: *Ampelitis*; a black, coal-like earth used to treat inflammations</note>

Ground-pine <note>original: *Chamæpitys*; a low-growing herb with a pine-like scent, used for joint pain and gout.</note>
Ground-spurge <note>original: *Chamæsyce*; a small trailing plant used to clear the skin and heal wounds.</note>
Greater Celandine <note>original: *Chelidonium majus*; famous for its yellow sap, used historically to treat jaundice and eye spots.</note>
Marigold <note>original: *Chrysanthemon*; literally "Gold-flower," used to treat various inflammatory conditions.</note>
Tree Medick <note>original: *Cytisus*; a shrubby plant often used as fodder, also applied in cooling remedies.</note>
Wild Basil <note>original: *Clinopodium*; named because its flower clusters resemble the feet of a bed-frame (*cline*).</note>
Wild Distaff <note>original: *Colus rustica*; Distaff Thistle, so named because its stems were used in wool-spinning.</note>
Dittany of Crete <note>original: *Dictamnus Creticus*; a rare and highly valued aromatic herb from Crete, famous for drawing out arrows and splinters.</note>
Dwarf Elder <note>original: *Ebulus*; also called Danewort, used as a powerful purgative to expel excess fluids.</note>
Hemp-nettle <note>original: *Galiopsis*; despite the name, it is a member of the mint family with medicinal properties.</note>
Crane’s-bill <note>original: *Geranium*; named for the long, beak-like shape of its seed-pod.</note>
Water-pepper <note>original: *Hydropiper*; known for its stinging, spicy taste and its ability to stimulate the skin.</note>
Cultivated Woad <note>original: *Isatis sativa*; primarily used as a blue dye, but also applied medicinally to stop bleeding.</note>
Nipplewort <note>original: *Lampsana*; a common edible plant often used in salads or as a soothing herb.</note>
Soapwort <note>original: *Lanaria*; literally "Woolly-plant," used for its soapy sap to clean wool and treat skin ailments.</note>
Lion’s-leaf <note>original: *Leontopetalum*; its leaves were thought to resemble the paw of a lion.</note>
White Dead-nettle <note>original: *Leucas*; a plant with white flowers, often used to treat female conditions.</note>
Rosemary <note>original: *Libanotis*; also called Frankincense-herb due to its strong, aromatic scent.</note>
Another Rosemary <note>original: *Libanotis altera*; a second variety or species of the Frankincense-herb.</note>
Lovage <note>original: *Ligusticum*; a tall, aromatic herb used both in cooking and to aid digestion.</note>
Privet <note>original: *Ligustrum*; an evergreen shrub whose flowers and leaves were used in cooling washes.</note>

### ON THE FACULTIES OF SIMPLE MEDICINES.

Lily <note>original: *Lilium*; its roots were often roasted and applied to soften hard swellings or treat burns.</note>
Mallow <note>original: *Malva*; prized for its mucilage, used to soothe internal and external irritations.</note>
Horehound <note>original: *Marrubium*; a bitter herb traditionally used to clear phlegm from the chest.</note>
Melilot <note>original: *Melilotus*; also called sweet clover, used in plasters to reduce inflammation.</note>

Mercury <note>original: *Mercurialis*; a common herb used as a gentle laxative and to "purge the bile."</note>
Moly <note>original: *Moly*; a wild species of garlic or allium with legendary status as a protective herb.</note>
Moss <note>original: *Muscus*; various tree or rock mosses were used for their cooling and binding (astringent) qualities.</note>
Watercress <note>original: *Nasturtium*; a sharp, biting herb used to "cleanse the blood" and stimulate the appetite.</note>

Burdock <note>original: *Personatia*; known for its large leaves and burrs, used to treat skin diseases and as a diuretic.</note>
Parsley <note>original: *Petroselinum*; specifically rock parsley, used to stimulate urine and expel kidney stones.</note>

Pycnocomon <note>original: *Pycnocomon*; a plant resembling Scabious, used for its thinning and dispersing effects on thick fluids.</note>

Fragrant Round Rush <note>original: *Juncus rotundus odoratus*; likely a species of Cyperus or Galingale, used for its aromatic and warming root.</note>

Savin <note>original: *Sabina*; a variety of juniper used as a powerful stimulant to the reproductive system.</note>

Marjoram <note>original: *Sampsuchum*; sweet marjoram, used in oils and ointments to treat cold-natured nerve pains.</note>
Groundsel <note>original: *Senecio*; a cooling herb used in poultices for hot inflammations of the skin.</note>

## CHAPTER VII.
### Condensers.

Condensers, densifiers, or restrainers <note>Greek: *pyknotika*</note> are clearly the opposites of rarifiers. They are not of an earthy or airy essence, but rather watery. They bind and close the channels or pores of the skin, making the substance of that part of the body firmer and more compact.

Burnt copper <note>original: *Aes crematum*; used topically as an astringent and to dry out wounds.</note>
Alkanet <note>original: *Anchusa*; a plant whose root provides a red dye, used to treat skin conditions.</note>
Cold water
Hemlock <note>original: *Cicuta*; a highly toxic plant used in controlled doses for its cooling and numbing properties.</note>
Duckweed <note>original: *Lenticula palustris*</note>
Poppy <note>original: *Papaver*</note>
Purslane <note>original: *Portulaca*; a succulent plant known for its cooling properties.</note>
Fleawort <note>original: *Psillium*</note>
Salt
Greater stonecrop <note>original: *Sedum majus*</note>
Lesser stonecrop <note>original: *Sedum minus*</note>
Green caltrop <note>original: *Tribulus viridis*</note>

The use of these is to ensure the skin is made firmer and more robust, both to avoid injury from external forces and to prevent excessive sweating or the dissipation of the vital spirits.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->Closing Agents<-

**Closing agents** <note>original: *Occludentia*</note>, as well as constricting, obstructing, or stuffing agents <note>Greek: *synaktikon* or *stegnotikon*</note>, are substances that narrow the openings of the veins and arteries, as well as other channels of the body, and draw them into a tight state. They are of a thicker substance, equally cold and dry, and entirely free from any sharpness or bitterness, belonging to the primary class of harsh and astringent medicines.

Starch <note>original: *Amylum*; often used in ancient medicine to soothe and bind.</note>
Armenian bole <note>original: *Bolus Armenus*; a medicinal red clay used to stop bleeding and treat wounds.</note>
Cheese <note>original: *Caseus*</note>
Dates <note>original: *Dactyli*</note>
Unleavened bread <note>original: *Panis azymus*</note>
Fats <note>original: *Pingvedines*</note>
Lemnian Earth <note>original: *Terra Lemnia*; a famous medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, prized as an astringent and antidote.</note>

These substances inhibit hemorrhoids and other flows of blood.

---

## CHAPTER IX.

->Opening Agents<-

**Opening agents** <note>Greek: *Anastomotika*</note> are medicines that unlock the mouths of the vessels. They dilate and enlarge all the channels of the internal parts, such as the veins, arteries, ureters, and intestines; they loosen and separate further those things which are closed or joined together. These should be of a moderate substance <note>Galen describes them as thick, sharp, and biting; original: *Gal. crassa, acri & mordaci*</note>, yet they must be warm so that they may penetrate deeply. They should not be excessively dry, so that they may relax the areas more easily without constricting the pathways.

<summary>This page defines 'Closing Agents,' which use cold and dry properties to stop bleeding, and 'Opening Agents,' which use warmth to dilate internal vessels and clear obstructions.</summary>
<keywords>Closing agents, Opening agents, Armenian bole, Lemnian earth, astringents, vascular health, Galen, medicinal clays</keywords>

**Thinning agents** <note>original: *Attenuantium*; medicines used to break up thick or "gross" fluids like phlegm.</note> are of no small use, for internal conditions as well as for stubborn external ones. Indeed, while they penetrate more deeply as the skin is opened, they not only liquefy cold, thick, and hardened humors by their heat, but through the thinness of their substance, they cut into and thin that very humor so much that it either vanishes of its own accord as breath and vapor, or is at least easily scattered by the force of "Drawing" medicines <note>original: *Trahentium*; substances that pull fluids or toxins toward the surface of the skin.</note>. They are likewise used internally for purging phlegm from the chest, stimulating the menstrual flow, and clearing the passages of the internal organs. However, these should not be used until the stomach and intestines have been purged of bad humors; otherwise, by the use of these thinning agents, those bad humors might be swept into the veins, and thus either further obstruct the organs or stir up fevers.

---

## CHAPTER XI.

### *Thickening Agents.*

A **Thickening agent**, <note>original: *παχυντικὸν* (pachyntikon)</note>, is the name given to that which makes thin, flowing, and liquid humors more solid and compact. It achieves this when its own thick material mixes with those thinner fluids, just as if earth were added to water to create mud. This power resides in a thick and earthy substance that is either cold or temperate in nature, without any sharp or biting quality, such as:
Hypocoon <note>original: *Hypocoon*; likely referring to *Hypecoum*, a plant with juice similar to poppy, used for its cooling and thickening effects.</note>
Henbane <note>original: *Hyoscyamus*; a potent plant used to cool the body and "thicken" the humors to stop excessive flowing or bleeding.</note>

<meta>catchword: Por-</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the list of "simple" medicinal substances and explains the theory behind "thinning" (attenuating) and "thickening" (incrassating) medicines in Galenic practice. It emphasizes the danger of using thinning agents before the digestive tract is cleared, as they may carry toxins into the bloodstream.</summary>

# CHAPTER XII.

## Absorbents.

Once the humor <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance was thought to determine health.</note> has been softened, thinned, and prepared by whatever other means necessary, it must then finally be absorbed and drawn out through the opened pores of the skin, until the entire swelling subsides and the symptoms of the affliction grow mild. Those substances that are powerfully drying act as absorbents; they possess such a great power of thinning and drying that whatever unnatural humor they encounter, they consume it without the need for it to dissolve into liquid.

->Vinegar<-
->Sea water<-
->Lime<- <note>original: *Calx*; likely quicklime or slaked lime, used for its caustic and drying effects.</note>
->Ash<-
->Lye<- <note>original: *Lixivium*; an alkaline solution leached from wood ashes.</note>
->Brine<- <note>original: *Muria*; a concentrated salt solution.</note>
->Oil of { Castoreum, Spurge, Petroleum, the Philosophers<- <note>Oil of the Philosophers (Oleum Philosophorum) was a chemical preparation made by distilling bricks soaked in olive oil, highly prized by alchemists for its "resolving" powers.</note>
->Salt.<-

These are beneficial for edematous <note>original: *oedematosis*; soft swellings caused by an accumulation of watery fluid.</note>, watery, and flatulent <note>original: *flatulentisque*; tumors caused by "wind" or gas trapped in the tissues.</note> tumors. They are also sometimes used for scirrhous <note>original: *scirrhosis*; hard, marble-like swellings.</note> and extremely tough tumors, provided they are in a state of decline and a thorough preparation of softening and thinning has already been applied.

## CHAPTER XIII.

->*Drawing Agents.*<-

Drawing medicines (Greek: *helktika kai odinagika* <note>original: ἑλκτικὰ καὶ ὠδιναγικὰ; terms for substances that pull or draw humors, sometimes also used for those that aid in childbirth.</note>), when applied externally, extract and transfer both watery and somewhat thick humors, as well as "spirits" <note>In Galenic medicine, "spirits" (pneumata) were subtle substances that carried vitality and heat through the body.</note>, from deep within the body to the surface. These are hot and dry, and are composed of thin parts. A substance that is hot and thin to the "second degree" <note>Historical medicine graded the intensity of a medicine's qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—on a scale of one to four.</note> does indeed draw; but that which reaches the "third degree" not only draws, but also dissipates what has been drawn. This is known as a *metasyncritic* <note>original: μετασυγκρίτικον; a term from the Methodic school of medicine referring to a treatment that alters the pores of the body and evokes humors to the surface for dispersal.</note> agent—that is, one that calls forth from the depths and scatters. Furthermore, regarding the power of drawing: some substances have it inherently, such as Dittany, Propolis <note>A resinous mixture produced by honeybees.</note>, Sagapenum <note>A bitter gum-resin from a Persian plant, similar to asafoetida.</note>, and Thapsia <note>Commonly known as "deadly carrot," a plant famous for its intense skin-irritating and drawing effects.</note>; others gain it from putrefaction, such as Yeast, Pigeon dung, Goose dung, and whatever falls from a hotter animal; others still by the similarity of their whole substance, such as all Purgatives and some Alexiterics <note>original: *Alexiteriorum*; medicines used to ward off poisons or contagious infections.</note>.

Drawing agents are recognized by almost the same signs as Thinning agents: since in both there is a thinness of parts and no small amount of heat, they seem to differ only by degree. Yet perhaps this distinguishes them more clearly: thinness of parts is more characteristic of Thinning agents, while heat is more specific to Drawing agents.

**Metals.** Magnet <note>Loadstone, believed to have a physical and spiritual "attraction."</note>

<header>BOOK THE FIRST.</header>

The use of drawing agents <term>Attrahentia: Medicines that pull fluids or "humors" toward the skin's surface.</term> is varied, namely so that the internal organs may be unburdened of corrupt humors. For when these are applied externally, the offending matter is drawn from the inner body to the surface. Nature's "critical efforts" <note>An ancient medical belief that the body undergoes a "crisis" to expel disease; these medicines were thought to help the body's natural drive to push infection out through an abscess or the skin.</note> are assisted by the same logic when drawing agents are applied to abscesses.

# CHAPTER XV.
## Repellents.

**Repellents** <term>Repellentia: Also called "apokroustika" in Greek or "repercussives." These are medicines intended to drive "humors" (excess bodily fluids) away from a site of swelling or inflammation.</term> are diametrically opposed to Drawing Agents. They are defined as those substances which hold back a flowing humor <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids like blood or bile; an "influx" of humor caused swelling.</note>, and which drive back—in the opposite direction—a humor that is flowing in or even one that is lightly settled in a body part.

This effect is achieved through the power of **cold**, the nature of which is to restrain, compress, repel, and push back. The most powerful cold for these purposes is that found in thick and "earthy" substances. This quality is typically detected in substances with a **harsh, tart, and astringent taste**. By pressing upon and tightening the substance of the body part, these agents force the incoming humor to retreat.

|:---|:---|
| **Metals.** | White lead <note>original: "Cerussa"; lead carbonate, used historically to cool inflammation despite its toxicity.</note> |
| | Lead |
| | Red ochre <note>original: "Rubrica fabrilis"; literally "smith's red," a type of iron-rich clay used in medicinal plasters.</note> |
| | Sinopian earth <note>original: "Rubrica sinopica"; a high-quality red earth from Sinope on the Black Sea.</note> |
| | Salt |
| | Salt-foam <note>original: "Salis spuma"; likely the frothy scum from salt production or a specific crystalline form.</note> |
| **Earths.** | Cimolian earth <note>original: "Cimolia"; a type of Fuller's earth or medicinal clay from the island of Cimolus.</note> |
| | Rich earth <note>original: "Pingvis"; literally "fat" or fertile soil, used for cooling poultices.</note> |
| **Roots.** | Ephemerum <note>Likely the wild iris or "spiderwort," used for its cooling properties.</note> |

The most suitable time for using these is at the beginning and during the peak of the illness, when the inflows of humors are certainly at their most vigorous.

## C A P T E R   XVI.

### Ripening Agents.

**Ripening agents** <note>original: "Maturantia"; also known as suppuratives. In humoral medicine, these substances were used to "cook" or mature a "raw" or corrupted humor so that it could be expelled or resolved.</note> are said to be those things which lead vitiated and corrupted humors back into a state more agreeable to nature.

These are moreover twofold: either <term>suppurants</term> <note>original: "ἐκπυητικὰ" [ekpyētika], "Suppurantia"</note>, which move pus by transforming corrupted and putrid blood into refined pus; or <term>maturants</term> <note>original: "πεπαντικὰ" [pepantika], "mitigantia seu concoqventia"; agents that "cook" or ripen the humors</note>, which soothe or ripen both yellow and black putrid bile, as well as phlegm <note>original: "pituitam"</note>. These do not turn the matter into pus, but rather, by suppressing the rot, they convert it into a more benign substance that is less troublesome to the body’s nature. By nature, these agents should be moderately warm and moist.

<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

These are of two kinds: either **Suppurants** <note>original: "ekpyētika"</note>, which induce pus by changing corrupt and putrid blood into refined pus; or **Concoctives** <note>original: "pepastika," also called soothing or ripening agents</note>, which convert putrid <term>bile</term> <note>Yellow and black bile were two of the four "humors" or vital fluids believed to govern health</note>—both yellow and black—as well as <term>phlegm</term>, not into pus, but rather, by restraining the putrefaction, they turn it into a more benign substance that is less troublesome to the body’s nature. By nature, these substances should be moderately warm and moist.

# CHAPTER XVIII.
## Purging Agents.

Purging agents, <term>kathartika</term> <note>original Greek: "καθαρτικὰ"; medicines used to cleanse or evacuate the body</note>, consist in heat and thickness of parts, but to a lesser degree than <term>Abstergents</term> <note>original: "Abstergentia"; highly effective cleansing agents that wipe away surface impurities</note>.

<margin>**Earths**</margin> Melian earth <note>original: "Melia"; a medicinal white clay from the island of Melos</note>.
<margin>**Metals**</margin> Vitriol <note>original: "Atramentum sutorium"; literally "shoemaker's black," an iron or copper sulfate used for its drying and cleansing properties</note>
Chrysocolla <note>original: "Chryfocolla"; a green copper mineral used as a pigment and medicinal powder</note>
Flower of copper <note>original: "Flos Aeris"; fine metallic particles produced during smelting</note>
Melanteria <note>original: "Melanteria"; a mineral related to vitriol, used for its astringency</note>
Nitre <note>original: "Nitrum"; in this period, likely referring to natron or soda (sodium carbonate) rather than modern saltpeter</note>
Salt
Flower of salt <note>original: "Salis flos"; the fine crystals that form on the surface of salt water</note>
Foam of salt
Dross <note>original: "Scoria"; the slag or waste residue of the smelting process</note>
*   of Silver
*   of Lead
Metallic ash <note>original: "Spodium"; the soot or ash residue from furnace chimneys, often used in topical salves</note>
Scales of copper
Antimony <note>original: "Stibium"; a semi-metal used as a purgative and in eye medicines</note>
Sulfur.
<margin>**Stones**</margin> Armenian stone <note>original: "Armenius"; likely azurite, used to treat ailments of the "black bile"</note>
Chalcitis <note>original: "Chalcitis"; a copper-bearing ore or brass-stone</note>
Indian stone <note>original: "Indicus"; likely referring to a type of hematite or magnetite from India</note>
Pumice.
<margin>**Marine substances**</margin> Trumpet shells <note>original: "Buccinæ"; shells of the whelk, used when ground into powder</note>
Purple snails <note>original: "Purpuræ"; shells of the murex snail, known for its dye and medicinal ash</note>.
<margin>**Roots**</margin> Anemone <note>original: "Anemones"</note>
Prickly poppy <note>original: "Argemones"</note>
Round birthwort <note>original: "Ariftolochiæ rotundæ"; named for its historical use in aiding childbirth and cleansing the womb</note>
Cuckoo-pint <note>original: "Aaron"; the root of the Arum maculatum</note>
Swallow-wort <note>original: "Afclepias"</note>

## CHAPTER XIX.
### Corrosives.

Corrosives, <term>καθαιρετικά</term> <note>original: "kathairetika"; from the Greek word meaning 'to take down' or 'diminish'</note>, are the name given to those medicines that consume useless flesh, whether it is decayed or overgrown. They remove polyps, swellings, warts, and calluses—not all at once or suddenly, but by liquefying and gradually wasting the tissue away without causing any corruption or decay to the healthy surrounding flesh. These substances are violently hot, classified in the fourth degree <note>the highest level of intensity in the Galenic system of medicinal properties</note>, and possess a very thin substance, allowing them to penetrate deep into the material they are meant to consume.

<margin>Metals.</margin> Adarce <note>original: "Adarce"; a salty, efflorescent crust found on reeds in marshy waters</note>

# CHAPTER XXI.

->Plastering Agents<- <note>original: "Illinientia"</note>

**Plastering agents**, or **plasters** <note>original: "ἐμπλαστικά" (emplastika)</note>, are **Glutinous**, **Besmearing**, **Smoothing**, **Staining**, and **Stuffing** substances that stand in direct opposition to Cleansing agents <note>detergents</note>. Their constituent parts are bound together so that they adhere to one another with great tenacity. Upon whichever part of the body such a substance is applied, it sticks quite firmly, smears the surface, and even—if the part is hollow or porous—obstructs it; in this way, it is truly a "staining" and "stuffing" agent. When introduced into the internal passages of the body, it blocks them,

### BOOK THE FIRST.

...and fills by stuffing <note>original: "infarctu implet"</note>: when smeared upon the passages of the skin with a fatty or tenacious substance, it adheres like glue and obstructs them just as well. The matter of this kind is in some way intermediate, suffused with much watery or airy moisture, yet it remains tenacious. It is temperate in the balance of heat and cold, having a dry and earthy consistency without the "bite" of a drying agent <note>meaning it lacks the stinging or corrosive quality of harsher desiccants</note>. Of this kind is what they call **Fatty**, which has a somewhat sweet or insipid taste, being neither sharp, nor biting, nor acidic, nor salty, nor bitter.

To restrain the rushes of blood and to check other discharges, we use **Emplastics** <term>Emplastica; substances with a sticky or "plastering" consistency that adhere to the skin</term>; likewise, they are used at times to promote **suppuration** <note>the process of ripening an infection or tumor so that it forms pus and heals</note>. For they block the pores <note>original: "meatus"</note> of the skin and keep in the heat, by which tumors are most effectively ripened. Furthermore, these substances are sometimes mixed with other medicines so that they may be prepared in the form of plasters, and thus adhere more easily and effectively to the parts of the body.

## CHAPTER XXII.
### Flesh-generating agents.

A sarcotic <term>Sarcoticum; from the Greek "sarkos," meaning flesh</term> medicine is one that produces new flesh where it is lacking in a wound or a hollow ulcer, filling the cavity itself with flesh. This is, indeed, a work of nature's own doing. However, any medicine that moderately dries an ulcer and cleanses its filth gently and moderately without biting <note>original: "morsum"; referring to the stinging or corrosive sensation often caused by stronger cleaning agents</note>—since it protects the blood, which is the material for creating flesh, and by removing obstacles, preserves the ulcer in a clean state (or at least in the state it was received)—is called a **Sarcotic**. Such a substance is of moderate consistency, and is moderately warm and dry, being below the second degree <note>Galenic medicine classified the intensity of a substance's qualities—heat, cold, moisture, dryness—into four "degrees" or orders</note>, so that it remains free of sharpness <note>original: "acrimoniae"; referring to a harsh or stinging quality</note>. For something too hot or too thin dissolves the flesh, while something too thick or too cold dries and binds it too much.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### Glutinants <term>Glutinantia; medicines that act as "biological glue" to fuse wound edges</term>.

A glutinant—or *kolletikon* <note>Greek: κολλητικόν; literally "gluing"</note>—is a medicine that joins together the brought-together edges of a fresh wound and restores them to their original wholeness. It achieves this by preventing fluid from either flowing into or growing between the edges as they attempt to close. To do this, the medicine must be astringent <note>having a tightening or contracting effect on tissues</note>, composed of a thick and earthy substance, and dry in the second degree <note>referring to the Galenic scale of intensity, where the 2nd degree is moderate—stronger than a mild effect but not corrosive</note>. It must also be temperate in its heat, so that it causes no pain through harsh cleansing or sharpness. The way to recognize these substances is established by the rules for astringents and driers.

# CHAPTER XXIV.
## Agents that Induce Scarring.

A scar-inducing agent—known as an *epulotic* <note>original: "ἐπουλωτικόν"</note> in Greek, or called *cicatrizative* by the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbaris"; a term used by Renaissance scholars to refer to Medieval or non-Classical medical authors whose Latin was considered "unrefined."</note>—is a substance that powerfully dries the surface flesh of a wound that has already been filled in, forcing it to form a scar very similar to skin. It is exceedingly dry, so that it may consume moisture; it is also of a thicker substance so that it may bind, contract, and thicken the flesh. It possesses no heat, but partakes of a certain coldness, and is entirely free from any stinging or biting sensation. These differ from "Gluing" agents only in being more or less intense in these qualities.

**Earths.** Armenian bole <note>original: "Armenia"; a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent.</note>

## CHAPTER XXIV.

### *Agents that Induce Scars.*

A scar-inducer—known as an *epulotic* <note>original Greek: "ἐπουλωτικὸν"</note> or called a *cicatrizative* by the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbaris"; a term used by Renaissance scholars to refer to Medieval or Scholastic authorities who did not use classical Latin.</note>—is a substance that powerfully dries the surface flesh of an ulcer that has already been filled in, forcing it to form a scar very similar to the skin. It is extremely dry, so as to consume excess moisture; it is also of a thicker consistency, so as to bind, contract, and densify the flesh. It possesses no heat, but rather partakes in a certain coldness, and is entirely free of any stinging or biting quality. These substances differ from "gluing agents" only in the degree of their intensity.

ON THE POWERS OF SIMPLE MEDICINES

# CHAPTER XXV.
## Putrefying Agents.

A **Putrefying Medicine**, called *Septikon* <note>original Greek: "Σηπτικόν"</note> or a **Corrupting agent**, is properly defined as that which, by the extreme sharpness of its heat, either dissipates our innate heat or converts it into a fiery state. At the same time, through a malignant quality, it dissolves the primordial moisture <note>The "primordial moisture" (humidum primigenium) was believed by early physicians to be the essential fluid that fueled life and vitality.</note>, wastes away and melts the entire substance of the affected part, and induces rot accompanied by a foul stench. This effect is produced by a substance of the highest heat with a moderately thick consistency; for a thinner substance can be easily overcome and dissipated by our own natural heat.

->Monkshood <note>original: "Aconitum."</note><-
->Pure Arsenic<-
->Sublimated Arsenic<-
->Orpiment <note>original: "Auripigmentum"; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note><-
->Cedar liquor<-
->Chrysocolla <note>A mineral often associated with copper; used here as a corrosive.</note><-
->Oak fern <note>original: "Dryopteris."</note><-
->Pine caterpillar <note>original: "Pityocampe"; the larvae of the pine processionary moth, known to cause severe skin irritation and necrosis.</note><-
->Sandarac <note>original: "Sandaracha"; in this medical context, it likely refers to "red arsenic" (realgar) rather than the plant resin.</note><-

Remedies of this kind are to be utterly abolished. Everything that needs to be removed or consumed should be treated instead with <term>Detergents</term> (cleansing agents), <term>Catheretics</term> (corrosives), <term>Escharotics</term> (scar-forming agents), or <term>Caustics</term> (burning agents) without such destruction to the patient. Or, if the patient is not overly fearful and possesses a steady mind and physical strength, those tissues should be demolished by incision or by the **falling iron** <note>original: "cadenti ferro"; a poetic or traditional term for the surgical scalpel.</note>, by which no foreign quality is introduced into the body. For the use of these putrefying agents is altogether dangerous and unnecessary for surgery, as they are destructive without providing any benefit. Unlike **Caustics**, they do not burn the part they touch or induce a protective crust (scab); rather, they leave the area they have corrupted in such a state that it must still be cut out by the surgeon's art.

<meta>catchword: CA- (likely beginning "CAUSTICA" or "CALIDUS")</meta>

<summary>This page defines and warns against "Putrefying Agents," substances that cause tissue rot and foul stenches. The author lists several dangerous materials, including arsenic and toxic plants, and argues they should be replaced by safer surgical methods or controlled chemical corrosives.</summary>

BOOK ONE.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

->Burning Agents<-

**Burning things**, called *Pyrotika* <note>original Greek: "Πυρωτικά"</note>, are those substances possessed of such vehement heat that they burn the skin no differently than boiling water or fire. These are distinguished by their own degrees (since they are all contained under a single category), so that some are milder, such as **Blistering agents** and **Scab-forming agents**; others are more powerful, such as **Caustics**. We use the latter for <term>Cauteries</term> <note>The application of a branding iron or caustic chemical to sear tissue.</note>, and the former for <term>Phænigmos</term> <note>original Greek: "φοινιγμός"; a treatment meant to redden the skin by drawing blood to the surface.</note>, **Pitch plasters** <note>original: "Dropaces"; medical plasters made of pitch and oil used to stimulate the skin or remove hair.</note>, and similar applications.

A **Blistering agent** <note>original: "Vesicans."</note> works in a similar way, but more lightly and sluggishly, because by the force of its heat it draws out moisture and only excites pustules <note>blisters</note>.

A **Scab-forming agent** <note>original: "Escharoticum"; also called an escharotic.</note> burns much more powerfully, causing ulceration so that it produces crusts <note>eschars</note>, yet it does not penetrate beneath the skin. Both of these belong to the highest and fourth order of hot substances; however, a Blistering agent consists of a thin substance, while a Scab-forming agent consists of a thick and dense substance.

A **Caustic** <note>original: "Causticum."</note> dissolves and breaks through not only the outer skin <note>original Greek: "ἐπιδερμίδα" (epidermida).</note> as the Scab-forming agent does, but also the true skin as well. Sometimes it even penetrates into the underlying flesh like a cauterizing iron—not indeed by gradually melting and eating it away, but by suddenly burning it, resulting in the formation of a thicker crust. This is more powerful than a Scab-forming agent, being endowed with a most fervent heat within a thick and earthy substance.

Burning agents are distinguished more by touch than by taste; for they are of such a nature that they scrape away and consume thick skin and the hardest of tumors.

<margin>Metals and Minerals.</margin> Adarces <note>A salty, crust-like substance found around reeds in Galatia.</note>
Verdigris <note>original: "Aerugo"; the green rust of copper.</note>
Burnt copper <note>original: "Aes ustum."</note>

We sometimes use burning agents to revive parts of the body that are dried out, wasting away, and nearly lifeless. Likewise, they are used for removing hair, and for treating hard and callous tumors, small swellings, warts, polyps, and similar growths. They are also beneficial for long-lasting diseases, such as for those suffering from gout, chronic headaches, and other "cold and moist" conditions of the brain <note>In early modern medicine, the brain was thought to be susceptible to an excess of cold, damp humors which required "hot" treatments to balance.</note>. They also check fistulas and suppress malignant ulcers. However, these agents must be used with caution and care, lest they trigger fevers or convulsions.

# CHAPTER XXVII.

->*Pain-Relieving Agents.*<-

Since the cause of pain is quite varied, anything that removes the cause truly settles the pain; however, such a thing is not necessarily called an Anodyne <note>original: "Anodynum"; a term derived from the Greek for "without pain."</note>. Rather, those things are properly considered Anodynes or **soothing agents** <note>original Greek: παρηγώρικα (paregorika), from which we get the modern term "paregoric."</note> which specifically target the pain itself, mitigating it even while the underlying cause and the disease remain. These are certainly moderate in heat, similar to our own bodies, and of a subtle essence—or at least not so hot that...

We soothe pain most especially at the time when danger threatens. Indeed, it often happens that we must set aside the underlying cause of a disease to focus on that which is most urgent; this is done so that the disease is not made worse by the pain, or so that other symptoms do not follow which are even more severe than the disease itself. The usefulness of Anodynes <note>Pain-relieving medicines.</note> is as great as the hardships caused by excessive pain.

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

## Numbing Agents.

Numbing agents, termed <term>Narcotics</term> <note>original Greek: Ναρκωτικά (Narkotika); substances that induce a state of stupor.</note> or <term>Hypnotics</term> <note>original Greek: Ὑπνωτικά (Hypnotika); sleep-inducing agents.</note>, should not be called Anodynes. This is because they do not actually remove or mitigate the pain; rather, they induce a numbness in the body parts, or they steal away the senses by bringing on sleep. In this way, no matter how great the pain may be, it does not affect the parts of the body, making them as if they were dead. All such substances are intensely "cold" in their nature <note>In ancient medicine, diseases were treated by balancing "humors." Pain was often seen as "hot," so "cold" medicines like opium or hemlock were used to counteract it by slowing down the body's vital heat.</note>, but they take away sensation not merely through coldness, but through a specific property.

<margin>Stones.</margin> Jasper
Memphis stone <note>original: "Memphites"; a type of Egyptian limestone believed to have local anesthetic properties when applied to the skin.</note>
Serpentine <note>original: "Ophites"; a mottled green stone named for its resemblance to snakeskin.</note>
<margin>Roots.</margin> Mandrake <note>original: "Mandragoræ"</note>
<margin>Leaves.</margin> Hemlock <note>original: "Cicula" (likely a misspelling of Cicuta); a highly poisonous plant used in small doses as a powerful sedative.</note>

---

We use numbing agents <note>original: "Obstupefacientibus"; substances that stun or dull the senses</note> in cases of the most violent pain, which we can settle neither with warming nor with soothing remedies. If these are consumed a little too freely, they even bring about death; for this reason, they are referred to as <term>Deleterious</term> <note>original Greek: "δηλητήρια" (deleteria); meaning poisonous or life-threatening</note> when used in such quantities. One must take care, however, that they are never applied to the vital organs—such as the Brain, the Heart, or the Liver—nor should they be given to children, the elderly, pregnant women, or others of a weakened constitution.

# CHAPTER XXIX.

->Poisons.<- <note>original: "Deleteria"; substances that are inherently destructive or fatal to the human body</note>

Those substances that kill a human being either by contact or through erosion must be considered **Poisons** to the entire human race. For these putrefying agents, even if they are consumed in the smallest amount, cause total corruption unless they are excreted along with waste products before they can inflict injury upon the body, or unless they are mixed with food or other substances that dull their potency.

# CHAPTER XXX.

->Substances that resist poisons.<-

Antidotes and counter-medicines <note>original: "Antipharmaca"</note> are the plain opposites of deleterious substances. Some of these resist poisons by a manifest quality <note>referring to the observable qualities of heat, cold, dryness, or moisture</note>; others resist through a hidden property <note>original: "occulta"; a "total substance" power that could not be explained by the four basic qualities</note> and a natural opposition of their entire substance, so changing and blunting the poisons that they are thereafter unable to harm us in the slightest.
<margin>**Earths.**</margin> Armenian bole <note>original: "Armenia"; a medicinal clay used to treat sores and counteract toxins</note>
Lemnian earth <note>original: "Lemnia"; a famous "sealed earth" or clay from the island of Lemnos, prized as a universal antidote</note>

<meta>catchword: Meli- (likely referring to Melitite earth or Melissa)</meta>

# CHAPTER I.

Tertiary Qualities are said to be those that are not directly traced back to the primary qualities <note>the four basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, but to the secondary ones, and through those intermediaries, to the primary ones. Thus, for example, "Hidrotics" <note>original: "Hidrotica"; sweat-inducing medicines</note> are not directly traced back to "hot" qualities, but to secondary qualities, which are thinning, digesting, and making porous <note>original: "rarefacere"; to make the skin or humors less dense to allow passage</note>.

<header>ON THE POWERS OF SIMPLE MEDICINES</header>

## CHAPTER III.

->Milk-producing substances.<-

Since milk is produced from the blood, there is no doubt that to increase the quantity of milk, the blood must be increased. Specifically, those substances are properly said to generate milk which produce a large amount of high-quality blood and, through a moderate power of "cutting," <note>original: "incidendi facultate." In early medicine, this referred to the ability of a substance to thin thick "humors" or fluids, allowing them to flow more easily through the body's channels.</note> direct it toward the breasts. These substances are therefore moderately warm and composed of fine particles. They are identified by a fatty or sweet taste, combined with a certain sharp or pungent quality, which is otherwise required for the enrichment of the blood.

# CHAPTER IV.

### *Spermatics: those things that generate Semen or stimulate Venus.* <note>original: "Venerem stimulantia"; substances that arouse sexual desire, named after Venus, the Roman goddess of love.</note>

Just as milk takes its origin from the blood, so too does semen. They differ, however, in this regard: the former <note>milk-producing substances</note> consist of better juices, whereas the latter <note>semen-producing substances</note> make the blood more "flatulent." <note>In Galenic medicine, "flatulent" (flatuosa) does not just mean digestive gas; it refers to the "windy" or "airy" spirits required to cause the physical expansion or erection of the male organs.</note> For this power exists within the semen so that, once warmed by the vital spirits, it distends the male member. These substances should be moist and tempered with heat, and they should possess a thicker and more viscous substance than those which generate milk. They should not be drying, but rather airy and slightly sharp if they are intended to provoke desire at the same time, so that the semen itself becomes more pungent.

## CHAPTER X.

->Diuretics.<- <note>Medicines that stimulate the production and flow of urine.</note>

Those things which stimulate urine, by the thinness of their substance and their dryness, thin and dissolve the blood; they separate the watery serum <note>The "serum" was understood in Galenic medicine as the watery byproduct of blood that needs to be expelled through the kidneys.</note> and lead it down into the Kidneys. In this category, some are said to be moderately cold, such as Pumpkins, Melons <note>original: "Pepones, Melopepones"; these were considered "cold" because of their high water content.</note> etc.; but the most effective of all are those which are hot and dry at the third degree of intensity <note>original: "3º recessu"; medicines were graded from 1 to 4 based on how much they altered the body's natural temperament.</note> through the thinness of their substance, such as Celery, Parsley, etc. They are recognized by their sharp taste.

### CHAPTER XI.

->Ornaments (Cosmetics)<-

**Cosmetics** <note>original Greek: "Koσμƞτική" (Kosmētikē)</note> is the name given to those things by which beauty and the dignity of form are provided to the body.

| These [ornaments] apply either to: | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | **The skin of the entire body** | |
| | **To parts that are exposed to the eyes of observers, such as:** | 1. The whole face |
| | | 2. The beard |
| | | 3. The hair |
| | | 4. The teeth and [gums] |
| | | 5. The hands |

The body may be defiled by filth, spots, or an unnatural color; or small swellings may break out; or the skin may be contracted by wrinkles or scars; or it may swell into excessive tumors.

Filth adhering either to the hands, the face, or the teeth is cleared away by **cleansing agents** <term>Abstergentibus: substances used to wipe away or purge impurities from the surface</term>. Likewise, skin eruptions <note>original: "Impetigines"; likely referring to scabby, itchy, or scale-like skin conditions</note> and spots are removed by these same agents or by moderate **astringents** <term>Adstringentibus: medicines that contract body tissues to reduce secretions or redness</term>.

For redness of the face, there are various remedies depending on the various causes: if the blood is too hot, it is tempered with **cooling agents**; if it is too agitated, it is driven back with **astringents**; if it is too thick and lodged in the skin, it is dispersed with **thinning agents** <term>Extenuantibus: remedies used to "thin" thick humors or reduce the density of a substance in the body</term>. Redness on the outer surface, appearing like spots, is cured with **wiping agents** <term>Tergentibus: cleansing agents similar to abstergents, focused on surface purification</term>. Pustules <note>original: "Pustulæ"; pimples or small inflammatory sores</note> are classified as actual diseases. We generally restore wrinkles to a proper smoothness of the skin using **relaxants**, **soothing agents**, and **emollients** <term>Emollientibus: substances that soften and soothe the skin, often used to reduce hardness or tension</term>.

<meta>catchword: Scars- <note>original: "Cica-", likely referring to "Cicatrices" (scars) which the author mentions in the text and will likely elaborate on the following page.</note></meta>

<summary>This page defines the field of "Cosmetics" within Galenic medicine, categorizing treatments for the skin, hair, and face based on their mechanical and humoral effects. It provides a systematic approach to treating blemishes, wrinkles, and redness using specific classes of medicinal actions.</summary>
<keywords>cosmetics, dermatology, cleansing agents, astringents, emollients, facial redness, skin care, Galenic medicine</keywords>

--- Page 269 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of cosmetic treatments (ornaments) begun on page 234, detailing the specific medicinal actions required for scars, facial texture, hair, and teeth, before transitioning into a new section on the general "fourth qualities" of simple medicines categorized by their effect on the body's systems.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

Scars are corrected by those things which strongly both dry and constrict <term>Adstringunt: substances that tighten or shrink tissues</term>.

Puffiness of the face <note>original: "Crassities"; refers to a thickening or coarseness of the facial features or a lack of definition</note> is corrected by **rarefying agents** <term>Rarefacientibus: substances that make the skin less dense or more porous to allow fluids to escape</term> or even by **drying agents**.

We grow hair using medicines which, through a mild heat, draw in proper nourishment and retain it with a moderate constriction. Hair is preserved by almost the same means. It is forcefully removed by strong **cleansers**; these are called **psilothra** <note>original: "ψίλωθρα" (psilōthra); a Greek term for depilatory agents used to remove unwanted hair</note> by the Greeks. Hair is made curly by things that are strongly drying and constricting, so that the strands of hair are contracted both by a lack of moisture and by the tightening effect.

**Dandruff** of the head <note>original: "Furfures"; literally "bran," referring to the scaly flakes of skin on the scalp</note> is removed by **dispersing agents** and **cleansers**.

**Teeth** are purified by **cleansers** and strengthened by **astringents**.

# SECTION VI.
## ON THE FOURTH QUALITIES OF SIMPLE MEDICINES.

## CHAPTER I.

**Fourth Qualities** <term>Qualitates Quartae: In traditional medicine, these are the "specific" properties of a drug that target a particular organ, beyond its general heating or cooling effects</term> are what we call those powers by which medicines—although they act by means of the primary and secondary qualities <note>Primary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry; secondary qualities include tastes like bitter or sweet</note>—nevertheless act upon some specific organ or a specific **humor** <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>.

->**Medicines that Strengthen the whole Body.**<-

These are the things which generate good blood and cleanse it from waste products; likewise, they are things which clarify and assist the **spirits** <term>Spiritus: the vital, subtle substances that were believed to circulate through the body to sustain life and thought</term>.

## CHAPTER II.
->**Head Medicines** <note>original: "Kephalika" (Greek)</note><-

Although the brain is refreshed by both music and paintings, these are not counted among the "cephalics" <note>Medicines for the head</note> because they are not drugs. There are, therefore, so many classes of head medicines that some heat the brain, others cool it, others purge it, and finally, others strengthen it; these are distinguished according to the brain’s specific ailments. Furthermore, these medicines are beneficial either because they oppose these diseases through a certain **antipathy** <note>original: "antipatheia" (Greek); a natural or hidden opposition between the medicine and the disease</note>, or because they fortify the brain in its whole substance against the malignant powers of diseases.

->*Medicines that Heat the Head.*<-

Sweet Flag <note>original: "Calamus aromaticus"</note>
Fennel

### CHAPTER IV.

#### Cleansing the Head.

The Brain is cleansed either through the nostrils, and these are called **Errhines** <note>medicines applied to the nasal passages to clear mucus</note>: or through sneezing, or through the palate, and these are called **Apophlegmatisms** <note>remedies chewed or held in the mouth to draw out "phlegm" or excess fluids</note>.

## CHAPTER VI.
### Pectorals.

Pectorals <note>Remedies specifically for the chest and respiratory system</note> are those substances which loosen and soften when applied externally; or they cut through and clear away humors <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to cause illness if unbalanced</note> that have become stuck in the passages of the lungs; or they thicken thin, runny discharges; or they temper sharp irritations and soothe the roughness of the windpipe <note>original: "arteriæ"; in early modern medicine, this term often referred to the trachea or bronchial tubes, as they were thought to carry air</note>. Here, one must beware of astringents <note>substances that shrink or constrict body tissues</note> as they are most harmful to the chest and lungs, both because they inhibit breathing and because they delay the coughing up of phlegm.

# CHAPTER IX.

## Cardiac Remedies <note>original: "Καρδιακα" (Kardiaka)</note>

The powers of cardiac remedies are chiefly to drive away all harmful and malignant influences and to bestow strength upon the Heart. Of those things which drive away the malignancy of the Heart, some are hot in nature, while others are cold.

# CHAPTER XI.
## Stomachics, or Gastric Remedies.

Medicines that are suitable for the Stomach either stimulate the appetite, aid weak digestion <note>original: "concoctionem"; the process by which the body "cooks" or matures food into humors</note>, or strengthen the retentive faculty <note>the body's ability to hold food long enough for digestion to occur</note>. The appetite is stimulated mostly by acidic things seasoned with a pleasant flavor; sometimes also by Orectics <note>original: "Orectica," from the Greek word for appetite; these are specific stimulants for hunger</note>, through which bile or other putrid humors are purged, namely those which contract the throat and stomach with a certain acidic force and delight with a pleasant taste. Those aid digestion which, either by a suitable warmth or an aromatic quality, foster the heat of the Stomach; or strengthen the stomach through some occult property <note>In early modern science, an "occult property" was a hidden power of a substance that could not be explained by the basic qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>. An impaired retentive faculty produces nausea, vomiting, and flows of the bowels <note>diarrhea</note>. It is corrected by astringents—not all of them, but those in which there is some power that makes them acceptable to the Stomach.

### Warm Stomachics.

<margin>Marine</margin> Amber <note>original: "Succinum"; fossilized resin used for its warming and strengthening effects</note>.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->Hepatic Remedies.<-

# CHAPTER XV.

## Splenic Remedies.

Medicines suitable for the Spleen <note>original: "Lien"</note> are those which, through a certain pleasantness, either soften or in some way liquefy, cleanse, and thin its earthy humor <note>referring to black bile, which was thought to be "earthy" in nature</note> without causing noticeable constriction. This is done so that once the obstruction is cleared, the humor may more easily pass into the bowels. Some of these are moderately cold and moist, which are suitable for cases where excessive bile has become scorched; however, most are moderately warm and consist of thin parts, so that they may thin and dissipate the thick and dreg-like melancholy.

### Warm Splenic Remedies.

<margin>Roots.</margin> Sweet Flag <note>original: "Acori"</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Celery <note>original: "Apii"; likely Smallage or Wild Celery</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Round Birthwort. <note>original: "Aristolochiæ rot."</note>

# CHAPTER XV.

## Splenic Remedies.
<note>original: "Splenica"; medicines intended to treat the spleen (lien).</note>

Remedies suitable for the Spleen are those which, by a certain sweetness, either soften or in some way liquefy, cleanse, and thin out its earthy humor <note>referring to the "black bile" or "melancholy" humor, which was thought to be heavy and earth-like</note>, without any noticeable astringency. This is done so that, once the obstruction is cleared, the humor may more easily pass into the bowels. Some of these are moderately cold and moist, which are appropriate for excessive, parched bile; however, most are moderately warm and consist of "thin parts" <note>substances with a light, penetrating molecular structure</note>, so that they may thin out and dissipate thick and dreg-filled melancholy.

### *Warm Splenic Remedies.*

## CHAPTER XVII.
->Warm Nephretic and Cystic Remedies.<-

Based on the very nature of the kidneys and the bladder and their specific diseases, those medicines are properly called <term>Nephretic</term> <note>relating to the kidneys</note> and <term>Cystic</term> <note>relating to the bladder</note> which soothe and, through moderate heat, cut into and thin [thick humors]. Beyond the power they possess to cut (in which respect they may be classified under <term>Diuretics</term> <note>agents that increase urine production</note>, which were discussed above), those which break and shatter stones are endowed with a specific property to crush stones that are even quite hard. This distinction must be observed in their use: since the bladder is further from the center of the body than the kidneys, stronger medications must be prescribed for it, lest their strength vanish before they reach the affected area.

->*Warm Nephretic and Cystic Remedies.*<-

<margin>Stone.</margin>
Jewish stone. <note>original: "Lapis judaicus"; fossilized spines of sea urchins, which were historically ground into powder and used to dissolve kidney and bladder stones.</note>

# CHAPTER IX.
## Uterine Remedies. <note>original: "Hysterica"; from the Greek 'hystera' for womb. In this era, 'hysterical' referred broadly to health conditions originating in the uterus.</note>

Regarding those things which are handed down as beneficial to the Uterus: some stop its immoderate flow; others move it when it is suppressed; others wash away and purge the uterus of a collection of foul humors; and others strengthen it. Such remedies ought to be judged by their sweet odor or aromatic flavor, which reveal the refinement of their substance.

BOOK ONE.

Blood-movers <note>original: "Hæmagoga"; medicines that stimulate blood flow or menstruation</note>. Chapter 11

## CONCOCTING OR DIGESTIVE MEDICINES.

### CHAPTER I.

We use digestives either to aid concoction <note>In early medicine, "concoction" refers to the process where the body's heat matures or "cooks" a raw humor so it can be expelled</note>, or to prepare the humors or the body for a better and easier removal. Thus, cold and moist substances "digest" bile <note>Specifically yellow bile, which was seen as hot and dry</note>. This is because they diminish the external heat of the body parts and restore them to a moderate state, which allows for better concoction. Likewise, by chance, syrups (which we will discuss in their proper place) can temper excessively hot matter or the heat of the body parts.

Melancholy <note>Black bile</note> is either present in the veins without fever, or without obstruction; or it arises from the blood, or from the "burning" <note>original: "adustione"; the overheating and thickening of a humor</note> of any humor. For this reason, we use either moistening substances, or those that are moderately warm and gently "opening" <note>medicines that open the pores or vessels</note> in cases of obstruction; or we use Cordials <note>medicines intended to strengthen the heart</note>. 

As phlegm <note>original: "Pituita"</note> is varied, so are the medicines that digest it. "Sweet" phlegm is digested by substances that are slightly cutting <note>original: "incidentia"; technical terms for medicines that break up thick, sticky fluids</note> and warm. "Acidic" phlegm requires more cutting and warmer agents. To these, "glassy" phlegm <note>a very thick, viscous, and transparent variety of phlegm</note> is added, requiring an increase in heat and thinning. Finally, for "watery" phlegm, because it is already thin, we do not use very cutting agents, but rather those that are warm enough to achieve concoction.

# ON SIMPLE
# *purgative medicines.*

## CHAPTER IV.

Medicines draw out the humors <note>the four vital fluids of the body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> in various ways: some by dissolving and attracting them; some by softening and soothing; others by cleansing; some by stimulating the body's natural forces; and at times they are seen to purge through their binding or astringent nature. 

Those, however, which are properly named **Purgatives**, possess another power beyond these faculties: through an innate property, they draw out and attract a specific humor even from the most distant parts of the body. Practical experience has noted three ranks of Purgatives. 

The first is the **Malignant**, which contain a poisonous force and substance, such as Bitter Apple <note>original: "Colocynthis"; a powerful and harsh laxative</note>, Scammony <note>original: "Scammonium"; a resinous root used for vigorous purging</note>, and others of that kind. 

The second is the **Benign**, which differ very little from the nature of food; such as Prunes, Manna <note>a sweet tree sap</note>, Violets, Whey, and the pulp of Cassia. 

The third is the **Moderate**; although these draw and eject humors, they are nonetheless harmless, provided the person taking them does not exceed the proper limit. By more recent Physicians, these are called **Harmless**, such as Black Cassia, Myrobalans <note>original: "Myrobalani"; astringent plum-like fruits from India used to purge different humors</note>, Tamarinds, Rhubarb, Agaric <note>original: "Agaricus"; a medicinal fungus grown on larch trees</note>, Senna, Aloe, Dodder of Thyme <note>original: "Epithymum"</note>, Polypody <note>original: "Polypodium"; a type of fern</note>, and so on.

<sig>S 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: Furthermore</meta>

<summary>This page concludes a list of simple medicinal ingredients and introduces Chapter IV, which classifies purgative medicines into three categories based on their intensity: malignant, benign, and moderate/harmless.</summary>

<keywords>purgatives, humors, malignant medicines, benign medicines, pharmacology, bitter apple, scammony, rhubarb, senna, aloe</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of purgative medicines from Chapter IV, detailing how specific substances target different humors, and begins Chapter V with a list of ingredients that specifically soften the bowels.</meta>

ON THE FACULTIES OF SIMPLE MEDICINES.

Furthermore, among those medicines that move the bowels <note>original: "Alvum movent"; referring to laxatives or purgatives</note>, some expel yellow bile, some black bile <note>original: "Melancholiam"</note>, some phlegm <note>original: "Pituitam"</note>, and others discharge thin and watery humors.

Note: The Ancient physicians believed that all purgatives were hot in nature, and because of this, some attributed the power of purging to heat itself. However, it is known from the experience of more recent doctors that the power to purge exists in some substances that are either cold or, at the very least, possess very little heat.

### Simple medicines that draw out bile, *cholagogues*. <note>original: "χολάγωγα" (cholagoga); from the Greek words for 'bile' and 'to lead/draw out'</note>

## CHAPTER XI.

->**Hemagogues**, that is, substances that cleanse the blood from<-
->putrid, salty, watery, and **burnt humors**.<-
<note>In the medical theory of the time, "burnt" (adust) humors were thought to result from excess heat, leading to melancholic or toxic conditions.</note>

These are called "blood-drawers" <note>original: "Sangvinem ducentia"</note> not because they physically draw the blood out of the body; rather, they either purge the blood of corrupt humors (for which reason almost all purges can be said to "cleanse" the blood), or because the vehemence of their action draws blood during <term>hypercatharsis</term> <note>an episode of excessive or violent purging</note>, or they move the blood—once it has been thinned and warmed—toward the outlets of the veins.

And so, kind Reader, with the help of God, the Best and Greatest, we conclude this first part of this Treasury, which concerned the properties of **Simple Medicines.** For we cannot rightly understand the **Compound medicines** themselves unless we first have a clear and thorough knowledge of the powers of **Simple Medicines.** By following the order of nature, we intended to address these in this first book; subsequently, in the following book, we shall discuss the theory and method of mixing these simples in various ways, namely, concerning **Compounds.** If anyone desires more information on this subject, let him read the most learned books of Galen, *On the Properties of Simple Medicines* <note>original Greek: "περὶ τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεων"</note>, as well as the works of Dioscorides, Avicenna, Mesue, Serapion, Aetius, and others who have written extensively and expertly on this topic.

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF MEDICINES,
## BOOK TWO.
### SECTION I.
#### ON THE COMPOSITION OF MEDI-
#### *cines in general.*
#### CHAPTER I.

A compound medicine is so named, not
because it emerged as such by its own origin, but because by
our art and industry it consists of a mixture of many things.
Thus, Composition is nothing other than a mixing together
of several simples <note>In early modern medicine, "simples" (Latin: *simplicia*) referred to individual natural ingredients—such as a single herb, mineral, or animal product—used as the base for more complex recipes.</note>. Moreover, there was a great necessity for mixing
and compounding medicines, both for simple
and for complex diseases.
1. Because of the scarcity of a simple. When, of course, a
simple is lacking that is entirely opposed to the disease, in its absence
we use a compound, the powers of which are equal to the disease.

<vocab>Medicine, Composition, Simples, Disease, Scarcity, Pharmacology</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces the concept of compound medicines, defining them as human-made mixtures of natural "simples." It argues that compounds are necessary when a single natural ingredient is unavailable or not powerful enough to counteract a specific disease.</summary>
<keywords>pharmacology, compound medicines, simples, medical composition, disease treatment, early modern medicine</keywords>

--- Page 328 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Composition of Medicines" from page 393. It elaborates on the second, third, and fourth reasons why medicinal "simples" are mixed into compound remedies, focusing on correcting ingredient flaws, targeting specific organs, and addressing complex diseases.</meta>

->### ON THE COMPOSITION OF MEDICINES.<-

2. Because of a faulty simple, which is either weak or harmful: a weak one is stimulated by the mixture of something sharper, such as <term>Rhubarb</term> with <term>Spikenard</term> <note>original: "Rhabarb. Spicâ"; Spikenard was often added to Rhubarb to enhance its digestive properties.</note> etc.; a harmful or wicked one is blunted by the mixture of something more benign.

3. Based on the substance, location, prominence, and sensitivity of the affected part. For when a part is dense and located far from the remedies, such as the <term>Kidney</term>, <term>Uterus</term>, etc., we mostly mix thinning agents with the Base <note>The "Base" (Latin: *Basis*) refers to the primary active ingredient in a medical recipe.</note>, which may penetrate there; and often others which, by their similarity of substance, direct the Base—that is, the principal simple medicine—to that place, such as <term>Betony</term> for <term>Cephalics</term> <note>original: "Cephalicis Betonicam"; remedies for the head.</note>, <term>Hyssop</term> for <term>Pulmonics</term> <note>original: "Pulmonicis Hyssopum"; remedies for the lungs.</note>, <term>Bugloss</term> for <term>Cardiacs</term> <note>original: "Cardiacis Buglossum"; remedies for the heart.</note>, <term>Agrimony</term> for <term>Hepatics</term> <note>original: "Hepaticis Agrimoniam"; remedies for the liver.</note>, <term>Hart's-tongue Fern</term> for <term>Splenics</term> <note>original: "Splenicis Scolopendriam"; remedies for the spleen.</note>, and <term>Mugwort</term> for <term>Hysterics</term> <note>original: "Hystericis Arthemisiam"; remedies for the womb.</note>. Thus a noble part or one of exquisite sensitivity also requires something familiar to its entire substance to be mixed in, which preserves itself and its own strength; for this reason, medicines adapted for the internal organs are supported by strengthening agents.

4. Most of all in the variety of conditions. Since no single simple has the power to drive out a compound condition, as many simples must be mixed as there are faculties desired, so that each condition may be driven out individually. Furthermore, the form of the Medicine is also useful, because solids draw more powerfully, while liquids penetrate and wash away more conveniently.

Furthermore, pleasantness <note>In early modern pharmacy, "jucunditas" referred to the palatability or "agreeableness" of a medicine to ensure the patient could keep it down.</note> is to be provided for Medicines as far as possible, provided it does not take away their power and faculty: for bitter and horrific things are neither easily taken nor kept down; instead, they upset the stomach <note>original: "Ventriculum"; specifically the stomach or "little belly."</note>, disturb the body, and often drain the strength through fainting of the spirit. Pleasantness is provided through smell, taste, and color.
