## Chapter II.

In the **composition** of any medicine, four things are generally required: 1. Those which drive away the **Disease**, the cause of the disease, and the **Symptoms**. 2. Those without which the former cannot remove or root out preternatural affections or constitutions <note>In early medicine, "preternatural" referred to anything "contrary to nature," such as illness or injury.</note>. 3. Those through which the primary and principal ingredients might more easily, swiftly, and effectively assist nature, providing help to dissolve, remove, and eradicate the disease. 4. Those which cherish and preserve the entire **form** of the compound, protecting and preventing it from corruption <note>This refers to preservatives or stabilizers that kept the medicine from spoiling.</note>. Let us speak briefly of each.

## Chapter III

Those medicines which drive away the Disease, the cause of the disease, and the symptoms, are called by Physicians the **Root** or the **Base** <note>original: "Radicem seu Basim"</note> of a compound. This is the ingredient from which the first or principal action of the medicine proceeds, and for the sake of which all the other ingredients are added. These medicines are mixed either from **homogeneous** <note>Ingredients of a similar nature.</note> or **heterogeneous** <note>Ingredients of a different nature.</note> substances. Furthermore, a **Base** is either simple or multiple. Indeed, it is varied whenever required by the **preternatural dispositions** <note>original Greek: "αἱ διαθέσεις παρὰ φύσιν"; refers to the underlying pathological state of the body.</note>, the **affected parts** <note>original Greek: "τὰ πεπονθότα μόρια"; the specific organs or areas suffering from the illness.</note>, or the **drugs** <note>original: "pharmaca"</note> themselves. One of these causes alone, or two or three together, may indicate that the Root needs to be increased, intensified, and varied by adding more ingredients, or conversely, that it should be softened and diminished.

## Chapter V.

The preternatural affections themselves cause the Base to vary, either because of the vehemence and magnitude of the disease, or because of the **timing** of the disease. For some medicines are suited for the beginning of a disease, while others...

It explains that a medicine's core must be adjusted based on the severity, location, and progression of the illness.</summary>

...varied <note>The text continues from the previous page: "Indeed, it is varied..."</note>; because one stage of the disease, the **growth** <note>original Greek: αὔξησις (auxēsis); the stage where the illness is intensifying.</note>, requires one thing; another, the **peak** <note>original Greek: ἀκμὴ (akmē); the highest point of the illness.</note>, requires another; and yet another, the **decline** <note>original Greek: παρακμὴ (parakmē); the stage where the illness begins to fade.</note>, requires something else. This variation may also depend on the cause of the condition itself—for the treatment of a disease caused by external factors is one thing, while that caused by internal factors is another—or it may be due to the **symptoms** <term>Symptoms: In early medicine, these were "accidents" or signs that followed the disease itself.</term> following the disease, or because of a gathering and complication of many different conditions.

### Chapter V.

The choice of the **affected site** <note>original: "Loci affecti"</note> changes the **Base** <term>Base: The "Basis" is the principal ingredient in a remedy that performs the main work of healing.</term> either by its location, its nature and temperament, its use and function, its connection and sympathy with neighboring parts, or by its natural constitution and construction.

### Chapter VI.

The **medicine** itself changes the Base: when it is too weak, it requires an increase in intention; when it is too strong, it requires a softening and restraint. When it possesses a substance or quality that seems likely to harm the body or the condition, or that might hinder the action of the entire medicine, it requires **correction**, which is achieved through burning, washing, or some other method <note>This refers to pharmaceutical "correction," where a harsh ingredient is processed to make it safer for the patient.</note>.

### Chapter VII.

**II.** Those things, however, without which the Base cannot drive away the condition, should be of such a kind that they either lead the Base to the affected part (when the entire substance is familiar to that part), or they lead their Base through passages narrowed by nature, obstruction, density, or compression, doing so by their sharpness, the thinness of their essence, or both, or even by...

### Chapter VIII.

**III.** Moreover, those things through which the Base acts better should be such that they make the action of the Base—and of the other things added to the Base—better, more perfect, more healthful, safer, faster, or slower, as the work requires and as necessity demands (based on the condition of the disease or the Base itself). They should assist the power of the others by diminishing the stronger ones through opposition (either of their whole substance, their qualities, or both); by increasing the weaker ones through similarity of substance or qualities; or by dulling, breaking, and correcting anything harmful to the body. They may also add grace and sweetness to the medicines through their color, odor, flavor, and consistency.

### Chapter IX.

**IV.** **Preservatives** <note>original: "Conservantia"</note> are mixed in for this reason: to preserve the form of the medicine and protect it from corruption, so that it is not destroyed by its location or by decay, and so that its **virtue** <term>Virtue: In early medicine, the "virtue" (virtus) was the specific healing power or "essence" of a drug.</term> does not dissipate or exhale. Therefore, all ingredients are dried, either by themselves or by the application of heat from fire or the Sun; or they are preserved in Honey, Sugar, or Vinegar, either alone or with Salt, Oil, etc.

### Chapter X.

**Compounds** <note>original: "Composita"</note> differ among themselves in material, form, use, and the method of preparation. For some are prepared and shaped from various simple ingredients (either alone or combined) that have been reduced to powder, or boiled in water, wine, or vinegar, or preserved with sugar or honey. Others are more suited to certain parts of the body than others, as shown by the names of some which are named after the parts they are primarily applied to and heal. For there are **Errhines** <term>Errhines: Medicines applied to the mucous membranes of the nose to induce sneezing or clear the head.</term>, **Stomatics** <term>Stomatics: Medicines intended for treating diseases of the mouth.</term>,

## ON DISTILLED WATERS.

### Chapter I.

Distilled water <note>original: "Aqua stillaticia"</note> is the thinner portion of a nourishing fluid. Although distillation can be performed on all simple substances, including animals and minerals, for the present we shall treat only of that which is made from herbs, flowers, roots, barks, spices, and certain animal parts. These should be processed in glass or earthenware vessels rather than leaden ones. Indeed, the use of lead vessels is not only harmful, but even damaging and deadly, as the great leader of physicians himself, Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years.</note>, affirms in the seventh book of his work *On the Affected Parts*, chapter 2; there, he writes that water carried through lead tubes or channels produces dysentery <note>A severe intestinal inflammation resulting in painful diarrhea with blood and mucus.</note>. We will present here only two methods, those being the most common and convenient; we leave the others, which are not so frequently used, to other writers.

The first method is that which is done by a "Mary’s Bath" <note>original: "Balneum Mariae"; a water bath or bain-marie, which allows for gentle, even heating by surrounding the vessel with boiling water.</note>, as they call it, using a double vessel. One vessel, which contains the boiling water, should be made of copper or bronze, and be round with a wide channel in the middle...

<summary>This page concludes the table of contents for medicinal oils and begins Chapter 1 of Book Two, defining distilled waters and providing instructions for their preparation. It highlights the dangers of lead poisoning and introduces the "Mary’s Bath" (bain-marie) as a preferred distillation method.</summary>
<keywords>distilled waters, distillation, Galen, lead poisoning, dysentery, bain-marie, medicinal oils, pharmacy equipment</keywords>

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF MEDICINES.
aaa. Balneum.
<meta>catchword: Balneum.</meta>

...[the base] being put in <note>original: "dium immisso"; likely "tripodio immisso" (put upon a tripod) or "incendio immisso" (put into the fire), referring to the placement of the heating unit.</note>, having a grate at the bottom to contain the fire and allow the ashes to fall through. Upon this channel, a lid is placed with a hole through which the smoke may exit. The lid should also have a copper vessel pierced with holes, so that the neck of any **Cucurbit** <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation.</note> can pass through any of the holes.

The other [vessel], holding the material to be distilled and called a **Cucurbit** or **Boccia** <note>From the Italian 'boccia', meaning a flask or bottle.</note>, should be made of glass. Upon this, an **alembic** <note>The 'head' or cap of the still where vapors condense.</note> is placed and carefully sealed to the Cucurbit with paste so that the vapors do not escape. It is then placed into the copper vessel filled with water, along with its **capitellum** <note>The 'little head' or uppermost part of the alembic.</note>, the beak of which should project toward the **receiving vessel** <note>The 'vasculum receptorium', where the final distilled liquid is collected.</note>, as is shown in the following figure.

In this [apparatus], those things are distilled whose powers we do not wish to be dissipated by the violence of the fire, and which we want to keep more mild and intact: such as herbs, flowers, fruits, roots, and all fresh meats collected in their peak of vigor and first ground or cut. The second method is that which is performed in sand, or in hot ashes, which have first been sifted. In this way, seeds, spices, and other things that rise with greater difficulty are distilled: having been **digested** <note>Slowly heated to soften or break down the material.</note> and **macerated** <note>Soaked to extract flavor or medicinal properties.</note> in wine or some other liquid, they will yield that same scent and flavor exactly.

## Chapter II.

### COMPOSITE DISTILLED WATERS.
<note>"Composite" waters are created by distilling several different ingredients together, rather than a "simple" water made from just one plant.</note>

### Chapter III.
## ARTIFICIAL OR
## MEDICATED WINES.

Since Wine is pleasing and familiar to [human] nature, whatever medicinal powers it receives, it readily spreads them into each and even the most hidden parts of the body, insinuating itself throughout—

...it diffuses and imparts; and it is the best vehicle for medicine. Moreover, so that the wine may be properly made, the plant material is gathered when its strength is at its peak and dried in the shade: then it is cast into the must <note>Must is freshly crushed grape juice that contains the skins, seeds, and stems; it is the first stage of winemaking.</note> while it is fermenting. After two or three months, when the wine has finished fermenting and has been cleared of dregs, it is poured off and stored away. Nor does the plant material undergo spoilage if it is allowed to soak for a longer time, unless by chance the wine turns flat because the cask has been emptied or was not properly sealed. Plant material or spices soaked even in older wine makes it quite effective, especially if they have been boiled once.

1 ounce each of anise and fennel; 3 ounces of licorice;
Half an ounce each of mace, cardamom, and orris root; <note>original: "Ireos," the root of the Iris plant, often used for its violet-like scent and fixative properties.</note>
3 ounces of white sugar. Let each be diligently ground and infused with the following:
<margin>Take:</margin> 9 ounces of Malmsey wine; <note>original: "Vini Malvatici," a sweet, high-alcohol wine originally from Greece, prized as a base for medicines.</note>
1 pound of borage water; 1.5 ounces of rose water;
3 ounces of melissa water. <note>also known as lemon balm.</note> Having been left for three hours near a furnace, let it finally be strained several times through a filter bag.

## THE STOMACH.

### *Wormwood Wine.* <note>original: "Absinthites." A bitter tonic intended to stimulate the appetite and digestion.</note>

<margin>Take:</margin> Throw an unspecified weight of common wormwood, whether fresh or dried, into a clean small barrel; pour in must, <note>freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented.</note> and set it aside to ferment until winter. There are those who, at any time of the year if necessity demands, suspend wormwood tied in a linen cloth in old wine for several hours. Some mix in other herbs and spices.
¶ This evacuates gas and excrement; it specifically draws out yellow bile and phlegm.

### *Black Cherry Wine.*

<margin>Take:</margin> 3 pounds of sour black cherries;
12 pounds of wine. The cherries, with their stems removed and crushed, are placed in a bag and sealed together in a vessel covered on all sides for a full year.

### *Hippocras.*

<margin>Take:</margin> 1 ounce of select cinnamon; 3 ounces of galangal;
1 ounce of ginger; 2 scruples <note>the symbol ℈ represents a scruple, a unit of weight equal to about 1.3 grams.</note> of cloves.

->PURGATIVES<-

->For Phlegm<- <note>original: "Pituitam," the cold, moist humor associated with the lungs and brain.</note>

->**Squill Wine**<-
<note>Squill, or "Sea Onion" (Drimia maritima), was a common diuretic and expectorant, though toxic in high doses.</note>

Take 1 pound of Squill; let it be cut into thin layers and dried in the shade for 10 days. Afterward, let it be placed in a glass vessel, and pour 12 <term>sextaries</term> <note>A Roman measure, roughly 1 pint or 0.5 liters.</note> of old white wine over it. Keep the vessel suspended for 40 days; afterward, the squill is to be taken out and thrown away, and the wine reserved for use.
¶ The greatest use of this wine is for purging Phlegm and slow, thick humors.

->**Squill Vinegar**<-

Take 1 pound of finely chopped Squill. 
8 pounds of the sharpest vinegar. For 40 days, in a glazed vessel with a narrow opening, expose it to the heat of the Sun; when these days have passed, let it be strained and stored. Sip this kind of vinegar in the morning. Its power is marvelous for preserving health.

->FOR YELLOW BILE<-

->Scammony Wine<-
<note>original: "Scammonites." Scammony is a resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia, known as a very potent and harsh purgative.</note>

Take 5 drams of ground Scammony root tied in a linen cloth; let it be put into a <term>congius</term> <note>A liquid measure equal to six sextarii, roughly 3 liters.</note> of <term>must</term> <note>Freshly pressed grape juice.</note> for 30 days.

->FOR BLACK BILE<-

->From Black Hellebore<-
<note>original: "Veratrum nigrum." Black Hellebore was famously used in antiquity to treat "madness" and conditions attributed to an excess of black bile (melancholy).</note>

Take 20 drams of Black Hellebore, 12 drams of <term>Sweet Rush</term> <note>original: "junci odor.", an aromatic grass.</note>, 
13 drams of Syrian <term>Spikenard</term> <note>original: "Spicæ Syriacæ," a highly valued aromatic root from the Himalayas.</note>. Once sifted and tied in a small linen cloth, let them be macerated in seven sextaries of wine for 40 days.

### Chapter IV.
#### ON EMULSIONS.

An <term>emulsion</term> <note>A milky liquid produced by grinding seeds or nuts with water or another fluid.</note> is drawn out from cleaned and crushed fruits and certain seeds. Because they release a great deal of juice and may become oily from grinding, they are sprinkled with liquid during the crushing process; this liquid, having been infused with the virtues of the simple ingredients, is then strained and pressed out. They should be stored in glass vessels.

Everything is boiled together in a glazed pot until reduced to half, or until a third part is consumed; afterwards, they are strained, sometimes adding Honey or Sugar for the sake of flavor. But when it is ready, for 1 <term>pound</term> of the decoction, half an <term>ounce</term> <note>original: "℥. ß." where "ß" denotes a half.</note> of Sugar or Honey is poured in. Sometimes they are also seasoned and sharpened with aromatics, adding 2 <term>drachms</term> of aromatics to 1 <term>pound</term> of decoction. Decoctions are usually prepared for three or four doses. Indeed, they can hardly be kept for more than a few days. Physicians also usually mix in 1 <term>ounce</term> of a suitable syrup for any given dose of the decoction. They differ from Syrups only by the length of boiling: for which reason they are called "long syrups" by some Physicians.

### ALTERATIVE DECOCTIONS.
<note>Alterative medicines (Decocta Alterantia) were intended to gradually restore healthy bodily function by "altering" or purifying the blood and humors.</note>

#### *Barley Water.*
<note>original: "Aqua Hordei." A staple of historical medicine, used for its cooling and hydrating properties.</note>

<margin>Take</margin> 2 <term>handfuls</term> of whole barley, well cleaned.
8 <term>pounds</term> of spring water. Let them boil until the barley bursts. At the end, add:
1 <term>ounce</term> of scraped Licorice.
Others add Plums and Fennel. Let them boil with a single boiling. <note>original: "unico fervore" — meaning a brief, single boil after the final ingredients are added.</note>

¶ It mitigates thirst, eases roughness, and also extinguishes inflammation.

#### *Common Decoction, or the Common Medicine.*
<note>original: "Decoctum commune seu communis Medicinæ." This was a "general-purpose" medicinal drink.</note>

<margin>Take</margin> 1 <term>pinch</term> of cleaned barley. 6 pairs of Plums.
<term>Raisins</term> <note>original: "Passularum".</note> and Licorice, half a <term>drachm</term> of each.

->Decoction to alter Phlegm<-
<note>In Galenic medicine, an "altering" (alterans) medicine was designed to change the qualities—heat, cold, dryness, or moisture—of a specific humor to bring the body back into balance. This recipe targets Phlegm (Pituita), which was considered cold and moist.</note>

## Chapter VI.
# ON EMETICS.
<note>original: "DE VOMITIVIS", referring to substances used to induce vomiting, a common practice in humoral medicine to clear the stomach of "corrupt" matter.</note>

Emetics are generally given in the form of drinks. However, the powders of emetic medicines are also mixed in. The dosage is 1 <term>drachm</term> <note>original: "ʒ. j."</note> or 1 and a half <term>drachms</term> according to their strength, with 3 <term>ounces</term> of distilled water or some decoction, adding emetic syrups in a dose of 1 <term>drachm</term> or 1 and a half <term>drachms</term>. Sometimes they are made without powders, using various waters, decoctions, and syrups to create something like a julep <note>A sweet, medicinal drink, often used as a vehicle for more potent drugs.</note>. Occasionally, they are made only with a decoction or other liquid without the addition of syrups.

->*Without powder and syrup.*<-

Take: Barley decoction, 3 <term>ounces</term>.
Vinegar, 1 <term>ounce</term>.
Oil, half an <term>ounce</term>. Mix to make a potion; let it be given warm after a meal or alongside food.

->*With Syrup.*<-

Take: Simple Syrup of Vinegar, 1 and a half <term>ounces</term>.
Decoction of Barley and Orache seeds <note>original: "Atriplicis"; Orache was a common garden herb often used as a mild laxative or emetic.</note>, 3 <term>ounces</term>. Mix to make a potion.

->*With powder and decoction.*<-

## Chapter VII.

### ON SYRUPS.

A syrup is a medicine cooked with Honey or Sugar to the thick consistency of Honey. They are called **Syrups** <note>original Greek: "Συρόποι"</note>, or as it were **"juices from Syria"** <note>original Greek: "οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Συρίας ὀποί"</note>, because they are believed to have been first brought from Syria. Others suggest the name comes from **"juices that are drawn"** <note>original Greek: "ὡς συρέντες ὀποί"</note>, although few are actually endowed with the power of drawing out humors. Actuarius <note>Joannes Actuarius, a prominent Byzantine physician of the 13th century.</note>, using a corrupted word, calls them **Serapia**, while Nicolaus <note>Likely Nicolaus Myrepsos, author of the "Dynameron," a standard pharmaceutical text.</note> names them **dewy-medicines** <note>original Greek: "δρόσατα" (drosata).</note>. Some syrups are Common <note>original: "Usuales"; standard preparations kept in stock by apothecaries.</note>, while others are Master-formulations <note>original: "Magistrales"; custom prescriptions designed by a physician for a specific patient.</note>.

#### ON COMMON SYRUPS.

These are made, much like decoctions <note>original: "Apozemata"; concentrated herbal infusions boiled down to a specific strength.</note>, from the juices of plants or from the broth produced by boiling them. Into three pounds of this liquid, while it is still warm, you shall add the whites of eggs and [beat] them for a long time with...

## Chapter VIII.

# MAGISTERIAL SYRUPS
->or Less Common ones.<-

<margin>
Syrups should be kept in a cooler place because they ferment easily in [warm] places.
</margin>
Syrups that are not kept ready-made in pharmacies, but are instead compounded from various medicines through the judgment, counsel, and skill of physicians when the need arises—as required by the disease and other circumstances—are called **M A G I S T E R I A L**. These are distinguished into digestive, purging, and restorative types.

### MAGISTERIAL DIGESTIVE SYRUPS.
Digestive syrups are prepared from the same materials as the "usual" ones previously listed, and are used for the same purposes; for example, to alter the bile:

Take: Escarole <note>original: "Scariolæ"</note>, Lettuce, Dandelion <note>original: "Rostri porcini," literally "pig's snout," a common name for dandelion due to the shape of its petals</note>, Bugloss, and Borage, 1 handful <note>original: "M. j." (manipulus)</note> of each.
Prunes and Sebesten <note>the Assyrian plum</note>, 5 pairs of each.
The four greater cold seeds <note>a standard blend of cucumber, gourd, melon, and watermelon seeds</note>, 2 ounces of each.
Anise, 1 drachm. Cordial flowers <note>usually borage, bugloss, roses, and violets</note>, 1 pinch <note>original: "P. j." (pugillus)</note>.
Let a decoction be made, and in 1 pound of it, dissolve a sufficient quantity of sugar to make a syrup.

### Dose for Purging Phlegm
<term>Phlegm: Also called "pituita," this humor was considered cold and moist; an excess was thought to cause sluggishness or respiratory issues.</term>

Take: Half an ounce <note>original: "℥. ß."</note> of cleaned raisins.
Safflower seeds and Polypody of the oak, 6 ounces <note>original: "℥. vj."</note> of each.
Anise, Fennel, and scraped Licorice, 1 and a half drams <note>original: "ʒ. j. ß."</note> of each.
Hyssop, 1 dram. Let a decoction be made.
In the strained liquid, dissolve 3 drams <note>The OCR lists "℥. iij." (3 ounces), but in the context of a single dose, drams "ʒ" are more likely</note> or half an ounce of Diacarthami <note>an electuary made of safflower</note>, or Diaphoenicon <note>an electuary made of dates</note>, or Benedicta Laxativa <note>a "blessed" laxative compound</term>.
Syrup of violets, 1 ounce. Mix them.

### [Dose for Purging] Bile
<term>Bile: Specifically yellow bile or "choler," associated with a hot and dry temperament.</term>

Take: Chicory, young Endive, and the Three Cordial Flowers <note>usually a blend of Borage, Bugloss, and Violet flowers</note>, 1 handful <note>original: "M. j." (manipulus)</note> of each.
Scraped Licorice, 1 dram.
Tamarinds, 1 ounce. Cleaned raisins, 3 ounces.
Damson prunes, 6 in number. Let a decoction be made.
In the strained liquid, dissolve 1 dram of fresh Cassia fistula <note>the "purging cassia" pod</note>.
Rhubarb, 1 and a half drams. Let this be the dose.

### [Dose for Purging] Melancholy
<term>Melancholy: Also known as black bile, this humor was associated with coldness, dryness, and a despondent spirit.</term>

Take: Chicory root, 1 ounce. Scraped Licorice, 2 drams.
Chicory, Escarole, Bugloss, Borage, Pig's Snout <note>a variety of dandelion</note>, and Dandelion, 1 handful of each.
Sebesten plums <note>the Assyrian plum</note>, 20 pairs.
Raisins, 10 pinches <note>original: "P. x." (pugillus)</note>. Anise, 2 drams. Tamarind, 1 dram.
Oriental Senna and the pith of Safflower seeds, 3 drams of each.
The Three Cordial Flowers, 1 pinch of each. Let a decoction be made in a sufficient quantity of water.
In the strained liquid, dissolve as much sugar as is sufficient to make a syrup.
To this, add:
Juice of Roses, 2 drams.
Laxative Syrup of Roses, 4 ounces.
Cinnamon, 2 drams. Mix them to make the dose.

BOOK TWO.

### RESTORATIVES.

Restoratives or "instauratives" <note>original: "Refectivi seu instaurativi"</note> are formulated by a doctor's decree from aromatic species—either simple or compound, such as Diatriasantal <note>a powder made of three types of sandalwood</note>, Diamargariton <note>a restorative compound featuring pearls</note>, Aromatic Roses, etc.—or from restorative herbs to rebuild strength that has been exhausted and consumed. They are mixed in the proportion of 2 drams <note>original: "ʒ.ij."</note> of powders or crushed aromatics to 1 pound <note>original: "℔.j."</note> of water. They should be sweetened with a sufficient quantity of sugar or mixed with other suitable syrups, such as:

Take: Cold powdered Diamargariton,
Electuary of Gems, half a scruple <note>original: "℈.ß."</note> of each.
Confection of Alkermes <note>a famous red-colored cordial made from kermes insects, valued for the heart</note>, 5 grains.
Water of Borage, Roses, and Bugloss, 1 dram <note>original: "ʒ.j."</note> of each.
Syrup of Lemons,
Syrup of Citron peel, half a dram <note>original: "ʒ. ß."</note> of each.
Mix them to make a drink.

¶ This is suitable for those whose strength is broken and those near death during "hot" diseases <note>illnesses involving high fever or inflammation</note>.

These syrups are frequently taken at daybreak after being first warmed; they are sometimes taken in the evening, specifically when they are used for the sake of inducing sleep.

## Chapter IX.
## ON THE JULEP.

Julep, or julapius—called <term>Zoulapion</term>, <term>Zolapos</term>, or <term>iolabon</term> <note>Greek: Ζουλάπιον, Ζόλαπος, or ἰόλαβον</note> by more recent Greek authors such as Actuarius and Simeon Seth <note>Byzantine medical writers</note>—is named as if it were an "infusion of violets" <note>the term Julep actually derives from the Persian word for rosewater, 'gulab', but early modern scholars often sought Greek etymologies</note>. It is prepared, accordingly, either from a "Cardiac" <note>heart-strengthening</note> or any distilled liquid, or from pure and clarified juice, such as that of Lemons or Pomegranates...

...etc., or from the juice of one or a few simples <note>individual medicinal plants</note>, especially aromatic ones such as Mint, Fennel, Hyssop, etc. Triple the amount of honey or sugar is added (though according to some, an equal quantity of sugar), and it is cooked slowly while skimming off the foam, until almost all the liquid is consumed and it reaches the consistency of honey. Finally, it is seasoned with spices so that it becomes an entirely pleasant drink. Now, however, it is usually made simpler and more liquid: and because it is simple, it differs from an Apozeme <term>Apozema</term> <note>a medicinal decoction or concentrated herbal tea</note>; being liquid, it differs from a Syrup. The dose is 1 and a half ounces <note>original: "℥. j. ß."</note>. Doctors also usually give one tablet of "altering" or "strengthening" electuaries <note>pastes made of honey and medicinal powders</note> appropriate to the disease along with any julep drink. In "hot" diseases <note>conditions involving fever or inflammation</note>, they give Santal compound <note>original: "Diatriasantali"</note>, cold Tragacanth compound <note>original: "Diatragacanthi frigidi"</note>, or "Hand of Christ" with pearls <note>original: "Manus Christi perlatæ"; a restorative sugar-based tablet</note>. In "cold" diseases, tablets of Rose aromatics, sweet Musk compound <note>original: "Diamuschi dulc."</note>, hot Tragacanth compound, Cumin compound <note>original: "Diacymini"</note>, Galangal compound <note>original: "Diagalangæ"</note>, and the like.

### Julep of Violets.

**Take:** Violet water, 2 pounds.
Sugar or Honey, 1 or 2 pounds. Let them be cooked while skimming the foam until they reach the consistency of honey, and let it be seasoned with spices.
¶ This mitigates inflammatory fevers <note>original: "Febris Phlegmonas"</note>, pleurisy, roughness of the throat and chest, and coughs.

### The Royal Parisian Julep, or
### The Alexandrian Julep, or
### Mesué’s other Rose Julep.

**Take:** Rose water, 3 pounds. White sugar, 2 pounds. Having been thoroughly purified with egg whites, let them be boiled down into a julep.
¶ This is most pleasing for all bilious and burning fevers, both for its flavor and because, when mixed with four times the amount of the best water, it effectively settles thirst.

## Chapter X.

### ON MEDICINAL JUICES.

Medicinal juice <term>Succago</term>, called *Apochylisma* <note>original: "Αποχύλισμα"</note> by the Greeks, and *Rob* or *Robub* by the Arabs, is the juice of fruits or herbs, purified and strained, and by the benefit of fire or the sun, boiled down to the somewhat firm consistency of boiled wine <term>Sapa</term> <note>grape juice boiled down to a third of its volume to create a thick, shelf-stable liquid</note> (so that it can be preserved and kept from corruption), thoroughly cooked to the thickness of an Electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note> or a Linctus <term>Lohoch</term> <note>a "lickpot" medicine intended to be dissolved slowly in the mouth</note>: and this is done either without the addition of honey or sugar, or with the seasoning of sugar or honey. To seven parts of the strained juice, they are accustomed to add parts—

### *Simple Rob of Redcurrants* <note>original: "Rob de Ribes sim."</note>

¶ It strengthens the stomach <note>original: "ventriculum"</note>, quenches thirst, and stops other bilious excretions <note>the discharge of "yellow bile," associated in this period with heat and digestive upset</note>.

### *Rob of Barberry* <note>original: "Rob de Berberis"</note>

**Take:** 4 pounds of purified Barberry juice.
2 pounds of the best sugar. Cook according to the art <term>f. a.</term> <note>an abbreviation for "fiat arte," a standard instruction for a pharmacist to use their professional skill to complete the preparation</note>.
¶ It is wonderfully effective in burning fevers, where thirst is pressingly intense. For it settles the thirst and strengthens the stomach. In the same way, you shall prepare Rob from Cornelian cherries <note>original: "Cornis"</note>, Cherries, the fruit of the Barberry bush <note>original: "Crespini"</note>, and similar fruits.

### *Walnut Syrup* <term>Dianucum</term> <note>a syrup made primarily from walnut husks; the name follows the Greek naming convention "dia" (made of) and "nucum" (walnuts)</note>

**Take:** 4 pounds of the juice of unripe Walnut husks.
2 pounds of the best skimmed honey. Cook according to the art to the proper thickness.
¶ It is helpful for the dripping <note>original: "destillationi"</note> of thin humors from the head and those exciting inflammation, such as Quinsy <note>original: "Anginæ," referring to severe throat inflammation or tonsillitis</note> and the like.

### *Galen’s Mulberry Syrup* <term>Diamoron</term> <note>a classic medicinal syrup made from mulberries, used since antiquity for mouth and throat ailments</note>

**Take:** 2 pounds of juice from cultivated Mulberries.
1 pound of Honey. After the juice has first been clarified, let it be cooked to the correct consistency.
¶ Used as a gargle, it is beneficial against spreading ulcers of the mouth <note>original: "depascentia Oris ulcera"</note>, for afflictions of the teeth, and damage to the gums, as well as for all defects of the mouth.

## Simple Quince Jelly <note>original: "Miva Cydoniorum sim."</note>

**Take:** 1 pound of purified Quince juice.

## Compound Quince Jelly <note>original: "Miva Cydonior. compos."</note>

**Take:** 4 ounces each of sweet and sour Quince juice.
5 ounces each of white sugar and the best skimmed honey.
3 ounces of white wine vinegar.
2 drams <note>original: "ʒ. ij."</note> of Long Pepper <note>a spice related to black pepper but hotter and more aromatic</note>. 1 scruple <note>original: "℈. j."</note> each of Galangal and white Ginger.
First, the juices, sugar, and honey should be cooked with the vinegar to the consistency of a thin syrup; afterward, add the spices, which must be very finely sifted, and let them simmer together over a slow fire until they reach the thickness of honey.
¶ This strengthens the stomach <note>original: "ventriculum"</note>, the liver, and the other internal organs; it stimulates the appetite, aids digestion, and settles vomiting and lientery <term>lientery</term> <note>a form of diarrhea where food passes through the body undigested</note>.

## Purgative Quince Electuary <note>original: "Diacydonites Catharcticum"</note>

**Take:** 3 pounds of Quince flesh.
2 pounds of sugar.
1 and a half ounces of Scammony <term>Scammony</term> <note>a harsh resinous juice from the root of Convolvulus scammonia, used as a powerful laxative</note>.
2 drams of Cinnamon.
Prepare according to the art. The dose is from 3 drams to half an ounce.
¶ It draws out bile and thin, watery humors from the more distant parts of the body.

## Sapa <note>Reduced Grape Must</note>

**Take:** As much as you wish of the freshest grape must. Cook it, skimming and purifying it, until it reaches a thick consistency.

## Chapter XI.
### ON INFUSION.

An infusion is a liquid in which medicines—whether lightly ground, powdered, or even solid and whole—are soaked without boiling <note>original: "absq; decoctione"</note> for several hours, a whole night, two days, or three days, depending on the nature of the medicine, so that its entire virtue <note>its medicinal power or active essence</note> is drawn into the liquid. It should be noted that for Purgatives <term>Purgantia</term> <note>laxatives or cleansing agents</note>, one should always add those things which restrain their violence and correct their harmful qualities <note>original: "malitiam," referring to the harsh side-effects of strong laxatives</note>, while strengthening the principal organs. This should be in a triple proportion, or at least a sub-double one; for example, to 3 ounces <note>original: "℥. iij."</note> of purgatives, add 1 dram <note>original: "ʒ. j"</note> or 1 and a half drams <note>original: "ʒ. j. ß."</note> of those that restrain them; thus, to 1 ounce <note>original: "℥. j."</note>, 1 and a half scruples <note>original: "℈. j. ß."</note> would correspond. All these are mixed and soaked in plant decoctions, broths, goat whey, or—most frequently—distilled herbal waters, for a space of 12 or 24 hours, or for as long as it takes until the liquids are affected by or imbued with the qualities of the added medicine. Afterward, they are strongly pressed out and seasoned with Sugar, Cinnamon, or even Serapio <note>likely referring to a medicinal syrup or oxymel named after the physician Serapion</note>; the quantity of which is determined by the amount of liquid and the qualities of the soaked drugs.

### The following are commonly infused.

**Rhubarb** <note>original: "Rhabarbarum." In this period, rhubarb was a highly prized medicinal root imported from Asia, used as a gentle but effective laxative that also "strengthened" the stomach.</note>

*   **Infused at a weight of 4 drams at most** <note>original: "ʒ.iiij." A dram was a measurement of weight roughly equal to 3.9 grams.</note>
    *   **In Winter**, with white wine
    *   **In Summer**, with:
        *   Whey <note>original: "Sero lactis," the liquid remaining after milk has been curdled</note>,
        *   Chicory juice,
        *   A decoction <note>a liquid made by boiling medicinal ingredients</note> that purges bile,
        *   Or distilled waters of the same.
*   **Corrected with a third part [by weight], or with:** <note>To "correct" a medicine meant adding ingredients to balance its harsh effects or improve its flavor.</note>
    *   Spikenard <note>original: "Spicę Nardi," a costly aromatic essential oil or dried herb from the Himalayas</note>
    *   Cinnamon
    *   Sweet rush <note>original: "junci odorati," a fragrant grass used in ancient and medieval pharmacy</note>,
    *   Mastic <note>a resin obtained from the mastic tree</note>.

Syrup of Endive,
Syrup of Sorrel,
And Syrup of Violets, of each half an ounce <note>original: "ana ℥.ß." An ounce was roughly 31 grams; "semissis" or "ß" indicates a half-measure.</note>. Mix.

**Turbith** <note>original: "Turbith." This is the root of *Operculina turpethum*, known as Indian Turpeth, used in the humoral system to purge "thick phlegm."</note>—

## Chapter XII.

### ON ENEMAS.

**Enema** <note>original: "Clyster."</note> **is not "Crister"; it comes from the Greek *klyzo*** <note>The OCR reads *κλύω* (to hear), but the context and medical tradition suggest *κλύζω* (to wash/cleanse). The author provides a specific etymology linking it to "hiding."</note> **that is, "I hide," because it hides within the body. It is the name of the instrument; the Greeks call it an *enyma* and the Latins call it an *Ablutio* (Washing). An Enema, or *Clysmus*, is a flooding and drenching of the bowels and intestines introduced into the anus by a syringe.** <note>original: "siphone."</note>

**Almost every enema consists of 1 pound of a decocted broth—made from peas, chickpeas, chicken, capon, etc.—or any liquid in which a sixth part, or at most a quarter part, of the medicinal ingredients are dissolved, along with a quarter part of oil. Sometimes Honey, Sugar, egg yolks, butter, and other things of that kind are added, as the illness requires. For children, the amount is kept lower; for adults, it is increased up to 1 and a half pounds** <note>℔. j. β.</note>**, though always taking into account the size of the body, the fullness of the belly, the patient's nature, the disease, and their age. The following proportion is usually observed:**

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF MEDICINES.

### DOSAGE FOR ENEMAS

| Ingredient Category | Recommended Dose |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Of decoction or liquid** | from 8 to 15 ounces. <note>℥ signifies an ounce, roughly 28 grams.</note> |
| **Of Purgatives:** | |
| — *Simples* <note>Single medicinal ingredients.</note> such as **Agaric** <note>A fungus from the larch tree used as a laxative.</note>, **Turpeth**, **Colocynth** <note>Bitter apple.</note>, and **Scammony** | from 2 to 3 drams. <note>ʒ signifies a dram, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> |
| — *Compounds* <note>Pre-mixed multi-ingredient formulas.</note> such as **Diaphoenicon** <note>A date-based purgative electuary.</note>, **Hiera Picra** <note>A famous "holy bitter" remedy made of aloes and spices.</note>, **Hiera of Logadius**, **Electuary of Eleschoph**, **Electuary of Laurel Berries**, **Electuary of Indigo**, and the **Blessed Laxative** | from 1 to 1.5 ounces, <note>ß signifies "half."</note> more or less. |
| **Of Oils** | 3 or 4 ounces. |
| **Of Fats, Honey, Butter, and Sugar** | 1/2 or 1 ounce. |
| **Of Egg yolks** | 2 or 3 in number. |
| **Of Salt** | 1 or 1.5 drams. |

Enemas are injected moderately warm by means of a bladder or a syringe <note>In the early modern period, enemas were administered using animal bladders attached to a pipe or via metal syringes.</note> two or three hours before food. The time they should be retained, however, is not one and the same; rather, it varies according to their different natures. Those used for cleansing and washing <note>Used to clear away waste or "filth" from the bowels.</note> are held for no more than half an hour; soothing enemas are held longer; and the healing ones <term>original: "glutinantes." Literally "gluing" medicines, used to coat the intestinal lining and heal ulcers or wounds.</term> are retained the longest of all. Purgative enemas usually tend to break out <note>That is, be expelled.</note> of their own accord. If, however, they linger too long in the body, it is proper to insert a suppository <term>original: "glandem." Literally an "acorn," referring to the traditional shape of a medicated plug inserted into the rectum.</term> so that the expulsive faculty <note>The body's natural power to drive out waste.</note> may be stimulated and the harmful substances expelled.

# Chapter XIII.
## ON GARGLES.

**Gargles** <note>original: "Γαργαρισμοὶ" (Gargarismoi)</note>, named from the Greek word *gargarizein* and the Latin *regurgitando* <note>meaning to wash the throat by bubbling liquid</note>, consist of decoctions of herbs, juices, roots, seeds, and even excrements taken from animals, as well as distilled waters and dry medicines reduced to powder. Depending on the specific nature of the ailment, there is added **Honey of Roses**, **Honey of Rosemary**, **Syrup of French Lavender**, or **Syrup of Calamint**; or **Mulberry syrup**, **Currant jelly**, **Hawthorn**, or **Hiera picra**. <note>"Hiera picra" (Sacred Bitter) was a famous ancient purgative powder made primarily of aloes and canella.</note> No certain weight is strictly observed for these. Some, however, prefer a ratio of three parts liquid to one part antidotes, medicinal juices, and syrups.

## Chapter XIV.

### ON ERRHINES, OR
### **Head-purgers.**
<note>original: "Errhinis, seu Caputpurgiis." These were medicines designed to be administered through the nose to "purge" the brain of excess fluids.</note>

**Errhines** are medicines that are placed or inserted into the nostrils. These are prepared in two forms: either liquid or dry. The liquids—which are either smeared into the nostrils or poured in—consist of juices or oils, or of leaves or powders mixed together. Of the dry forms, some are ground into a powder and blown into the nostrils through a reed; others are kneaded with wax or oils and shaped into long, pyramidal masses. These are inserted with a thread tied to them so that they can be pulled back out when necessary.

Squill honey, 1 drachm of each. Let them be mixed and drawn up through the nostrils. <note>An "Errhine" is a medicine applied to the nose to induce sneezing or mucus discharge.</note>

->*An Errhine for restraining blood.*<-

<margin>Take</margin> Frankincense, 2 scruples. Aloes, 1 scruple. Once ground into a powder, let them be worked together with egg white; with the addition of very soft hare’s fur, let them be formed into the shape of a small plug to be placed in the nostrils.

->*An Errhine for purging Phlegm.*<-

<margin>Take</margin> Juice of Squirting Cucumber, or Beet, or Mercury, or Cyclamen, 2 drachms. Troches of Agaric, 2 drachms.
A little wine. Let a decoction be made. In the strained liquid, dissolve a sufficient quantity of honey to make an errhine.

One thing must be uniquely observed: those who take these medicines should first fill their mouth with water, so that the juices do not flow down from the nostrils through the passages or channels [into the throat]. They should tilt the head backward; nor should they use these treatments unless the body has first been emptied by a purgative medicine or by <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>The practice of opening a vein to draw blood, a common medical procedure of the time intended to balance the body's humors.</note>.

¶ We use these for long-lasting afflictions of the head, especially the <term>Comitial disease</term> <note>original: "morbo Comitiali"; a historical name for epilepsy, so called because a seizure was seen as a bad omen that would cause the Roman "comitia" or assemblies to be dismissed.</note>, dimness of the eyes, obstructions and ulcers of the nostrils, difficulty in smelling, the <term>Cynic convulsion</term> <note>original: "Convulsione Cynica"; a type of facial paralysis or spasm, likely Bell’s Palsy, named for the way it can make a patient look like a snarling dog.</note>, and the <term>royal disease</term> <note>original: "morbo regio"; a historical term for jaundice.</note>.

# BOOK TWO

Mix, and let an <term>epithem</term> <note>A medicinal compress or a small bag filled with herbs, soaked in liquid and applied externally to the body to treat internal conditions.</note> be made.

### An Epithem for the Stomach

<margin>Take</margin> Red roses, 2 small handfuls.
Both types of plantain <note>Typically referring to the broadleaf and ribwort varieties.</note>, 1/2 handful each.
Shoots of wormwood, 1/2 handful.
All types of sandalwood <note>A mixture of red, yellow, and white sandalwood.</note>, 2 drachms each.
Red coral, 3 drachms.
Let all these be placed in a small bag and cooked in water with a dash of vinegar to which some wine has been added; let a doubled linen cloth, soaked in this warm broth, be applied to the stomach.

### An Epithem for the forehead to induce sleep

<margin>Take</margin> Rose water, 3 ounces. Rose vinegar, 1 ounce.
The white of one egg.
Mix, and let a <term>frontale</term> <note>A medicated cloth or pad applied specifically to the forehead to cool the head or aid sleep.</note> be made.

#### Another

<margin>Take</margin> Red roses, water-lily flowers, violets, 1 small handful each.
Betony, melilot <note>A fragrant herb also known as sweet clover.</note>, 1/2 handful each.
Let these be placed between two pieces of fine linen, and let a quilted compress be made, which is to be applied to the forehead and the temples.

These epithems are applied after an <term>evacuation</term> <note>A medical clearing of the body, often through laxatives or emetics.</note> has been performed or after bloodletting, and especially during the peak of a fever, when all symptoms are most severe; they are applied frequently, in the evening and the morning. In short, they are used whenever any part of the body is inflamed or affected by any other "hot" condition.

¶ Their use is most effective in <term>hectic fevers</term> <note>Persistent, wasting fevers often associated with chronic illness.</note>, as well as for foul, burning, and pestilential fevers; for inflammation of the internal organs and a general "fire" or burning of the whole body. They are likewise used for palpitation of the heart, <term>cardiac passion</term> <note>A historical term for severe heart distress or agonizing chest pain.</note>, <term>erysipelas</term> <note>A painful, red bacterial skin infection.</note>, and weakness of physical strength.

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF MEDICINES

### ON FOMENTS

Foments (<note>original: *Fomenta*; the Greeks call them *pyrias*</note>) are named from the word for "cherishing" or "warming," because they soothe and warm the parts of the body to which they are applied. They are prepared in various ways: sometimes from hot water, to which wine or vinegar is occasionally added toward the end; sometimes from milk; sometimes from lye (<note>a solution made from wood ashes</note>); sometimes from "blacksmith’s water" (<note>the water used by smiths to cool hot iron, thought to contain restorative minerals</note>); and sometimes from oil or decoctions of herbs, flowers, and seeds boiled down until only a third or half the liquid remains. 

They may also be made from the liquid used for <term>cataplasms</term> <note>A warm, moist medicinal poultice</note>, which is then placed in an ox bladder, or a vessel made of brass, clay, or glass. Alternatively, the liquid can be soaked into a sponge, a filter, or linen cloths folded two or three times, and then applied to the affected part—specifically the eyes, chest, belly, liver, spleen, kidneys, bladder, uterus, joints, and so on. The method and quantity of both the dry ingredients and the liquid should be adjusted to the size and location of the area being treated; however, it is customary to add one pound of liquid for every two handfuls of herbs. The specific materials suited to each ailment and body part must be chosen based on the particular case.

->*Foment for Inflammation of the Eyes*<-

<margin>Take</margin> Leaves of eyebright, 1 handful. Oat chaff, 2 handfuls.
Fenugreek (washed in fennel water), 3 ounces.
Anise and Fennel seeds, 1 ½ ounces each.
Flowers of Arabian lavender (<note>original: *Stoechados*</note>), ½ pinch.
Make a powder from which two square bags are to be made; let these be infused in a small amount of white wine and fennel water, and then let the eyes be bathed.

->*Foment for Pleurisy*<-

<margin>Take</margin> Mallow, Sage, Wormwood, Southernwood,
Scabious, ½ handful each.
Boil in a pint (<note>original: *sextario*</note>) of water until reduced by a third; bathe the affected part with a sponge squeezed out of the broth of this decoction.

## Chapter XVI.

### ON EMBROCATIONS.

An *Embrocation* <note>original Greek: Ἐμβροχὴ (*Embrochē*)</note>, derived from the word "to soak" <note>original Greek: ἐμβρέχειν (*embrechein*)</note>, is called *udibrochē* by Galen, *Diabrochē* <note>original Greek: Διαβροχὴ, meaning a thorough soaking</note> by Alexander, and is known to the Latins as *Perfusio* (a pouring over) or *Irrigatio* (irrigation). An embrocation occurs when a liquid is dripped from a height, like rain, onto a specific body part, or applied with gentle rubbing. It is composed of herbs, flowers, roots, seeds, etc., boiled in water, wine, lye, or oil. For the most part, the recipe follows a ratio: 2 handfuls <note>original: *manipulus*, abbreviated as M.</note> of herbs or flowers, 1 ounce <note>original: ℥</note> of seeds, and 1 pound <note>original: ℔</note> of liquids; these are boiled until half the volume is consumed.

->*An Embrocation for cold diseases of the Head.*<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| <margin>Take</margin> | Roots of Sweet Flag <note>original: *Acorus*</note>, Galingale <note>original: *Cyperus*</note>, and Orris <note>original: *Iris*</note>, 2 ounces of each. |
| | Betony, Marjoram, Sage, |
| | Oregano, Calamint, ½ handful of each. |
| | Dried Lemon peel, 3 ounces. |
| | Flowers of both types of Arabian Lavender <note>original: *Stœchas*</note>, 1 pinch <note>original: *pugillus*, abbreviated as P.</note> of each. |

Boil in a sufficient quantity of water until half remains to make an embrocation with which the head may be irrigated. If the disease is stubborn, add ½ ounce of <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>literally "water of life," referring to concentrated distilled alcohol or brandy</note>.

->*For Gouty Pain.*<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| <margin>Take</margin> | Thyme, Oregano, Sage, |
| | Calamint, 1 handful of each. Water, 1 pound. |

Let them be boiled until half the volume is consumed, with which the affected parts may afterwards be bathed or fomented. ¶ This is used hot, and mostly for a head filled with <term>viscous humors</term> <note>thick, sticky bodily fluids thought to cause sluggishness or illness in Galenic medicine</note> or for obstructed joints, so that the falling droplets may dissolve, disperse, and consume the stuffed-up humors.

## Chapter XVII.
### ON BATHS.

A bath <note>original: *Balneum*</note> is a remedy for the entire body, which is moistened by water or vapor, either for the purpose of cleansing, or for pains, or for fatigue, or for defects of the skin, or for an <term>intemperance</term> <note>an imbalance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> of the whole body. Some baths are natural and are called Thermal Springs <note>original: *Thermæ*</note>; others are artificial.

### ON NATURAL BATHS, OR THERMAL SPRINGS.

Those are called natural baths which arise of their own accord or naturally. Thermal Springs are named from "heat" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς θέρμης (*apo tēs thermēs*)</note>. Their differences are various; for they may consist of sulfur, alum, salt, niter <note>likely referring to natron or soda ash rather than modern gunpowder niter</note>, bitumen, brass, iron, copper, gold, or mixtures of these.

#### *Saline Baths.*

¶ These are beneficial for cold and moist imbalances <note>original: *intemperies*</note> and for diseases of the same kind. Consequently, they heal those suffering from <term>dropsy</term> <note>swelling caused by excess fluid; original: *Hydropicis*</note>, cold pains of the nerves, <term>gout</term> <note>original: *Podagra*</note>, asthma, discharges of the chest, a cold and moist stomach, loose tumors, phlegmatic conditions, those infected with the itch <note>original: *scabie*</note>, and the head and chest when they are subject to fluxes <note>excessive fluid discharges</note>.

#### *Nitrous Baths.*

¶ These do not differ from the powers of saline baths, except that they are more potent in all those respects; they do not constrict as much, but they cleanse powerfully. For this reason, they clean those with the itch, heal ulcers of the ears, and disperse both the ringing sounds <note>tinnitus</note> and tumors of the ears.

#### *Aluminous Baths.*

¶ These are for the spitting up of blood, a stomach inclined to vomit, hemorrhoids that flow immoderately, and women who inordinately—

...purged adequately <note>original: *natè*, likely the end of *ordinatè* (orderly) or *inordinatè* (inordinately)</note>, and for women who frequently miscarry. Finally, they are beneficial for those who are weakened by excessive sweating and for varicose veins of the legs.

### *Sulfurous Baths*

¶ They provide heat, soften the nerves, and soothe pains. However, they weaken and upset the stomach. They wipe away all defects of the skin: they assist those with <term>dropsy</term> <note>swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, <term>alphos</term> and <term>leuce</term> <note>types of skin discoloration or leprosy; original: *Alphis, Leucis*</note>, skin eruptions, chronic ulcers, the buildup of fluid in the joints, a hardened spleen, the liver, the uterus, paralysis <note>original: *resolutionibus*</note>, hip pains <note>sciatica</note>, and the itch <note>scabies</note>.

### *Bituminous Baths*

¶ They fill the head <note>cause congestion or pressure</note> and harm the sense organs, yet they heat vigorously and soften extensively if one remains in them for a longer time, especially benefiting the uterus, the bladder, and the colon. Furthermore, they are suitable for those affected by "water under the skin" <note>another term for dropsy or edema; original: *aqua intercute*</note>.

### *Iron Baths*

¶ They are useful for the stomach, the spleen, and the kidneys.

### *Bronze Baths*

¶ They are beneficial <note>original: *Aerea*—referring to *aes*, an alloy of copper like bronze or brass</note> for the eyes, the mouth, the tonsils, and the <term>uvula</term> <note>the fleshy hangings at the back of the throat</note>.

### *Copper Baths*

¶ They help with joint pains, <term>gout</term> <note>original: *Podagricis*</note>, asthma, kidney diseases, and malignant ulcers.

### *Gold Baths*

¶ They provide relief for colic pains, <term>volvulus</term> <note>a painful twisting of the intestines</note>, fistulas, gout, and malignant ulcers.

Those baths which consist of mixed qualities act according to the proportion of whichever quality is dominant.

## Chapter XVIII.

### ON ARTIFICIAL BATHS.

Artificial baths are either "aerial" <note>gas or vapor based</note>, such as the **Laconicum**, or liquid and watery, such as the **Solium**. The **Solium** is nothing other than a vessel in which people sit to wash themselves; at other times it is called a **Labrum** <note>tub</note>, **Lavacrum** <note>bath</note>, **Piscina** <note>pool</note>, or **Tina** <note>vat</note>.

The **Laconicum** [which is also called a **Sudatorium** <note>sweat-room</note> or **Calidarium** <note>hot-room</note>, or in the common tongue a **Stupha** <note>stove-room or sauna</note>] is a space enclosed on all sides. The air inside is heated in the center, either by hot and dry vapors from a lit fire, or by hot and moist vapors from herbs boiled in a vessel, or by water sprinkled over heated stones. It is prepared either from "simples"—such as plain hot water, wine, milk, or oil—or from "compounds," such as herbs, flowers, seeds, barks, herbal juices, minerals, and other items of that kind. These are placed in a bag and boiled in water until the liquid is reduced by a third.

->The amount of liquid for a bath should be appropriate, and should not rise above the pit of the stomach of the person sitting.<-

| Ingredient Type | Appropriate Quantity |
| :--- | :--- |
| <margin>*</margin> Herbs | From 5 to 10 or 15 **handfuls** <note>original: *M.* for *manipuli*</note>, more or less according to the nature of the disease and the strength of the patient. |
| Flowers | From 3 to 10 or 12 **fistfuls** <note>original: *P.* for *pugilli*</note>. |
| Roots | From 3 **ounces** to 3, 4, or 5 **pounds**. |
| Seeds | Up to 1 **ounce**. |
| Legumes | From 6 **ounces** to 2 **pounds**. |
| Minerals | From 3 **ounces** to 3 **pounds**. |

The appropriate time for the **Laconicum** <note>vapor bath</note> is considered to be winter and the beginning of spring, or any time that is not excessively cold or hot. For the **Solium** <note>sitting bath</note>, however, Spring, Summer, and the end of Summer are best—provided the body has first been purged, and not while one is still weary from the exertion of a journ—

[...the body should not be] exhausted or overly full, or filled with raw and bad humors <note>In traditional medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that needed to be kept in balance for health</note>. The most suitable hour of the day is in the morning, one hour after sunrise, with an empty stomach, and after the waste of the bowels and bladder has first been discharged, either naturally or by art <note>such as by using a suppository or enema</note>. An evening hour is also seen as appropriate, specifically when the digestion of the midday meal is complete. The duration of the stay in the morning bath should be longer than in the evening; namely, in the morning from one hour up to two or three hours, more or less according to the patient’s nature and the strength of their constitution. For those who are bilious <note>hot and dry-tempered</note>, thin, and weak cannot endure a long stay; on the contrary, those who are strong, stout, cold, and moist <note>phlegmatic</note> can endure a longer one. The evening stay should be two hours at the most.

### *A Warming Bath*

Take 1 handful <note>original: *M.* for *manipulus*</note> each of Pennyroyal, Oregano, Hyssop, Thyme, and Savory.
Half a handful <note>original: *M. ß.* for *manipulus semis*</note> each of Sage, Laurel leaves, Rosemary, Ground-pine, and Pellitory-of-Spain.
Cook these in a sufficient quantity of water for a bath.

### *Another, Softening Bath*

Take 4 handfuls each of Mallow with its root, Bear's-breech <note>original: *Branca ursina*</note>, and Violets.
2 handfuls each of Mercury herb, Pellitory-of-the-wall, and Beet.
1 ounce <note>original: *℥.*</note> of Flaxseed; 2 fistfuls <note>original: *P.* for *pugillus*</note> of Chamomile flowers.
Let a decoction <note>a concentrated liquor made by boiling</note> be made for a bath.

### *Another, Cleansing Bath*

Take 2 handfuls each of Myrtle leaves, or Mastic tree leaves, or Plantain, Great Mullein <note>original: *Thapsus barbatus*</note>, Mouse-ear hawkweed, Horsetail, and Knotgrass.
2 fistfuls of Roses.
2 ounces each of Orris root, Bistort, and Cinquefoil.
Let a decoction be made, in which dissolve 3 pounds <note>original: *℔.* for *libra*</note> of common salt.

¶ A fresh-water bath <note>original: *Solium Aqvæ dulcis*</note> that is moderately warm is beneficial for children and the elderly; it warms, moistens, relieves fatigue, soothes, disperses "fullness" <note>likely referring to congestion or an excess of bodily fluids</note>, softens hard parts, dispels gas, and induces sleep. A lukewarm bath, however, moistens and cools; it is beneficial for drying fevers, hectic fevers <term>hectic: a persistent, wasting fever often associated with chronic consumption</term>, and severe cases of sunstroke. That which is hotter than is right certainly warms, but it does not moisten in the same way.

# Chapter XIX.

## ON SITZ-BATHS.

Sitz-baths <note>original: *Insessiones* or *Insessus*</note>, which the Greeks call *egkathismata* <note>original: *έγκαθισματα*</note>, are nothing other than decoctions of herbs, flowers, roots, and seeds, in which the sick sit only up to the stomach, with their legs and arms kept out. These were invented as a substitute when full baths are unavailable, or because the patient is too weak to use a full bath.

<note>The following proportions are grouped together:</note>
Quantity of herbs: from 5 to 8 handfuls <note>original: *M.* for *manipulus*</note>.
Quantity of roots: from 2 to 4 ounces <note>original: *℥.*</note>.
* Quantity of seeds: from 6 to 8 ounces.
Quantity of water: as much as seems sufficient for the bath.

Everything is placed in a bag and boiled in water until the liquid is reduced by a third. 
These are applied when the kidneys, bladder, colon, anus, or intestines are affected.

### For inflamed Kidneys.

Take <note>original: *℞* for *Recipe*</note> 4 handfuls each <note>original: *ana*</note> of Mallow and Marshmallow.

They should not be used, however, when the body is filled with raw and bad humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which early medicine sought to keep in balance</term>. The stay in the bath should last for about an hour, more or less, depending both on the severity of the condition and the weakness of the patient's strength.

## Chapter XX.

### ON LOTIONS.

The Head, Armpits, Hands, Feet, and Private Parts are washed. Head washes <note>original: *Capitales ablutiones*</note> are composed of "head herbs" and flowers <note>plants believed to benefit the brain or scalp</note> boiled in lye <note>original: *lixivio*; a solution made from wood ashes used as a cleansing agent</note>. Those for the armpits are made from astringents, such as wild olive <note>original: *Oleastro*</note> and mastic <note>original: *Lentisco*</note>, with certain fragrant substances added. Those for the feet are made from herbs or flowers, either hot or cold in nature, boiled in water or lye. The quantity of these is commonly from 4 to 8 or 10 handfuls <note>original: *M.* for *manipulus*</note>.

Warm head washes are to be administered in the morning before food, when the body is empty of waste <note>referring to the evacuation of the bowels and bladder</note>; however, the head must be wiped immediately and dried with warm cloths. Foot washes, on the other hand, should be used in the morning or evening before food, or even before sleep; the feet are not to be wiped dry again, but are to be washed with a damp cloth.

Lye washes <note>original: *Lixivia*; cleaning solutions made from wood ash</note> cleanse the sweat and grime of the head and open the pores of the skin; they also strengthen the brain and the memory. Foot baths, however, draw humors from the upper parts of the body down to the lower parts, dispel fatigue, and induce sleep.

## Chapter XXI.

### ON OILS.

Oil, or *Elaion* <note>original: *Ἔλαιον*; the Greek word for olive oil</note>, is defined by Galen <note>a Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium</note> in the strict sense as that which is pressed from mature olives, being free from almost any extreme quality <note>Galen believed pure olive oil was "temperate," meaning it was not excessively hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>. To us, however, it refers to any oily, fatty, or greasy juice prepared by any method. It is nothing other than the "airy" portion of a moist substance, and just as it carries the scent and flavor of its source, it also reflects its medicinal powers to a great degree.

## ON SIMPLE OILS.

An oil is called "simple" when it is made without any additional ingredients. Those skilled in the study of nature <note>original: *naturæ periti*; naturalists or physicians</note> have found this to be of two types: one **terrestrial**, the other **aerial**.

I. **Terrestrial oil** is thick and viscous, and is physically mixed within the body <note>the plant or mineral matter</note> in which it resides. This is prepared either by **pressure** or by **maceration**.

->*Oils produced by expression <note>original: *expressionem*; the process of squeezing or pressing</note>.*<-

1. By **pressure**, oils are produced from oily fruits and seeds. These are crushed in a mortar, warmed by the steam of hot water, and placed into a small bag or a cloth made of hair <note>original: *setaceo panno*; a sturdy cloth made of bristles or horsehair used for straining</note>; they are then squeezed in a press <note>original: *torculari*</note> until the pure oil flows out. However, if the material to be expressed is quite dry, such as linseed <note>original: *semen lini*; flaxseed</note> and the like, it ought first to be thoroughly roasted in a cauldron while being stirred and turned; then, while boiling hot, it should be placed in the press and squeezed while wrapped in the hair-cloth.

<summary>This page classifies oils into "simple" and "mixed," further dividing simple oils into terrestrial and aerial types based on their density and extraction method. It details the process of "expression," using heat and mechanical pressure to extract oil from seeds and fruits.</summary>

# Chapter XXII.

## OILS MADE BY MACERA-
## tion. <note>original: *macerationem*; the process of soaking a substance in liquid to extract its medicinal properties</note>

2. Simple substances are macerated in fresh, common oil—namely flowers, herbs, fruits, or roots—in such a way that they are entirely covered by the oil. Cold ingredients are placed in "washed" oil <note>oil purified by shaking with water</note>, while hot ingredients are placed in pure oil. They are then exposed to the sun <note>original: *insolantur*</note> for several days. After a strong pressing, the spent herbs are discarded, and fresh ones are added; this exchange is repeated a second and third time. Finally, once the leaves have been pressed and thrown away, the mixture is exposed to the sun and cooked in a double vessel <note>original: *duplici vase*; a water bath or bain-marie</note> until the moisture <note>original: *succus*; the watery juices of the plant</note> has been consumed. These oils are generally the following:

Let the buds be ground, then macerated in oil and wine for seven days: finally, let them be cooked in a double vessel <term>a water bath or "bain-marie," used to provide gentle, even heat</term> until the wine is consumed <note>evaporated during the boiling process</note>.

# Chapter XXIII.

## SUBTLE OILS.

II. Airy, or thin oil, is inseparably inherent in its body. This is produced by distillation: and that either by ascent <term>where vapors rise, condense, and are collected</term> or by descent <term>where the source material is heated from above so the oil drips down into a receiver</term>.

->OILS MADE BY DESCENT<-

Those substances which yield oil more stubbornly <note>referring to woods, resins, or seeds that do not easily release their essence through simple pressing</note> are distilled by descent. The work is performed in this manner: Take a flask...

[...Take a] flask <note>original: *boccia*, a gourd-shaped vessel</note> turned upside down, fill it with chopped wood, and seal it well to the furnace with lute <term>a paste made of clay and other materials used to seal chemical apparatus and prevent the escape of vapors</term>, specifically at that part where the body of the flask meets the furnace. Some also distill from gums and resins in this way; but because we have a better method, we leave this behind and follow that one instead.

## Chapter XXIV.

### OILS DISTILLED BY ASCENT.

We extract oils by ascent <note>upward distillation, where vapors rise before condensing</note> from those materials that yield their oil more easily. This is done in various ways, as will appear from the following:

1. By a <term>Copper Still</term> <note>original: *Vesica Cuprea*, literally a copper bladder or vessel</note>, if the herbs and fruits are fresh, in this manner: The herbs or fruits are chopped or coarsely crushed, then steeped in rainwater and allowed to digest <note>soak in gentle heat</note> for several hours. Afterward, they are placed into the <term>copper still</term>. A glass <term>Alembic</term> <note>the "cap" or head of the still</note> is placed on top, with its beak passing at an angle through a barrel filled with cold water, extending all the way to the receiving vessel. Finally, the oil is distilled, first with a slow fire and then a stronger one. You shall then separate the oil from the water in the manner we will teach shortly.

### OILS FROM RESINS AND GUMS.

Gums, resins, or tears are placed into a glass retort that has been well-luted <note>original: *lutatam*; "luting" refers to sealing the joints of the apparatus with a specialized paste or clay to prevent the escape of medicinal vapors</note>, and are distilled either by themselves, or mixed with sand, gravel, or other materials. However, the retort should be placed into a cupel <note>a shallow, bowl-like container</note> filled with sand in such a way that it does not touch the bottom of the vessel; rather, sand should be present on all sides.

## Chapter XXV.

# OILS FROM METALLIC SUBSTANCES.

From certain metallic substances—such as <term>Vitriol</term> <note>a historical term for sulfate minerals; blue vitriol is copper sulfate, green is iron sulfate</note>, Antimony, Sulfur, Tartar, Bricks, and many others—oil is also distilled by means of a retort. But since they do not all have one and the same method of procedure, we shall treat at least of those which, because of their excellent use in Medicine, are accepted by Physicians and <term>Pharmacists</term> <note>original: *Pharmacopæis*; those who prepare and dispense medicinal drugs</note> today.

->*Oil of Vitriol.*<-

<term>Take:</term> 6 pounds of blue or green or Roman Vitriol [because this excels all others]; cast it into a new, large, and very well-fired pot. Place it in a deep furnace over live coals. When it begins to boil, let it be stirred with a spatula so that it liquefies completely, and let it boil until it no longer produces any bubbles and until the whole mass becomes thick. Afterwards, once the Vitriol has cooled in the pot, let it be ground very finely in a mortar; then let half of it be cast into a fresh pot, and again lowered into a deep furnace, and burned for some time until it turns more reddish. In this way, having been <meta>catchword: prepared</meta>

Once the material is prepared, let it be mixed very well in a mortar, stirring it gently so as not to stir up a dust that would irritate the nose and throat. Put the whole amount into a glass <term>retort</term> <note>a flask with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> that has been properly <term>luted</term> <note>covered with a protective layer of clay or paste to withstand high heat</note>, ensuring that a portion of the retort is left empty. Soon, let it be placed in the middle of the furnace upon a transverse iron beam that is also covered in lute [on which a fragment of a pottery sherd should be placed, lest the glass be cracked by the glowing iron]. Position the retort so that it sits in the very center of the furnace, with its beak projecting outward little by little. Attach a large <term>receiver</term> <note>the vessel that collects the distilled liquid</note> made of the finest glass [for the larger it is, the more freely it will receive the <term>spirits</term> <note>the volatile vapors released during the process</note>]. Secure the joint where they meet most diligently with lute, so that no spirits may escape.

You must also construct a roof over the furnace to enclose the retort, covering this also with lute, but leaving a hole at each corner about the width of a thick thumb. Once all these things are set up, allow the lute to dry for an entire night. In the clear morning, light the fire with one of the upper holes open. Let the fire be increased gradually until evening, at which point the second hole should be uncovered; on the following day, open the third. 

Toward the night of this second day, increase the fire further. After midnight, let the cover of the fourth hole be removed, and thus keep the fire at its full strength until you no longer see any spirits coming out. Let the vessels cool for a day and a night. Then, remove the receiver with the liquid it contains, and let the pure oil be separated from the <term>phlegm</term> <note>the watery, inactive byproduct of distillation</note> by a second distillation in a <term>Bain-marie</term> <note>original: *Balneo*; a gentle water bath</note>.

->Or in this way, as I am accustomed to prepare it.<-

Take a very large <term>alembic</term> <note>a distilling apparatus consisting of a gourd-shaped vessel and a cap with a beak</note> with a narrow mouth and a very short beak. While this burns, fresh sulfur is added. From this, it happens that from the rising smoke, the oil flows down drop by drop through the neck into the receiver in a short time. This should then be carefully collected and reserved for use.

¶ It thins and draws out [humors] considerably; it draws out <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyron"; quicksilver</note> that has been absorbed into the body. Smeared on immediately after bathing, it heals the itch <note>original: "scabiem"</note>, leprosy, and foulness of the skin; it is conveniently applied for <term>venereal disease</term> <note>original: "morbo venereo"; likely referring to syphilis, which was commonly treated with mercury—this oil was intended to counteract mercury's toxic buildup</note>. It is beneficial for fistulas, malignant ulcers of the mouth, and defects of other parts at the first or second application.

| <term>Tripoli Stone</term> <note>original: "Lap. Tripolis"; a porous, siliceous earth used here to manage the heat or act as a filter</note> | one and a half pounds |
| <term>Sugar Candy</term> <note>original: "Sacchari Candi"</note> | one pound |

All these, ground and diligently mixed, should be distilled over an open fire, starting lightly and at the end becoming glowing hot. When <term>rectified</term> <note>purified by a second distillation</note> through sand, it is golden in color. One drop of it purges the body.

¶ Three grains taken in a drink of wine, <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>distilled alcohol</note>, and <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "Calchanti"</note> cure "water under the skin" <note>edema or dropsy</note> within a few days. Two grains swallowed with two <term>drachms</term> <note>original: "ʒ. ij."; a unit of apothecary weight</note> of <term>theriac</term> <note>original: "theriacæ"; a complex herbal paste used as a universal antidote</note> heal the plague and venomous diseases. ...they heal the plague and venomous diseases: taken in the amount of three small drops or more in <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; literally "water of life," referring to high-proof distilled spirits</note>, it assists with convulsions, <term>apoplexy</term> <note>original: "morbo attonito"; literally the "thunderstruck disease," a term used for a sudden loss of sense or motion</note>, and other afflictions of the brain: it settles gouty and colicky pains, dispels fevers: it aids an ulcerated bladder: it wonderfully heals malignant ulcers, cancer, fistulas, <term>spreading sores</term> <note>original: "phagedænā"; a type of "eating" or gangrenous ulcer</note>, <term>shingles</term> <note>original: "herpetem"</note>, and all defects of the skin.

### Oil of Tartar.

Take 3 pounds of white <term>tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartari albi"; the potassium bitartrate crust that forms on the inside of wine barrels</note> reduced to a powder. Let them be placed in a clay-coated <term>retort</term> <note>a glass or ceramic vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> and positioned in the furnace; with a large receiving vessel attached, let the joints be closed with <term>lute</term> <note>original: "luto"; a sealing paste used to make the apparatus airtight</note>. Afterward, let it be pressed first with a small fire, and then a stronger one, until no more "spirits" <note>vapors</note> appear. Then, once the vessels have cooled, let it be corrected in a warm <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "Balneo calente"</note> and the oil separated from the water.

¶ It is most effective for healing wounds. Drunk with wine, it crushes and expels <term>stones</term> <note>original: "calculos"</note> of the kidneys and bladder, moves the urine, and cleanses ulcers.

### Oil of Bricks, or of the Philosophers.

Take old red bricks broken into small pieces; burn them in hot coals until they are glowing red-hot throughout. Then, once removed, quench them in old oil and leave them until they have filled themselves with the oil. Afterward, when they are removed from the oil, crush them into a very fine powder and distill them through a glass <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: "cucurbitam"; a gourd-shaped distillation vessel</note>.

¶ It warms, penetrates, softens hard things, and resolves and dispels cold tumors; it aids with <term>spasms</term> <note>original: "Spasmo"</note>, <term>epilepsy</term>, paralysis, <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Podagræ"</note>, and all cold afflictions of the joints and nerves.
