# ->CONCERNING SUBSTITUTES:<-
## ->that is, regarding <term>Succedanea</term><note>medicines used as substitutes when the primary ingredient is unavailable</note>,<-
### ->A treatise by Guillaume Rondelet, formerly Royal Professor at Montpellier.<-

After I had spent a long time thinking about the nature of substitutes, I finally came across a treatise by that most learned man and excellent practitioner, Guillaume Rondelet <note>1507–1566; a famous French physician and naturalist known for his work on fish and medicine</note>. We have chosen to include the entire work here as it is highly useful, though we have at least rearranged the simple medicines into alphabetical order to make them easier to find.

Since we are not infrequently forced to use substitutes—for "not every soil bears everything" <note>a reference to Virgil’s *Georgics*: *non omnis ferre omnia tellus*</note>, nor are appropriate medicines found everywhere—

<meta>catchword: occur- (likely "occurring")</meta>

<summary>This page concludes a table of pharmaceutical abbreviations and introduces a treatise by Guillaume Rondelet on medical substitutes (succedanea), emphasizing the necessity of using alternative ingredients when specific plants or minerals are unavailable.</summary>
<keywords>Guillaume Rondelet, Succedanea, pharmaceutical abbreviations, Montpellier, medical substitutes, pugillus, ana, weights and measures</keywords>

--- Page 598 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Guillaume Rondelet's treatise on medical substitutes, picking up from the previous page's discussion on the alphabetical arrangement of these materials.</meta>

<page-num>630</page-num>
<header>ON SUBSTITUTES,</header>

as they occur. For in the countryside, one must make use of <term>easily obtainable materials</term> <note>original Greek: εὐπορίστοις (*euporistois*), referring to medicines that are readily found in nature or at hand</note>; and since the medicines necessary for sudden accidents are often not within reach, one must use what is present. Those things should be selected which can be substituted for our <term>simples</term> <note>medicines consisting of only one primary ingredient, usually a single plant or mineral</note>, just as we read that Galen <note>the influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> did. When <term>Euphorbium</term> <note>a caustic resin derived from the *Euphorbia* plant, used for its drawing properties</note> was missing for the purpose of extracting spear-heads, thorns, and other fixed objects, he used <term>propolis</term> <note>a resinous mixture honeybees collect from tree buds, also known as "bee glue"</note> from beehives in place of the Euphorbium with successful results. 

The use of <term>Succedanea</term> <note>substitutes; from the Latin *succedere*, to follow or take the place of</note> is truly more necessary today than it ever was. We lack many of the things that once provided a rich and fertile harvest for the ancients in their native and exotic lands. Furthermore, counterfeit goods—adulterated by the crafty wit of the Hebrews and merchants—are being imported; if these must be rejected, it is necessary to substitute others. In addition to this, most of the ancient simple medicines are now obsolete; those very well known and commonly used in antiquity are ignored today.

Many useful compositions and highly effective remedies devised by the Arabs were once accepted into use, but their <term>simples</term> are now entirely unknown to us because of the "barbarity" of their names <note>a reference to the linguistic difficulty European Renaissance scholars had with Arabic pharmaceutical terminology</note>. We do not know what they intended to mean by those foreign names, or we simply lack the substances. 

In the selection and use of substitutes, we must also rightly reject that terrible habit of Physicians which has prevailed for many years now to the great disadvantage of the sick. In the composition of remedies, they rashly pile up every single thing that has been recommended for the disease, the affected part, or a specific symptom. When they have used up every similar ingredient at once, they no longer have anything left that can be substituted for a missing herb or medicine.

If they were instead content with one, two, or three herbs, the pharmacist would never be left destitute of a substitute. If a necessary quantity were required for one handful <note>Latin: *manipulus*</note>, add two; for two, add three or four. From this, two advantages follow:

->RONDELET'S WORKS. 631<-

...methods; the operation of the medicine will be more certain, and its preparation easier and very swift. The Physician who is permitted to repeat, change, or substitute <term>drugs</term> <note>original Latin: *pharmaca*</note> will abound with many remedies and <term>substitutes</term> <note>original: *succedanea*</note>—the greatest ornament of the Medical art. Such a doctor will know more than the common crowd of physicians and those who practice only at the bedside.

For example, if he prescribes <term>Borage</term> <note>*Borrago officinalis*, a herb often used in decoctions for its cooling and "cheering" properties</note> in his decoction and it is missing, he will substitute wild <term>Bugloss</term> <note>*Anchusa arvensis*, a plant closely related to Borage with similar medicinal uses</note>, or vice-versa. If <term>Prickly Lettuce</term> <note>Latin: *Scariola*</note> is lacking, he may substitute its juice or syrup. If <term>Chicory</term> <note>*Cichorium*</note> is missing, <term>Dandelion</term> <note>Latin: *dens Leonis*, literally "lion's tooth"</note> or <term>Endive</term> <note>Latin: *Endivia*</note> may be used. If <term>Ground Pine</term> <note>*Chamæpitys*, used for gout and joint pain</note> is unavailable, <term>Wall Germander</term> <note>*Chamædrys*</note> may be substituted if it is missing, or vice-versa. But what will a doctor do if all these ingredients are heaped together into one and the same medicine? Surely nothing else than that poetic chaos: <note>original: *Rudis indigestaque moles*, a famous line from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* describing the state of the universe before creation</note> "A raw and confused mass."

Doctors should keep that saying of <term>Arnaldus de Villa Nova</term> <note>a famous 13th-century physician, alchemist, and religious reformer</note> before their eyes: where <term>simples</term> <note>medicines made of a single primary ingredient</note> are available, it is a deception to use compound medicines.

Therefore, they should turn away from this corrupt habit and avoid such practices like dangerous reefs. Likewise, they must beware of bad, greedy, wicked, unlearned, and imprudent pharmacists who, hungry for coin and profit, praise a hodgepodge of medicines that are even half-rotten. Some do this to show off their vast stock, whether out of ignorance or pride; even some learned men do it so they do not appear poorly practiced in the knowledge of remedies.

Furthermore, since there are certain useful compositions devised by the ancient Physicians, accepted and proven by experience and reason, it is necessary to investigate, recognize, and supply several substitutes. In this way, the most noble drugs can be prepared, and for that reason, they should by no means be excluded or rejected. Indeed, it is no great misfortune that certain substitutes—which are not inferior to the originals—sometimes fulfill all the promises of the genuine medicine just as well.

# RONDELET <note>original: *Rondeletii*, referring to the French physician Guillaume Rondelet (1507–1566)</note>

Oil for oil, whether simple or compound.
Ointment for ointment.

### *The universal or common theorem.*

A medicine which must be substituted, whether for internal or external use:

*   **Must agree in:**
    *   **Powers** <note>original: *viribus*</note>
        *   Hidden <note>occult powers often referred to properties that were not immediately explainable by the four humors</note>
        *   Manifest <note>properties like heating, cooling, drying, or moistening</note>
    *   **Consistency**
*   **Is also made similar in:**
    *   **Taste**
    *   **Smell**
    *   **Age**
    *   **Origin and region**
    *   **Nature and temperament** <note>the specific balance of qualities like hot/dry or cold/wet</note>

Some things are permitted as substitutes in external remedies which are not allowed to be used internally. For example, the juice of the <term>Carline thistle</term> <note>original: *Cardopatium*</note> can be substituted for the juice of <term>Lettuce</term> <note>original: *Lactuca*</note> in external applications; however, since it is a poison, it is not taken internally.

The whole <term>simple</term> <note>a "simple" is a medicinal herb or substance used on its own</note> is not always substituted, but rather certain parts. For instance, the <term>mucilage</term> <note>original: *Muccago*, a thick, gluey substance</note> of <term>Psyllium</term> <note>fleawort or plantain seed</note> seed is substituted for the mucilage of <term>Quince</term> <note>original: *Cydonia*</note> seeds, but not the whole seed; this is because the interior part differs in temperament from the mucilage and is considered poisonous. Neither is the Quince fruit itself a suitable substitute for its own seed, because it differs in both its powers and its consistency.

Certain medicinal formulas may succeed one another, such as a <term>preserve</term> <note>original: *conservatio*, a preparation of fresh plants or fruits with sugar or honey</note> in place of a syrup made from the same simple fruit, flower, or root. A preserve of <term>Maidenhair fern</term> <note>original: *capill. Veneris*, or *Adiantum capillus-veneris*</note> can be substituted for the syrup when making an <term>opiate</term> <note>a thick medicinal paste or electuary</note>; however, it cannot be substituted when a syrup consistency is required, because the formula of the remedy does not allow for it.

# ON SUBSTITUTES <note>original: *De Sūccedaneis*</note>

For liquids, liquids should be substituted: therefore, if a syrup is lacking, water or a decoction <note>an extract made by boiling plant material</note> of herbs may be substituted.

In certain preserves, one may substitute the "syrup of preservation," because the items are stored in it; for example, the syrup used to preserve Citron instead of a syrup made specifically from Citron peels. The syrup of preservation of Bugloss root <note>Bugloss, or *Anchusa officinalis*, was a common herbal remedy used to "gladden the heart" and temper melancholy</note> may be used instead of the standard syrup of bugloss.

Likewise, one may use plasters instead of ointments, and vice versa, provided the affected part of the body allows for it: such as the <term>Plaster of the son of Zacharias</term> <note>a specific historical compound plaster</note> instead of the <term>Resumptive ointment</term> <note>an ointment intended to restore strength or "resume" the body's healthy state</note>; and the Resumptive instead of the Plaster. However, in ailments of the chest, these should not be used unless they are first dissolved or softened <note>original: *malaxetur*</note>, because applied plasters hinder the expansion of the ribs and respiration. A plaster of <term>White Lead</term> <note>original: *Cerussa*</note> may be used instead of white ointment, unless inflammation prevents it; for an inflamed area can bear neither hard nor heavy things.

### *Various other medicines may be substituted for others, provided their powers correspond.*

Pills may be used for confections, and confections for pills, such as <term>Hiera simplex</term> <note>a "holy" bitter purgative based on aloes</note> for <term>Hiera</term> pills and <term>Benedicta</term> <note>the "Blessed Laxative," a compound used to purge phlegm</note>, and vice versa. And for phlegmatic conditions <note>original: *pituitosis*, referring to an excess of the humor of phlegm</note>, the <term>Electuary of Diacarthamum</term> <note>a laxative paste made from safflower seeds</note> or a solutive of citron. For bilious conditions, the Electuary of the juice of Roses, and vice-versa—provided the specific quantity of each is observed. The doses of Hiera and similar electuaries <note>medicinal pastes mixed with honey or syrup</note> must be increased because of the bulk of the honey, which diminishes the strength of the medicine.

Syrup may be used for a <term>Linctus</term> <note>original: *Eclegmate*, a medicine intended to be licked or dissolved slowly in the mouth</note>, if it is to be taken by licking, such as syrup of jujubes instead of the <term>Looch sano & experto</term> <note>a "healthy and proven" cough medicine; *Looch* is an Arabic-derived term for a linctus</note>. Syrup of poppy may be used instead of <term>Diacodium</term> <note>a sedative syrup made from poppy heads</note>.

Powder may be used for a <term>troche</term> <note>a medicinal lozenge or tablet</note> and vice versa, such as <term>Diarrhodon</term> <note>a rose-based medicinal powder</note> for Diarrhodon troches. Troches of <term>Squill</term> <note>a sea onion used as an expectorant for coughs</note> for a linctus...

# RONDELET

...with a decoction <note>original: *apozemate*</note> of Squill <note>the sea onion, *Drimia maritima*, often used as a diuretic or expectorant</note>, with the quantity increased or decreased according to the reason, the indication of the disease, and the goal of the Physician.

In Simples <note>medicines consisting of a single ingredient</note>, the specific types are sometimes not strictly observed, such as using Turpeth <note>a purgative root</note> instead of Agaric troches <note>lozenges made from a medicinal fungus</note>, and vice versa. Here, a simple is used in place of a compound, or a compound in place of a simple; for example, Colocynth <note>the "bitter apple," a powerful laxative</note> in a smaller quantity instead of Agaric. Or a double or triple amount of Safflower <note>original: *Carthami*</note> instead of Agaric, and vice versa.

It is difficult, however, to find a simple medicine for substitution that truly agrees in every way and in every part, as Avicenna <note>the famous 11th-century Persian physician</note> testifies in his *Canon*; therein, he notes that barely two simple medicines can be safely substituted for one another due to a lack of other substances with similar powers. Since this is so difficult, he sometimes substitutes two, or occasionally three, of equal weight and measure—sometimes doubling or tripling them, and adding a fifth or eighth part of another medicine. This is because very few medicines possess an entirely similar temperament <note>the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, or the same consistency, thickness, or thinness of parts, and hidden properties.

The use of medicines in compositions is varied, either:

*   On account of heat
*   On account of cold
*   On account of moisture
*   On account of dryness
    — at the beginning of the first degree, in the middle of the first degree, and so on for others <note>This refers to the Galenic system of grading the intensity of a drug's effect from 1 to 4</note>.

*   On account of the viscosity of the parts:
    *   their thinness
    *   their thickness
*   On account of taste
*   On account of smell
*   On account of color

Therefore, that which temper—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of medicinal substitutes (succedanea) by Guillaume Rondelet. The previous page discussed the difficulty of finding perfect substitutes due to differences in "temperament" (the balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness) and consistency.</meta>

# ON SUBSTITUTES

...responds to the temperament, it often differs in the thickness or thinness of its parts, or in another faculty. For example, some judge that Sweet Flag <note>original: *Acorum*</note> should be substituted for Asarabacca <note>original: *Asarum*, a plant used as an emetic and diuretic</note>. But it is not suitable in every operation: for Sweet Flag cannot do everything that Asarabacca can. It certainly moves urine and the menses (for which reason it should only be substituted in diuretics <note>medicines intended to increase urine flow</note>); but it is not at all able to provoke vomiting or draw out waters <note>likely referring to the treatment of dropsy or edema</note> as Asarabacca does.

By the same logic, Hyacinth <note>the bulb or flower</note> is substituted for Alkanet <note>original: *Anchusa*, a root used for red dye and medicinal properties</note>. But if Alkanet is needed for its color, as in ointments, Hyacinth is not suitable. In its place, Lac <note>a resinous secretion</note> is substituted, or Brazilwood <note>original: *Brasilia*</note>, Red Sandalwood <note>original: *Santala rubra*</note>, painter’s Lac, or Kermes <note>original: *Coccos baphica*, a red dye derived from insects</note>. Sweet Asa <note>likely Benzoin resin; original: *Assa dulcis*</note> is not allowed in place of Foetid Asa <note>Asafoetida</note> because of the odor, as Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian physician</note> substituted in disorders of the Uterus; this is because it would attract the uterus upward with its pleasant scent, for [the uterus] follows fragrant things and flees from foul ones <note>this refers to the historical "wandering womb" theory, where the uterus was thought to move within the body in response to smells</note>.

Some things are used for their taste: but they do not agree in every respect. In certain formulas for remedies, Honey and Manna <note>a sweet plant exudate used as a mild laxative</note> can be substituted for Sugar, such as in laxative medicines; but not at all in astringent ones <note>medicines intended to stop flow or tighten tissues</note>, because Manna loosens the belly more than Sugar or Honey. Mucilage <note>original: *Muccus*</note> is useful in a flux of blood, and is used for its stickiness. Fenugreek <note>original: *Foenum graecum*</note> yields a mucilage, but a warm one, and therefore it should be rejected in the spitting up of blood. This is much like in external remedies, such as Ophthalmia <note>inflammation of the eye</note>, in which Egg white <note>original: *Ovi albumen*</note> is preferred at the beginning and during the increase <note>the first two stages of a disease's progression in Galenic medicine</note>: but in the peak <note>original: *statu*</note> and decline <note>original: *declinatione*</note> of the condition, the mucilage of Fenugreek is recommended.

Things that are substituted are not substituted in every formula of a remedy, such as Myrrh for Bdellium <note>a semi-translucent oleo-gum resin</note> in pills and ointments: but in pills of Bdellium it is by no means allowed, because Myrrh, like the menses, elicits a flow of blood and hemorrhoids. Therefore, these things must be observed in substitutes.

# RONDELET

so that a substitute, used in place of a genuine item that is corrupted or unavailable, might produce the same effects that the genuine one provided; such as whether it warmed, cooled, moistened, or dried, or whether it acted as an astringent, a laxative, or promoted concoction <note>The process by which the body "ripens" or processes raw humors to restore health</note>. For Wormwood <note>original: *absinthium*</note> simply stated in the compositions of the Greeks, use Sea-Wormwood <note>original: *Serphium*</note> or Santonica <note>original: *Santonicum*, also known as Tartarian Southernwood</note>. For Wormwood from Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note> or Mount Taurus, use Roman Wormwood. For Roman Wormwood, use that of the place where you live.

It is permissible to follow this practice in the selection of all herbs that belong to a particular region, provided you take that herb from a neighboring region, or at least one very similar. An example of such a place is the Crau <note>A desert-like plain in Provence, France, known for its distinct flora</note> in the French province of Provence, or Crete, where our narrow-leaved Thyme and Epithyme <note>original: *Epithymus*, a parasitic plant also known as Dodder of Thyme</note> are best and most abundant. In the second place, herbs from humid regions—provided the summer has been dry and parched—can be substituted in place of those from hot regions. Galen <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> teaches that this was done in the preparation of Theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote containing dozens of ingredients</note>: for Macedonian Parsley <note>original: *Petroselinum*</note>, you may substitute Parsley from another region.

But one must observe the similarity of the region, for the region increases or diminishes the efficacy and quality of the medicine; for Illyrian Iris, we take the Venetian one, and for African Iris, the Florentine.

# ON SUBSTITUTES

For **Acacia juice** <note>original: *Acaciæ succo*</note>, use the juice of **Sloes** <note>The fruit of the blackthorn</note>; the juice of **Sumac** <note>original: *Rhois*</note> is also approved by Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of the foundational herbology text *De Materia Medica*</note>.

**River water** is preferred over spring water, contrary to what Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> prescribes in his recipe for **Diacodion** <term>Diacodion: A medicinal syrup made from poppy heads used to induce sleep or soothe coughs</term>; this is because river water is composed partly of rain and partly of springs.

For **Spring water**, use **River water**.

For **Citron juice**, use **Lemon juice**.

For **Sowbread** <note>original: *Cyclaminis*</note>, use **Iris** <note>specifically the root, or Orris</note>.

For **Liquorice juice**, use an infusion or decoction of the same; or use **Raisin juice**, or cooked wine, otherwise known as **Sapa** <term>Sapa: Grape juice boiled down to a thick, sweet syrup</term>.

For **Box-thorn** <note>original: *Licio*, referring to *Lycium*</note>, use **Gentian juice** for treating ulcers.

For **Box-thorn** <note>original: *Lycio*</note>, use **Amurca** <term>Amurca: The bitter, watery, dark sediment that settles out of olive oil after pressing</term>.

For **Unripe grape juice** <note>original: *Omphacii*</note>, use **Sumac**, and vice versa.

For **Opium**, use **Meconium** <note>A less potent extract made from the whole poppy plant rather than just the latex of the seed pods</note>, or the juice of **Wild Lettuce**, or **Garden Lettuce** in a larger quantity.

For **Balm of Gilead** <note>original: *Opobalsamo*, a rare and costly aromatic resin</note>, use **Pure Liquid Myrrh** <note>original: *Stacte*</note>, unadulterated **Liquid Storax**, or **Oil of Myrrh**. In eye washes <note>original: *suffusionibus*</note> used to break down humors, use **Oil of Lavender Spike**, which has equally thin and penetrating parts.

For **Spurge Olive juice** <note>original: *Thymelææ*</note>, use **Mezereon juice** <note>original: *Chamelææ*</note>.

### ON LIQUIDS AND GUMS <note>original: *Lachrymis*, literally "tears," referring to the droplets of resin that bleed from trees</note>

For **Fir resin**, use **Pine resin**.

For **Asphalt** <note>original: *Aspaltho*</note>, use **Petroleum** or **Jet** <note>original: *Gagates*, a minor gemstone formed from fossilized wood</note>, and vice versa. Also, **Stone coal** from the bowels of the earth, which blacksmiths use, may be used.

For **Cedar oil** <note>original: *Cedria*</note>, use oil prepared from **Juniper shavings** through distillation <note>original: *per descensum*, a method of "downward" distillation where the oil drips into a lower vessel</note>, or **Juniper gum**.

For **Cypress resin**, use **Larch resin**.

For **Lac** <note>A resin secreted by the lac insect</note>, use **Myrrh**.

For **Manna of Frankincense**, use the **Bark** to which some Frankincense still clings.

# ON SUBSTITUTES

For **Mastic** <note>A resin from the mastic tree, used as a binder or for digestive health</note>, use **Fir resin**, either hardened or fried.
For **Mummy** <note>original: *Mumia*; in this period, it referred to either actual mummified remains or a specific type of bitumen used in medicine</note>, use **Pissasphalt** <note>A natural mixture of bitumen and pitch</note> <margin>as according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose works were the foundation of western herbal medicine</note></margin>.
For **Myrrh**, use **Bdellium** <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum resin</note> or the juice of **Alexanders** <note>original: *Smyrnii*</note> or **Celery**.
For the **Tear of the Olive** <note>The resin exuded from the bark of olive trees</note>, use **Elemi gum**.
For **Opobalsam** <note>Balm of Gilead, a rare and expensive aromatic resin</note>, use **Stacte** <note>The finest, purest form of Myrrh</note>, which is liquid Myrrh prepared by nature or by art, or use **Turpentine liquor**. For **Opocarpasum** <note>A toxic substitute for balsam fruit</note>, do not use **Laurel oil**, nor **Myrtle liquor**, nor **Myrtle seed and Zedoary** <note>A root similar to ginger</note>, as our teachers have determined. Instead, for **Carpobalsam** <note>The fruit of the balsam tree</note>, use the seed of the **Lentisc** <note>The mastic tree</note> or the **Turpentine tree**, of which there are many species. Or use **Cubebs** <note>Tailed pepper</note> in a smaller dose, or two parts **Turpentine** to one part **Cubebs**.
For **Opopanax** <note>A gum resin from the herb-bennet</note>, use **Gum Ammoniac**, or **Galbanum**, or **Bdellium**, especially when we wish to soften; <margin>Galbanum is especially useful for external applications.</margin>
For **Pitch**, use cooked **Pine resin**.
For **Liquid Pitch**, use **Pitch** dissolved in oil, or Pitch liquefied from **Juniper oil**.
For **Pissasphalt**, use **Pitch** and **Bitumen**.
For **Storax** <note>A fragrant resin used in incense and medicine</note>, use **Benzoin**.
For **Turpentine**, use **Mastic**.
For **Xylobalsam** <note>The wood of the balsam tree</note>, use shoots of the **Lentisc**.

### ON MINERALS

For **Antimony**, use **Burnt lead**, and vice versa, according to Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician from the 11th century</note>.
For **Cadmia** <term>Cadmia: An oxide of zinc or a cobalt-bearing ore found on the walls of smelting furnaces</term>, use **Calamine stone** <margin>and **Burnt tin**.</margin>
For **Flower of Copper** <note>The fine scales that flake off when copper is heated</note>, use **Verdigris** <term>Verdigris: The green pigment or patina that forms on copper or brass</term>.
For **Litharge** <note>Lead oxide, often used in ointments</note>, use **Burnt lead** or **Molybdenum** <note>In historical texts, this often referred to lead-like minerals or ores</note>.
<margin>For</margin> **Lead**, use **Tin**.
For **Pompholyx** <note>A white zinc oxide residue, sometimes called "white smoke"</note>, use **Spodium** <note>A substance produced by burning metallic ores or organic matter</note> as according to Dioscorides.
For the **Sandarac of the Greeks** <note>A toxic red arsenic mineral</note>, use **Orpiment** <note>A yellow arsenic mineral</note>, and vice versa.
For **Spodium** <term>Spodium: Historically refers to the soot or ash of metals, but sometimes to burnt ivory or bone</term>, use **Antispodium** <note>A substitute for spodium</note> made from **Myrtle**, **Lentisc**, **Olive**, **Wild Olive**, **Quince**, or **Burnt stag’s horn**.
